comments.title: Comment Submitted by Aimee Bosland
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and ask DHS to withdraw the proposal.

As a Career Specialist at Portland Community College, I help students explore career options, prepare for employment, and connect their education to their goals. I am submitting this comment in my individual capacity, informed by my work supporting students.

Practical experience is an important part of career preparation. It helps students apply classroom learning, build confidence, strengthen their skills, and develop professional relationships. OPT gives eligible international students an opportunity to gain that experience in their field of study.

PCC has indicated that it cannot cover the proposed fee. Students could complete their programs and meet the eligibility requirements, yet lose access to OPT because their college cannot afford the cost. After investing considerable time, effort, and money in their education, these students would face a financial barrier unrelated to their eligibility or preparation.

I understand the importance of preventing fraud and protecting workers. International students already undergo visa screening, and OPT requires a separate school recommendation and federal approval. Those reviews serve different purposes and cannot prevent every later violation. However, DHS should explain how this fee would address specific weaknesses in the existing process.

Colleges have a responsibility to review student eligibility, maintain records, and meet reporting requirements. DHS is responsible for federal enforcement, including investigating fraudulent employers. The agency’s limited capacity to carry out that work should not become a $70,000 financial obligation for colleges.

The proposal states that the fee is intended to reduce participation and that the revenue would not be retained by ICE to fund OPT oversight. I question how making the program unaffordable would improve its integrity. A college’s ability to pay does not establish whether a student’s practical training is legitimate.

If there are gaps in oversight or institutional compliance, I ask DHS to address those gaps directly. Investigating documented misuse and holding those responsible accountable would better address the stated concern than imposing a fee that also excludes eligible students and compliant colleges.

In career services, we encourage students to gain experience and build connections in their field. This proposal would prevent eligible international students at PCC from taking that next step. Their access would depend on institutional financial resources rather than whether they meet the program’s requirements.

International students are part of our college community. Their perspectives and experiences contribute to classroom discussions, collaboration, and learning. They deserve fair consideration and an affordable opportunity to apply what they have learned.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue measures that address fraud and enforcement needs while preserving access to OPT for eligible students.
comments.reason: The commenter asks DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee because it creates an insurmountable financial barrier for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As an international educator at a private university, I respectfully express concern regarding the proposed fees for international students seeking post-graduate practical training.

While I recognize the importance of protecting our immigration system and preventing fraud, these fees create significant financial and operational burdens that undermine higher education, limit opportunities for international graduates, and may harm U.S. interests.

1. Misalignment with Statutory Intent

The proposed $70,000/$30,000 fee structure goes far beyond reasonable administrative cost recovery and creates a prohibitive financial barrier. When fees prevent eligible individuals from accessing legally established training opportunities, they function more as penalties than administrative charges.

Furthermore, if collected revenue goes to general Treasury funds rather than supporting OPT oversight, compliance, or fraud prevention, the connection between the fees and their stated purpose is unclear. Fraud prevention measures should be targeted, justified, and proportionate to the costs and risks they address.

2. Financial and Operational Impact on Higher Education

Assigning financial responsibility for these fees to institutions and employers creates an unreasonable burden, particularly for nonprofit, faith-based, and mid-sized institutions with limited resources. Absorbing these costs could negatively affect students, academic programs, and other institutional priorities.

Many valuable training opportunities are offered by nonprofit, religious, educational, and research organizations with limited budgets. Fees of this magnitude could make participation financially impossible, leaving opportunities primarily available through the largest and best-funded employers. This would disadvantage graduates pursuing careers in education, nonprofit service, humanitarian work, and other fields that provide substantial public benefit.

3. Institutional Oversight and Regulatory Responsibilities

Universities already fulfill significant regulatory responsibilities through Designated School Officials (DSOs), who maintain SEVIS records, report required information, and support compliance with student visa regulations. These responsibilities provide an established framework for monitoring international students and maintaining accountability.

While stronger oversight is appropriate, extraordinary financial burdens do not necessarily improve reporting accuracy or compliance. Institutional accountability should be reasonable and proportionate to actual responsibilities.

Post-graduate practical training is also a natural extension of higher education, allowing graduates to apply their knowledge, develop professional skills, and contribute to their fields. Creating substantial financial barriers between graduation and practical experience undermines this important educational connection.

4. Economic and Workforce Consequences for the United States

International graduates contribute to the U.S. workforce through research, innovation, specialized knowledge, and service in fields where qualified talent is needed. Practical training allows them to apply their education while contributing to American businesses, universities, research institutions, and nonprofit organizations.

Excessive fees risk diminishing the United States' ability to retain talent educated at its own institutions. International students consider career opportunities after graduation when choosing where to study. Prohibitive fees may encourage talented students to pursue opportunities in countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia, allowing those nations to benefit from the educational investment and talent developed by American institutions.

Restricting these opportunities could reduce the pool of qualified workers, limit innovation, and weaken the competitiveness of American higher education.

Conclusion

I support responsible immigration administration and effective fraud prevention. However, these goals should be pursued through measures that are proportionate, financially reasonable, and consistent with U.S. educational and economic interests.

I respectfully urge the Department to reconsider the proposed $70,000/$30,000 fee structure and evaluate its legal justification, relationship to actual administrative and enforcement costs, and consequences for universities, employers, international graduates, and the American workforce.

Effective oversight should not require prohibitive financial barriers or unnecessarily restrict legitimate opportunities for graduates to apply their education. A balanced approach can protect our immigration system while preserving the valuable contributions international graduates make to American education, research, innovation, and service.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create prohibitive financial and operational burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by University of Dayton
comments.commentText:
University of Dayton comment on Optional Practical Training Fees, Docket ICEB-2026-0100. Cites are to 91 Fed. Reg. 64566.
The University of Dayton is a private Catholic research university in Ohio with 9,000 students, about 450 of them international, 270 of those graduate students, (17% of graduate enrollment). We are SEVP-certified and fall in the small-entity class analyzed in the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (64592). We share the Department's commitment to program integrity and urge reconsideration of this rule.
In FY 2026, 397 students began OPT. Under the Department's methodology—$70,000 per initial OPT, $30,000 per extension, and the 56% uptake rate (64583)—that single cohort carries a fee obligation to the university of about $34.5 million; the FY 2025 cohort of 230 starts would have cost $19.96 million. The obligation recurs each year and exceeds any reasonable level of support the University could provide.
The mitigation paths the rule suggests, passing costs to F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers (64578), are inconsistent with our values and do not hold up. Charging a nonimmigrant student $70,000 allocates a federal work authorization by family wealth. Charging all students raises tuition on domestic (including Ohio) students, to fund a federal fee—a transfer the rule never analyzes despite its American-worker rationale. Declining to recommend a student for OPT generates no fee and so appears costless to the Department, while imposing real costs on students, families, employers, and region. This would also make American higher education at our university unattractive to int’l students.
The rule states the fees are on par with one or two years of education (64575). Int’l graduate tuition at the university is about $20,000 a year, so the initial fee is equal to 3.5 years of tuition and the full obligation equals five.
The claim that only 20% of F-1 students use OPT (64,578) uses the wrong denominator of all 1.4 million F-1 students, including many who are not yet eligible. Since the fee is triggered by a DSO recommendation at program completion, the more relevant measure is OPT use among graduating internal students. In the most recent year, we conferred 393 degrees to int’l students and recorded 397 OPT starts—evidence that OPT use in our graduating cohort is far higher than 20%.
Participation is also not stable. Our starts rose 73% in one year, from 230 to 397, against the assumption of no change in recommendations (64582). Clemens projects a 79% decline in starts where institutions bear a $100,000 fee. NAFSA estimates a $102.3 million loss to Ohio in 2026-27 from falling int’l enrollment, and IIE projects up to $3.4 billion in lost revenue and 40,000 fewer jobs.
The administrative burden is understated. The rule estimates an hour of staff time per instance (64584, 64595), conceding it cannot estimate budgeting, recordkeeping, banking, or refund costs (64590). At our volume, roughly 397 payment events totaling $34.5 million a year, each needing finance approval, treasury handling, reconciliation, and audit records. Payment must precede the SEVIS recommendation (64599), which follows graduation timelines rather than our budget cycle, forcing unbudgeted rolling commitments. Refunds are discretionary, unavailable once an EAD issues, and carry no appeal, so they are not a reliable receivable.
The small-entity analysis does not support its conclusion. The rule reports 841 of 1,389 small institutions face impacts above 1% of revenue and 98 above 20% (64595-96), yet concludes the impact is minimized. Its rejection of an exemption counts institutions rather than participants or incidents of fraud (64596). The conduct described is employer-side—shell companies, staged worksites, residential addresses, third-party placements (64571)—not a function of school size. Targeting by compliance history or recertification outcome is a significant alternative under 5 U.S.C. 603(c) the analysis never addresses.
Less burdensome alternatives warrant analysis: adjust SEVP fees to fund fraud detection; use appropriated funds; pre-hire employer rules such as E-Verify, a valid EIN, and no residential worksites, self-employment, or third-party placement; extend STEM OPT safeguards to all OPT; and a risk-tiered fee. The only alternative fee discussed is a higher one (64577), which we oppose. The Department's own cost estimate is $4.1 billion/year, up to $8.2 billion (64579), while revenue goes to the Treasury and ICE may not use it (64576), so the fee funds none of the enforcement. The investigation tied suspect employers to about 3% (64571); why does the full fee reach the other 97%?
We ask that the Department reopen the comment period after further analysis of cohort-level participation, transaction and administrative costs,and where participant and fraud actually sit by institution type; address each alternative on the record; and reconcile the analysis with its findings.
comments.reason: The university argues the massive OPT fees are unaffordable, inconsistent with values, and will harm students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Charles Bennett

Dear Secretary Mullin,

I am Charles H. Bennett, a physicist and information theorist at IBM Research Division

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

My most famous scientific paper had six authors from four countries. Such cosmopolitan collaboration is the rule rather the exception in my field because world-class talent is scarce and thinly spread. I have advised young students from many countries who, because of programs like OPT remained in the US, became citizens and will continue for decades to come strengthening American STEM.

Ever since the Second World War the US has thrived from being the at the receiving end of the brain drain from other countries. If we abandon this position and encourage the best talent to go elsewhere our science will stagnate

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Charles Bennett
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessive and will harm the U.S. STEM talent pipeline.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**Parent Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees – Docket ICEB-2026-0100**

I am writing as a concerned parent to strongly oppose the proposed rule, *Optional Practical Training Fees*, under DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (RIN 1653-AB01).

My child has completed their entire education in the United States since first grade. From elementary school through high school and now higher education, our family has invested many years of time, effort, financial resources, and personal sacrifice in our child's education and future.

From a very young age, my child has dreamed of becoming a medical professional and contributing meaningfully to society. This is not simply a career choice. It is a dream that has guided my child's academic decisions, dedication, and preparation for many years.

As a parent, I am deeply concerned about the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. Although these fees would technically be imposed on educational institutions rather than directly on students, their practical impact could ultimately fall on students. A university may be unable or unwilling to absorb such an extraordinary cost associated with an individual student's OPT.

International families already make substantial financial commitments toward tuition, housing, insurance, books, transportation, and educational expenses for medical student. Students pursuing demanding professional careers, particularly medicine and healthcare, face many years of education and training. A $70,000 fee could become a significant barrier at a critical stage of a student's professional journey.

My child has been educated in the United States since first grade. Our family has made long-term educational decisions and substantial financial investments in good faith, with the expectation that legitimate educational and professional pathways would remain reasonably accessible.

It is deeply concerning that after years of education and sacrifice, a qualified student could potentially face a major barrier to legitimate practical training because an educational institution may not be able or willing to bear an excessive fee.

I fully support the government's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud, protect American workers, and ensure compliance with immigration laws. However, measures intended to address fraud should be targeted toward actual fraud and noncompliance rather than creating excessive financial barriers that could affect legitimate students.

There are more targeted approaches available, including stronger institutional oversight, compliance reviews, audits, investigations, and meaningful penalties for institutions or employers that violate immigration requirements.

The United States benefits from talented students who study here, become part of their communities, and eventually contribute their knowledge and skills to the USA. This is particularly important in healthcare, where the United States benefits from well-trained and dedicated professionals.

I respectfully request that the Department of Homeland Security:

• Withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

• Protect legitimate practical training opportunities for qualified international students.

• Avoid policies that could discourage universities from supporting deserving students.

• Consider reasonable and proportionate administrative fees rather than excessive financial barriers.

• Ensure that students pursuing professional careers, including medicine and healthcare, are not unnecessarily disadvantaged.

I am not asking for special treatment or an exemption from immigration laws. I am asking for fairness, proportionality, and a reasonable opportunity for hardworking students who have completed their education in the United States from Elementary to High School to pursue their legitimate professional goals.

Behind every international student is a family that has invested years of sacrifice, hope, and commitment in that child's future.

For our family, this is deeply personal. My child's educational journey in the United States began in first grade, and throughout that journey, the dream of becoming a medical professional has remained a constant goal. We have supported that dream through years of education, financial investment, hard work, and sacrifice.

At the time (mid-1970s), there were almost no jobs in physics, and very few US citizens wanted to study physics. As a result, when I had obtained my PhD, all three nuclear weapons labs would have wanted to hire me if it wasn't for my visa status, F-1 at the time. Instead, I did a post-doc at s University, but it was only when I went to work with a defense contractor who could only hire me if they supported my application for a permanent residency. At the time that was free, so they did that. I they would have had to pay a year's salary for the purpose, they wouldn't have and I would have happily returned to the Netherlands.

My study in the US was funded by the DOE, presumably because the US wanted to entice foreign scientists to come and stay in the US. Adding fees to the process makes that more difficult.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

I'm retired, so it doesn't affect me at all. But it would have if I weren't.

The main reason is that the US appreciates other human endeavors that those that makes people want to do science. An accessory reason is that US high schools don't all teach mathematics at a good enough level to prepare students for STEM study. So, the US educates too few physicists and medical doctors, among other specialties. Other countries with more of an intellectual tradition (like Finland, Germany, or indeed Russia and China) educate too many of their citizens for the demands of their economy, and (for physicists) of their defense industry. So, the US makes up for its inferior early education and its excessive appreciation for money and sports, by importing capable foreigners. But, it shouldn't be like that. Ideally, each country, or country block, should be able to educate their own people to fill their own needs. But, it isn't so. Same with just about everything that a country imports, be it pineapples or coffee or rare earth metals. If you can't make them yourself (at an acceptable price) you import them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 student pursuing dual master's degrees in Health Tech and Information Systems at Cornell Tech, expecting to graduate in May 2028. Before coming to the United States, I trained as a physician at Sun Yat-sen University in China. I chose to study in the United States, and pay full international tuition, in substantial reliance on the availability of Optional Practical Training (OPT), which would allow me to apply my clinical and technical training in the U.S. health technology sector. I respectfully oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT, for the following reasons.

1. The fees bear no relationship to the cost of administering OPT. An OPT recommendation is a SEVIS data entry by a school official, followed by the same Form I-765 adjudication for which students already pay a filing fee. Nothing in the proposal demonstrates that processing one student's practical training costs the government anything approaching $70,000. A charge of this size, deposited into the general Treasury, is a revenue measure directed at one group of students, not a fee calibrated to the cost of a service.

2. The flat structure is arbitrary. The same $70,000 would be triggered by a ten-week pre-completion summer internship as by twelve months of post-completion employment. There is no rational connection between the fee and the duration, value, or oversight burden of the training.

3. The proposal would end OPT in practice while claiming only to fund it. The Department itself acknowledges that schools may pass the cost to students or stop recommending OPT altogether. No student in my position could pay $70,000 on top of tuition and living expenses, and most schools cannot absorb such a cost either. Smaller institutions, and the hospitals, universities, and nonprofit health organizations that hire many OPT graduates, would be affected first and worst.

4. It would directly harm the U.S. healthcare workforce pipeline. My field, health technology and clinical AI, depends on people who combine clinical training with data science, and international students supply a large share of that pipeline. A $70,000 barrier will not protect U.S. workers in these shortage fields; it will move the talent, and eventually the employers and the research, to Canada, the United Kingdom, and other countries competing for the same graduates.

5. Fraud prevention does not justify a blanket fee on the compliant. Fraud in the F and M programs is properly addressed through SEVP school certification, site visits, and enforcement against bad actors. Charging every lawful student $70,000 because a small number of actors abuse the system punishes the compliant majority and the schools that follow the rules.

6. The rule disregards reliance interests. Hundreds of thousands of students, including me, selected U.S. institutions and committed years of study and substantial tuition in reasonable reliance on the longstanding availability of OPT. Raising the effective price of participation to $70,000 for students already enrolled is fundamentally unfair.

I respectfully request that the Department withdraw this proposal. If any fee is adopted, it should be capped at the demonstrable, per-student cost of administering the OPT recommendation, and students already enrolled in their programs should be exempt.

F-1 student, Cornell Tech, Class of 2028

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a Designated School Official (DSO) at a large private university in the Midwest. I have worked as a DSO for nearly 15 years at multiple institutions in different states. At my current institution, we have about 4,600 enrolled international students and about 2,100 students on OPT and STEM OPT. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. My concerns relate to the rationale for the fee, its impact on institutions and students, and its broader economic consequences.

Lack of evidence supporting the fee

The proposed rule appears to be based in part on concerns about fraud within the OPT program. However, DHS has not provided evidence demonstrating widespread fraud that would justify imposing a substantial fee on all applicants. In my professional experience, international students are highly motivated to comply with immigration regulations because the consequences of status violations are severe. While some instances of fraud may occur, I have not observed evidence that fraud is so prevalent as to justify this broad financial burden. DSOs share DHS's interest in maintaining program integrity. Throughout my career, I have worked with colleagues who take their reporting and compliance responsibilities very seriously. If DHS believes additional oversight is needed, more targeted approaches are available. For example, SEVIS already contains extensive data that could potentially be used to identify patterns of noncompliance without imposing significant new costs on every OPT applicant.

Impact on institutions and DSOs

OPT is a long-standing benefit available to eligible F-1 students. Introducing a substantial financial barrier creates difficult questions for institutions, particularly if schools are expected to absorb any portion of the cost. Institutions could be forced to decide whether, and for whom, financial assistance should be provided. Such decisions might require schools to establish criteria based on financial need, academic achievement, or career prospects rather than immigration eligibility. These are not determinations DSOs are trained or authorized to make as part of the immigration advising process. The proposal has already increased advising demands on my office. International students often plan their coursework, internships, research activities, and graduation timelines years in advance. The uncertainty created by this proposal has made it more difficult for students to make informed decisions and for advisors to provide meaningful guidance.

Impact on students

Practical training opportunities are a critical component of the educational experience for many international students. Whether graduates remain in the United States or return to their home countries, OPT allows them to apply their education, gain professional experience, and contribute to the workforce. The uncertainty surrounding this proposal is already affecting student decision-making. I have worked with students who have modified academic plans, accelerated graduation timelines, or abandoned research interests because they are concerned that future access to OPT may become financially unattainable. It is disappointing to see students making major educational decisions in response to uncertainty surrounding an immigration benefit for which they are otherwise eligible. A decline in international student enrollment would also affect US students and institutions. International students contribute valuable perspectives to classrooms, research, and campus communities. These interactions are an important part of preparing students to succeed in an increasingly interconnected world.

Economic consequences

Even the proposal of this fee has created uncertainty that affects planning by students and employers. In conversations with students, I increasingly hear that they are considering opportunities outside the US because they are uncertain about future access to practical training, and that employers are cancelling interviews due to the uncertainty. OPT is an important bridge between higher education and participation in the US workforce, particularly in STEM fields. Adding a substantial new financial barrier risks making the US less attractive to talented students from around the world. Reduced international enrollment would have significant consequences for universities, research programs, local economies, and employers seeking highly skilled graduates.

Administrative process

Finally, I am concerned about both the process and timeline associated with this proposal. If DHS seeks to address fraud or program integrity concerns, it should pursue measures that are narrowly tailored to those objectives and that minimize burdens on compliant students, institutions, and employers. Given the significant impact this proposal could have on students, educational institutions, and employers, a longer comment period would have allowed for more meaningful stakeholder engagement and a more thorough evaluation of its consequences.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I urge DHS to withdraw this fee structure and preserve affordable access to legitimate, degree-related practical training.

As a scientist who works in biotechnology and bioinformatics, I am concerned about the consequences for scientific research, workforce development, and medical innovation. Practical training allows graduates to apply specialized knowledge, develop professional skills, and contribute to research teams. Access to these opportunities should depend on qualifications and compliance with program requirements, rather than the ability to finance an extraordinary fee.

Although educational institutions would be responsible for payment under the proposal, that does not eliminate the financial burden. Institutions may limit recommendations, pass costs to students, or seek payment from employers. Qualified graduates could consequently lose training opportunities even when they meet every other eligibility requirement.

In biotechnology, many valuable training opportunities exist at small companies, academic laboratories, and organizations operating under limited research budgets. A substantial additional fee could make it financially impractical for these organizations to support a graduate’s participation. DHS should evaluate the potential effects on research continuity, federally funded projects, and the development of treatments and diagnostic technologies that could benefit American patients.

I support protecting American workers and addressing fraud. However, the ability to pay is not a reliable measure of whether a training opportunity is legitimate. DHS should explain the evidence supporting these particular fee amounts and assess whether they would deter misconduct or primarily discourage lawful participation. Reduced participation alone should not be treated as proof of successful fraud prevention.

More targeted approaches deserve meaningful consideration, including verification that training relates to the student’s degree, focused compliance reviews, employer accountability, and enforcement of applicable worker protections. These approaches would address specific problems without imposing the same financial barrier on compliant students and institutions.

I also urge DHS to consider the reliance interests of students already enrolled in U.S. educational programs and graduates already participating in OPT. They may have invested years of study and substantial financial resources with the expectation that they could pursue practical training under the existing framework. A short transition period would not adequately account for those commitments.

The agency should also examine whether these fees could increase students’ debt or dependence on employers willing to finance participation. Making workers financially dependent on a limited number of sponsors could undermine their ability to leave unsuitable employment or report mistreatment.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure. If the agency pursues an alternative, it should provide a transparent justification, evaluate substantially lower fees and meaningful waivers, and protect students and participants with existing educational commitments.

The United States benefits when its educational institutions can translate advanced training into scientific discovery and productive work. I urge DHS to protect that pathway through proportionate oversight and evidence-based enforcement.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Strong Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. These excessive fees would undermine American higher education, economic competitiveness, innovation, and fairness without adequately addressing the stated concerns about program integrity.

1. Harm to American Universities and the Economy

OPT allows international graduates to apply their education through practical training in the United States. These fees would discourage talented students from choosing American universities and push skilled graduates toward competing countries, harming American research, technological advancement, and economic growth.

3. Disproportionate Impact on Smaller Institutions

A $70,000 fee per student would disproportionately burden smaller universities, public institutions, and research programs with limited financial resources. This could effectively eliminate OPT opportunities at many institutions, regardless of students’ qualifications or compliance with immigration requirements.

4. Unfair and Ineffective Approach to Fraud Prevention

Excessive financial barriers do not directly address immigration fraud. Legitimate students and compliant institutions should not face extraordinary financial penalties because of misconduct by others. Targeted enforcement, improved verification, and stronger oversight would be more proportionate and effective alternatives.

5. Insufficient Economic Justification

DHS should demonstrate that the proposed fees are reasonably connected to actual administrative and enforcement costs and that their benefits outweigh the substantial economic consequences. The proposal risks causing far more economic harm than any anticipated regulatory benefit.

Conclusion

The proposed OPT fees are excessive, economically counterproductive, and inconsistent with America’s long-term interests in education, innovation, and global competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for each subsequent OPT recommendation, and use targeted measures to prevent fraud and protect U.S. workers.

DHS has a legitimate responsibility to enforce immigration law and address abuse, including fictitious worksites and “pay-to-stay” arrangements. Enforcement should nevertheless be proportionate and avoid needlessly burdening legitimate students, schools, employers, and research institutions.

The fees must be paid by SEVP-certified schools before a designated school official can recommend a student for OPT. The $70,000 fee applies to the student’s first OPT recommendation, whether pre-completion or post-completion. A $30,000 fee applies to each subsequent OPT recommendation, including a STEM OPT extension. The fee is not tied to a specific employer or proven violation. A student using post-completion OPT followed by a STEM extension could therefore trigger $100,000 in school payments.

This risks deterring legitimate participation along with abuse. Schools with limited budgets may be unable or unwilling to absorb these costs. A qualified graduate with a genuine, degree-related job offer could lose OPT—not because of misconduct, but because the school cannot justify the expense.

DHS cites an investigation involving more than 10,000 F-1 students working for highly suspect employers. These concerns warrant action, but association with a suspect employer is not proof that each student committed fraud. DHS should disclose how many cases resulted in substantiated violations, who was responsible, and what proportion of OPT participation involved confirmed misconduct. Policy should rest on verified outcomes, not suspicion.

OPT participants may compete with U.S. graduates for some jobs, and effects on wages and hiring deserve evaluation. But every OPT position lost will not necessarily become a job for an American; employers might leave positions vacant, reduce projects, or move work and investment elsewhere. DHS acknowledges uncertainty about how much participation the fees would reduce. It should assess effects on U.S. hiring, wages, vacancies, and investment before concluding that these fees protect American workers.

The impact on doctoral researchers and innovation also deserves attention. Eligible F-1 doctoral graduates contribute to scientific discovery, medical research, engineering, artificial intelligence, and other fields with long-term value. Their work strengthens research teams, advances technology, and trains future scientists and engineers. DHS should assess how these fees could affect universities, laboratories, hospitals, and research programs that may lack resources to pay them. Discouraging legitimate early-career researchers could weaken U.S. research capacity and push projects or talent abroad.

The public value of technical work extends beyond research output or immediate job creation. In my work on health-related technology, I have seen U.S. users describe how features helped them recognize potentially serious health conditions or seek timely medical attention. Some described these experiences as life-changing or even life-saving. No single feature deserves sole credit for a health outcome, but this shows how engineering can benefit Americans. These contributions cannot be measured only by counting jobs filled.

DHS estimates about $12.4 billion in annual fee transfers under its primary scenario; collections would go to the U.S. Treasury, not be earmarked for OPT oversight or enforcement. DHS argues fees would deter abuse and encourage school scrutiny. It should explain why these amounts are necessary, how they relate to oversight costs or demonstrated risks, and how success will be measured. A fee that sharply reduces participation is not necessarily effective enforcement.

DHS should evaluate alternatives: risk-based audits and worksite verification; stronger employment and training-record checks; scrutiny of high-risk employers and schools; and meaningful penalties for proven misconduct. A pilot or phased approach could test these measures before imposing a uniform fee.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the fees in their current form; publish data distinguishing suspected from substantiated fraud; assess labor-market and research impacts; and compare targeted alternatives using transparent measures of cost and effectiveness. Protecting U.S. workers and program integrity is essential, but should not undermine legitimate education, research, and innovation without evidence these extraordinary fees are necessary and effective.

Thank you for considering this comment.

DHS should demonstrate why these particular amounts would effectively distinguish misconduct from lawful participation. Targeted audits, verification of genuine training arrangements, enforcement against fraudulent institutions and employers, and enforcement of applicable worker protections would address misconduct more directly. DHS should compare the effectiveness and costs of those alternatives before imposing a broad financial barrier.
Regarding Sections V.C and VI, DHS should give greater weight to students who have already committed substantial time and resources to U.S. education under the existing framework. Although OPT approval is not guaranteed, the opportunity to apply under reasonably predictable conditions can influence major educational decisions. If DHS proceeds with changes, it should protect already-enrolled students and existing OPT participants, including their otherwise eligible STEM extensions, through meaningful grandfathering provisions.
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees, preserve affordable access to legitimate practical training, and pursue proportionate, evidence-based measures against documented abuse. Protecting American workers and maintaining America’s attractiveness to global talent should be complementary policy objectives.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 international student currently pursuing my master's degree in the United States, and I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, including for STEM OPT extensions. I believe these fees could have serious consequences not only for international students but also for American universities, research institutions, employers, and the broader U.S. economy.

International students make enormous financial and personal sacrifices to pursue higher education in the United States. Many of us depend on educational loans, family savings, and years of financial planning. We already pay substantial tuition, living expenses, health insurance, and immigration-related fees. OPT provides a valuable opportunity to apply our education, develop professional skills, and gain practical experience in our fields.

Although the proposed fees would be imposed on educational institutions, their consequences could extend far beyond university budgets. Institutions may be unable or unwilling to absorb such substantial costs, potentially limiting OPT recommendations or passing costs on to students. This could make practical training inaccessible to many qualified international graduates, regardless of their academic achievements or professional abilities.

I am also concerned about the impact on American higher education. International students contribute tuition revenue, diverse perspectives, research assistance, and academic expertise to universities across the country. If studying in the United States becomes significantly less attractive because of reduced post-graduation opportunities, universities could experience declining international enrollment and associated financial losses. Research laboratories and academic programs could also lose access to talented students and graduates who support research, teaching, and innovation.

The consequences could extend to American businesses and the economy. International graduates contribute specialized knowledge and skills to fields such as technology, healthcare, engineering, science, and research. OPT allows employers to benefit from graduates educated at American institutions. If these opportunities become financially inaccessible, employers may lose access to qualified candidates, research projects may lose contributors, and the United States may lose valuable opportunities for innovation and economic activity.

Furthermore, international students have choices about where to pursue their education and build their careers. If the United States introduces financial barriers of this magnitude, prospective students may increasingly consider countries offering more accessible post-study work opportunities. Over time, this could weaken the global competitiveness of American universities and reduce the country's ability to attract and retain international talent.

As a master's student approaching graduation, this proposal is particularly concerning to me. After investing years of effort and substantial financial resources into my education, the possibility that practical training opportunities could become inaccessible creates uncertainty about my professional and financial future. Students who have followed immigration regulations in good faith should not face disproportionate barriers to applying the education they worked so hard to obtain.

I recognize the importance of preventing fraud, protecting American workers, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, I believe targeted oversight, stronger verification procedures, and proportionate enforcement measures would address those concerns more effectively without creating financial barriers that could harm legitimate students, educational institutions, and employers.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw or substantially reconsider the proposed OPT fees and carefully evaluate their potential economic, educational, and workforce consequences. Policies intended to protect the United States should also consider the value that international students and graduates bring to its universities, research institutions, businesses, and communities.

Thank you for considering the concerns of international students whose educational investments, professional opportunities, and financial futures may be affected by this proposal.

For international students, the availability of degree-related practical training may be one factor in those decisions.

That is why I am particularly concerned about the proposed 60-day transition period under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(3).

A student who has already invested several years in an American degree cannot easily adjust to a substantial change in the financial conditions associated with OPT. Changing institutions or pursuing education in another country may no longer be realistic.

Even when a new fee is formally imposed on universities, students may experience the consequences if their institutions cannot support OPT recommendations.

This raises a basic question of fairness: How should regulatory changes account for students who made long-term educational commitments under the existing framework?

I request that DHS reconsider the proposed transition provision and provide meaningful protections for students already enrolled before any final rule takes effect.

A reasonable transition policy should reflect the time and financial commitments required to complete a university education.

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 graduate student in computer science at Santa Clara University, and I oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension.

OPT is the bridge between my degree and my career. My practical training is how I apply what I learn in the classroom to real work in the U.S. technology industry, and it is the path I planned my degree around.

Schools will recommend fewer students, or only those they can afford to recommend, and students like me will lose the training our degrees were built around.

DHS says the fees will combat fraud and protect U.S. workers, but the proposal does not show that charging $70,000 per student is a proportionate or effective way to do that. A fee this large does not target fraud — it prices ordinary students out of the program entirely.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
One potential consequence of the proposed OPT fees deserves more attention: the location where new intellectual property is developed and commercialized.

American universities produce research with applications in medicine, materials science, engineering, computing, and other fields. Turning a research finding into a commercial product often requires additional experimentation, technical validation, and collaboration with industry.

OPT can provide eligible international graduates with opportunities to participate in that process through degree-related practical training.

If substantial fees make those opportunities less accessible, some graduates may pursue professional development outside the United States. The research knowledge they acquired here may then contribute to commercial activities in other countries.

This does not mean that graduates take ownership of university intellectual property or that research results automatically leave the country. Patent ownership, confidentiality, and technology transfer are governed by separate legal and contractual arrangements.

The concern is about where future inventions, improvements, and commercial applications are developed.

The proposed fees under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) should be evaluated for their potential effects on domestic technology commercialization, patent-related activity, and research-to-industry transitions.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee provisions pending an assessment of these longer-term economic consequences.

Targeted enforcement against fraudulent training arrangements would address compliance concerns more directly without imposing the same broad financial obstacles on legitimate graduates.

The United States has invested heavily in building a research environment that produces valuable knowledge. Regulatory decisions should consider whether they help retain the economic benefits of subsequent innovation within the country.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees harm domestic innovation and explicitly requests DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous

I strongly oppose the proposed substantial increase in fees associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT).

As an international student pursuing higher education in the United States, I am deeply concerned about the financial and professional consequences of making OPT prohibitively expensive.

Imposing excessively high fees would effectively restrict OPT to students from exceptionally wealthy backgrounds. Access to professional development should not depend primarily on a student’s financial privilege.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Public transportation systems do not improve on their own.

Cities need transportation planners, traffic engineers, geographic information specialists, and data analysts to understand congestion, improve bus routes, evaluate safety, and plan infrastructure investments.

Much of this work requires practical experience. A transportation planning graduate may understand modeling techniques in a classroom but still need professional training to work with actual ridership data, public budgets, and community needs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tobias Marriage
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security / U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement:

My name is Tobias Marriage. I am a professor of physics and astronomy at Johns Hopkins University, where I lead a lab that builds novel telescopes to study the early universe. Regarding DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, “Optional Practical Training Fees,” I am writing to oppose the new fees in Section V.A of the proposed rule: $70,000 for a school’s initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension.

Over the past eleven years, I have advised five international students who have used OPT. Their OPT followed clearly from their degree and advanced US science: developing multiplexed readout for quantum detectors, analyzing data for multiple astronomical surveys, and designing novel telescopes. Both during their degrees and during OPT, these talented young international scientists worked side by side with strong US students and scholars, a collaboration that elevated their collective research, benefitting the whole team and US science more broadly. All five of them remain in the United States, where they help train and inspire the next generation of American STEM innovators.

Because the proposed rule places the fee on the school, the decision about whether a student can pursue OPT would move from the student and employer to the university’s budget office. At $100,000 per STEM student, I expect that institutions like mine would be unable to absorb the cost for most of the excellent international students completing our programs. In practice the rule would close this pathway for most international students regardless of merit. The strongest of them would go to countries that offer post-study work routes, such as the UK’s Graduate Route or Canada’s Post-Graduation Work Permit, and they would take their expertise and future contributions with them.

In Section IV.C, DHS states that the fees are intended to combat fraud, strengthen program integrity, and protect U.S. workers. I share the goal of a program free of abuse. However, a flat fee falls equally on legitimate research training and on any fraudulent arrangements. Furthermore, in my experience, OPT participants, far from displacing US workers, raise the level of research for everyone involved, US-born and foreign-born alike. If DHS has identified patterns of fraud, I encourage it to address them through targeted measures, such as strengthened employer verification, audits of training plans, or enforcement against noncompliant employers, rather than a flat fee that uniformly chokes off the remarkable creativity and productivity of collaborations that stem from OPT.

In summary, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees, which would deal a blow to American innovation. Instead, DHS should pursue more targeted measures to combat any observed patterns of fraud. U.S.–international collaboration is a central reason American science and technology leads the world, and OPT is a primary pathway that sustains it.

Sincerely,
Tobias Marriage
Professor of Physics and Astronomy, Johns Hopkins University
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they harm university budgets and international STEM collaboration.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,
I am an international graduate student who has invested years of time, money, and hard work in pursuing an education in the United States. I am concerned that the proposed OPT fees, combined with restrictions on Curricular Practical Training (CPT), could make it increasingly difficult for international students to gain experience and build careers in the fields they studied.

Internships are essential to professional development, particularly for students in STEM-designated programs. They allow us to apply classroom knowledge, build skills, and demonstrate our abilities to employers. When CPT opportunities become harder to access, students may graduate without the experience employers expect, making it more difficult to compete for jobs during OPT. Adding substantial OPT fees creates another barrier for students and institutions that already face significant costs.

What is the purpose of investing years in an American education if opportunities to apply that education become increasingly inaccessible?

I recognize the importance of enforcing immigration rules and protecting American workers. However, violations by some individuals should not justify broad barriers for students who comply with the rules. Targeted oversight and enforcement can address abuses without unnecessarily limiting legitimate educational and training opportunities.

These decisions could also affect universities and local communities. International students pay tuition, rent housing, spend money in local businesses, contribute to research, and participate in campus life. The Institute of International Education reported declines in new international student enrollment in fall 2025. Although multiple factors affect enrollment, uncertainty about practical training can influence whether prospective students choose the United States or another country.

Employers may also face consequences. Some industries struggle to recruit people with specialized skills, language abilities, and international experience. Limiting the pool of qualified candidates can increase hiring difficulties and workloads for existing employees. In fields such as hospitality, staffing challenges can affect turnover, stress, and service quality. Businesses may also consider expanding recruitment or operations elsewhere if access to talent becomes more difficult.

International students have options. Other countries offer strong academic programs and pathways to professional experience. If studying and training in the United States becomes too costly or uncertain, students may choose to take their tuition, skills, and future contributions elsewhere.

After years of sacrifices, I am now questioning whether I will have a fair opportunity to use the education I worked so hard to earn. I am not asking for guaranteed employment or special treatment. I am asking for the chance to gain experience, compete fairly, and contribute.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider the proposed OPT fees, examine their effects on students and educational institutions, and consider how CPT restrictions compound these barriers. Immigration compliance and workforce protections matter, but so do the long-term interests of American universities, employers, communities, and students who have followed the rules.

Thank you for considering this perspective.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed OPT fees create financial barriers and limit legitimate training opportunities for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed imposition of additional fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT). This proposal risks undermining one of the United States’ greatest competitive advantages: its ability to attract, educate, and retain talented individuals from around the world.

International students already make substantial financial contributions to the American economy. They frequently pay higher tuition rates, face significant restrictions on employment while studying, and must navigate an expensive and complicated immigration system. Imposing additional fees simply for the opportunity to gain practical experience in their fields would create yet another financial obstacle for individuals who have already invested considerable resources in American education.

More importantly, OPT is not a privilege that benefits international students alone. It is a program that benefits the United States. International graduates contribute their knowledge, skills, innovation, and productivity to American businesses. They help fill specialized positions, support research institutions, and strengthen the country’s position in an increasingly competitive global economy.

The United States should be encouraging talented graduates to contribute to its workforce, not making that opportunity progressively more expensive.

There is also a fundamental issue of fairness. International students pursue their education under a system that offers limited opportunities for authorized practical training. Introducing additional financial burdens on access to that training risks disproportionately affecting students from lower-income backgrounds. A student’s ability to gain professional experience should not depend on their financial capacity to absorb an ever-growing series of administrative fees.

Furthermore, the agency should demonstrate that any proposed fee is necessary, proportionate, and supported by a transparent accounting of actual administrative costs. Regulatory fees should reflect legitimate administrative expenses, not function as financial barriers to lawful participation in an established immigration program. Without a convincing justification, additional fees risk appearing arbitrary and unnecessarily burdensome.

The long-term consequences deserve serious consideration. International students have choices about where to pursue their education and begin their careers. Countries around the world are competing to attract highly educated individuals. If the United States continues increasing the financial and administrative obstacles facing international graduates, it risks pushing talent, investment, and innovation toward competing economies.

This is not simply an immigration issue. It is an issue of economic competitiveness, educational opportunity, and the future of American leadership.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement to reconsider this proposal, provide a rigorous justification for any additional costs, and fully evaluate its potential economic and educational consequences.

The United States should not invest in educating the world’s brightest minds only to create unnecessary financial barriers when they are ready to contribute to the American economy.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the agency to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they create financial obstacles and harm US competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yiming Chen
comments.commentText:
I’m an international student here on an F-1 visa, and I came to the U.S. to study. Between tuition, rent, daily living and travel, I spend about $200,000 a year, and most of that money goes to my school and to small local businesses.

I agree that OPT fraud is a real problem and that the government should stop it. I’m also fine with OPT users paying a reasonable fee to cover the cost of enforcement.

This proposal doesn’t do that. Nowhere does it say what enforcement actually costs or how that cost turns into $70,000 per student, plus $30,000 for each OPT after that. It just picks a huge number meant to scare people away. A charge meant to discourage behavior rather than cover a cost is really a tax, and only Congress can create a tax.

It also doesn’t fit the problem. The fraud examples in the rule are almost all fake or shell employers, but this fee doesn’t check employers at all. It charges every student and every school the same amount. Fraud rings with money can still pay. Honest students mostly can’t, so many will simply choose another country. That means fewer students, less tuition and less spending in college towns, which hurts ordinary Americans and small businesses the most.

The problem is real, but this fix doesn’t match it. Please withdraw this proposal and replace it with a fee based on real enforcement costs, along with stronger checks on the employers who are actually committing fraud.

The NPRM itself says the money would be deposited in the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt under 31 U.S.C. 3302, that ICE would not retain or use it for SEVP or enforcement, and that deterrence is the point regardless of whether Congress later appropriates it. DHS estimates $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion a year, $12.4 billion as its primary estimate. A charge of that scale, untethered to cost and paid into general revenue, is a tax and a deterrent penalty, not a user fee. DHS should withdraw it and, if any fee is proposed, justify it with actual program costs.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee is an unjustified deterrent tax and should be withdrawn by DHS.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) and the Legal Authority discussion - Oppose for lack of statutory authority. DHS relies principally on INA 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), the power to prescribe the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission. Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), upheld DHS authority to create OPT; it did not hold that DHS may impose a $70,000 charge on a third party, a school, as a condition of a recommendation, or levy billions of dollars for the general Treasury. Congress has set specific immigration fees elsewhere in the INA. It has never authorized this charge, on this payer, at anything near this magnitude. A decision of this economic and political significance - effectively pricing a national training program out of existence - requires clear congressional authorization, which INA 214(a) does not supply.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11) and 214.13(i) - Oppose because this is a de facto elimination of OPT, not regulation of it. DHS acknowledges schools may stop paying, reduce pre-completion OPT, and become selective about which students they recommend, and that DSOs will become financial gatekeepers who may deny a recommendation to a student who is not judged a strong candidate. A qualified student would lose practical training - training directly related to the degree the F-1 program contemplates - not because the student is ineligible, not because the job is unrelated, and not because of any misconduct, but because the institution will not pay $70,000. If the government wishes to end OPT, that choice belongs to Congress after open debate. It should not be achieved indirectly by pricing every recommendation beyond what schools can rationally pay.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Antonio Redondo
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

I am Antonio Redondo, a scientist at Los Alamos National Laboratory and former head of its Theoretical Division.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

As a private citizen with direct knowledge of the positive contributions of foreign nationals to research I strongly oppose the proposed increases in OPT fees. The proposed increase will make it very difficult for academic institutions, as well as research laboratories, national and private, to continue to recruit the best candidates in the world.

Sincerely,
Dr. Antonio Redondo

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Oliver Kelly
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Oliver Kelly, and I am a chemistry student at West Virginia University.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

Over time, the field will see less contributions from international students in materials science, pharmaceuticals, etc., greatly damaging our national research capabilities.

International students and graduates are important to American science because they increase total diversity. Highly trained graduate students will be prevented from entering the U.S. workforce where they would have contributed to the advancement of American science.

Sincerely,
Oliver Kelly
