comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (FR Doc. 2026-20660). This comment addresses a cost the NPRM never names: harm to U.S. foreign relations and to the exchange purpose that student visas have always served.

1. DHS's own history ties student visas to exchange.
Footnote 23 of the NPRM notes that the 1952 INA addressed the student visa and "amends the United States Information and Educational Exchange Act of 1948, 22 U.S.C. 1446." Congress built the student category alongside its public diplomacy law. The Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 states a goal of increasing mutual understanding between Americans and people of other countries through educational exchange (22 U.S.C. 2451). The NPRM lists "Cultural exchange program" among its CFR subjects. Yet its analysis treats OPT only as a labor and fraud issue.

2. DHS dropped its own exchange premise without discussion.
The NPRM quotes the 2016 STEM OPT rule, which rested on "the widely accepted proposition that educational and cultural exchange, a strong post-secondary education system, and a focus on STEM innovation are, on the whole, positive contributors to the U.S. economy and U.S. workers and in the overall national interest." The NPRM responds that participation grew. It never says the exchange benefit is false or smaller than DHS once thought. An agency that changes course must address the facts behind its earlier policy.

3. The F-1 design depends on graduates going home.
DHS stresses that F-1 students must have a foreign residence they do not intend to abandon (INA 101(a)(15)(F)(i), cited at footnote 122). That is the point. Most OPT participants are expected to return home. They take back a year or more of work inside U.S. firms, labs and agencies, plus colleagues, norms and contacts. Those ties are a long-term asset to the United States abroad. A $70,000 charge per student, and $30,000 more for STEM OPT, cuts that experience short or removes it. The rule pushes students toward the outcome DHS says it fears, which is study as a narrow path to a job, while removing the part of the program that builds lasting goodwill.

4. The cost analysis has no foreign-relations line.
DHS uses unpaid fees as a proxy for opportunity costs. It lists the value of labor to employers, contributions to the economy, educational outcomes and school enrollment revenue. It lists nothing for diplomatic or foreign-relations effects. It also assumes U.S. schools "remain highly attractive." In Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026), the court found DHS likely acted arbitrarily when it relied on a similar unsupported assumption in the companion Duration of Status rule. The same gap exists here.

5. The rule creates an unexplained gap with State Department exchange programs.
The fee applies only to F-1 students. J-1 students in State Department-designated exchange programs may receive academic training employment under 22 CFR 62.23(f), generally up to 18 months and longer for postdoctoral training, with no comparable fee. The NPRM does not mention J-1 academic training. It does not explain why one form of post-study training needs a $70,000 price screen and the other does not. Nor does it consider whether students and schools will shift to J-1 programs, which would move workload to State without any analysis.

6. No interagency foreign-relations review is described.
The NPRM notes that the State Department uses SEVIS data and cites Executive Order 14150, a foreign policy directive to the Secretary of State (footnote 84). It does not say whether DHS asked State to assess effects on exchange programs, alumni networks, or partner-government responses, including any measures affecting U.S. students and institutions abroad. A rule with 10-year transfers DHS estimates at $109.4 billion (primary estimate, 3 percent discount) should not skip that review.

7. Requests.
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS re-proposes any OPT change, it should (a) assess effects on foreign relations and exchange goals with the Department of State and publish that assessment; (b) explain the different treatment of F-1 OPT and J-1 academic training; (c) state whether it still accepts the 2016 exchange premise and, if not, give its evidence; and (d) address fraud through employer-focused enforcement that does not penalize the many students who use OPT as intended.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states opposition to the proposed rule and argues it causes harm to U.S. foreign relations.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees. A student could complete a demanding degree, follow every immigration requirement, and find a legitimate opportunity related to their education, yet still lose access because a $70,000 payment cannot be arranged. That is an unacceptable outcome.

Requiring the school to pay does not resolve the problem. If the school passes the cost to students, access depends on personal wealth. If the school absorbs it, access depends on the institution’s budget. Either way, a qualified student could be turned away for reasons unrelated to academic merit or compliance.

Students should be judged on whether they meet the requirements and whether their training is legitimate. The ability to produce an enormous payment tells us neither. DHS should withdraw this proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the OPT fees are excessive and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The United States puts tremendous effort into educating talented people. This proposal could make it much harder for those graduates to apply what they have learned here through lawful practical training. I strongly oppose that direction.

A graduate’s skills do not become less useful because a university cannot finance an OPT fee. A promising research or engineering opportunity does not become suspicious because its funding is limited. Yet those are precisely the kinds of situations in which this policy could close the door.

DHS needs to consider what happens when capable graduates take their knowledge elsewhere because legitimate training becomes financially inaccessible. Their departure could also affect colleagues, unfinished projects, and future collaboration. These consequences deserve serious consideration before such a substantial barrier is imposed. Please withdraw the proposed fees.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees create financial barriers and asks DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
What troubles me most is the possibility that a strong educational recommendation could become meaningless unless someone can finance the fee. A professor or supervisor might see clear value in a graduate’s continued training, while the institution’s finance office sees an expense it cannot approve.

Those are different judgments. One concerns whether the work is relevant, supervised, and educationally worthwhile. The other concerns available money. This proposal risks allowing the second judgment to override the first.

Research teams can spend considerable time developing specialized knowledge and working relationships. Interrupting that process could harm other researchers as well as the individual graduate. DHS should examine those consequences carefully. I strongly oppose charging institutions amounts that could prevent sound educational decisions from being carried out.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees will harm educational decisions and research, explicitly stating strong opposition.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Saying that universities will pay these fees is not a satisfactory answer to concerns about affordability. Universities still have to find the money.

For illustration, just 100 initial OPT recommendations would mean $7 million in fees. A university facing that expense could restrict recommendations, seek reimbursement, or redirect money from other purposes. None of those choices is harmless. Nor should domestic students face higher charges or reduced services because their institution is trying to preserve training opportunities for international graduates.

The proposal places schools in a deeply uncomfortable position: support an eligible student’s educational plans or protect a limited budget. DHS should not create that conflict without a much stronger justification for the amounts involved. I strongly oppose the proposed fees and urge the agency to withdraw them.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees strain university budgets and explicitly states strong opposition to the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
An employer could offer relevant work, proper supervision, and fair treatment, and still lose a qualified graduate because the graduate’s school cannot arrange the required payment. I cannot support a policy that could produce that result.

The fee is triggered by the school’s recommendation, so a compliant employer’s careful planning would not necessarily protect the placement. Recruitment could have to start again. Projects could be delayed. Existing employees could be left carrying additional work while a replacement is sought.

It is reasonable to investigate whether a job is real and whether training requirements are being followed. Those checks should focus on the actual employer and placement. A large payment made by a university does not answer those questions. DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue oversight that examines compliance directly.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fee harms employers and graduates, and explicitly states DHS should withdraw this proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
A small company may be able to offer a graduate close supervision, meaningful responsibility, and valuable practical experience. It may also have very little spare cash. This proposal could make that financial limitation decisive.

Although schools would formally pay the fees, the proposal allows costs to be shifted to employers. Larger organizations might be able to absorb that expense while smaller businesses abandon otherwise worthwhile placements. Even when employers are not charged directly, they could lose applicants whose schools decline to fund recommendations.

That would be a troubling way to determine who gets access to talent. A company’s bank balance does not establish the quality of its supervision or its respect for the rules. I strongly oppose a fee structure that could favor financial strength over the merits of a training opportunity.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees will harm smaller businesses and restrict access to talent.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Some worthwhile work does not generate much money. Community research, environmental projects, and nonprofit services can offer serious, degree-related training while operating within very tight budgets.

I strongly oppose making those opportunities harder to access through enormous OPT fees. A placement should not become less available simply because the work serves people who cannot pay much for it. Nor is it enough to suggest that everyone involved can share the cost. A community may benefit from a project without the student, university, or host organization having enough cash to finance the payment.

DHS should take that distinction seriously. Educational and public benefits do not automatically turn into available funding. This proposal could discourage valuable work for the wrong reason, and it should be withdrawn.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees make low-paying community work inaccessible and should be withdrawn.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Nate Tate
comments.commentText:
**Re: DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees**

I am a Sociology PhD student at Portland State University, and I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule.

International students contribute substantially to American higher education through research, academic collaboration, and the exchange of knowledge. Imposing $70k initial and $30k subsequent OPT fees would create major financial barriers, potentially undermining educational opportunities, university research, and international student enrollment.

I am particularly concerned about the proposal's evidentiary justification. In Section VII.A.5.b, DHS acknowledges potential losses in enrollment, student earnings, and employer productivity but uses unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for the opportunity costs of lost participation. This assumption does not adequately establish the actual educational and economic consequences of the rule.

Furthermore, while preventing immigration fraud is a legitimate policy objective, the proposal does not convincingly demonstrate that fees of this magnitude would be more effective or proportionate to simply strengthened institutional oversight. These fees risk penalizing compliant institutions and students without directly addressing the sources of fraudulent activity.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue evidence-based, proportionate alternatives that protect program integrity without unnecessarily restricting legitimate educational and research opportunities.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create financial barriers and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
American workers deserve fair wages and real opportunities. That goal requires a careful examination of what this proposal would actually accomplish.

If an OPT placement disappears, the job does not necessarily pass immediately to an American worker. The employer might leave it vacant, reduce the project, or move the work elsewhere. Other employees could also be affected when a team loses someone with skills they depend on. DHS needs to examine those possibilities alongside any potential benefits from reduced competition.

Where employers underpay workers or misuse training arrangements, those practices should be addressed directly. Collecting a large fee does not itself improve wages or working conditions. I strongly oppose this proposal because its payment mechanism does not provide a convincing answer to the worker-protection concerns used to justify it.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong opposition because the fee does not address worker-protection concerns and harms operations.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I take OPT fraud seriously. Fake employers and fabricated jobs undermine the program and harm people who follow the rules. But a $70,000 payment does not establish that a job exists, that supervision is adequate, or that the work relates to a student’s degree.

Those facts require verification. DHS should focus on checking employment records, investigating suspicious arrangements, inspecting worksites where appropriate, and holding people accountable for documented violations.

A universal fee could exclude honest participants with limited resources while leaving well-funded misconduct undetected. Before imposing such a barrier, DHS should demonstrate why it would work better than measures directed at the actual fraud. I strongly oppose making legitimate educational opportunities financially inaccessible without that demonstration. Please withdraw the proposed fees.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees are a financial barrier that harms honest participants and asks DHS to withdraw the proposed fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed 60-day transition is especially troubling for students who are already enrolled. They may have spent years progressing toward a degree and planning around the possibility of lawful practical training. Those decisions cannot simply be undone in two months.

Recognizing that disruption does not mean promising anyone a job or automatic OPT approval. Students would still have to qualify. It means acknowledging the difference between failing an existing requirement and suddenly facing an enormous new financial barrier near the end of a degree.

Families, universities, and employers also make commitments well before graduation. Their reliance deserves more consideration than a short adjustment period. I strongly oppose the proposed fees. DHS should withdraw them; if it proceeds anyway, it should provide meaningful protection for students already enrolled.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against the proposed OPT fees and asks DHS to withdraw them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Electricity reliability depends on a workforce that understands both engineering theory and actual infrastructure.

Power utilities and engineering contractors need specialists in grid modeling, electrical systems, energy storage, and control technologies. Developing these skills takes practical experience beyond a university degree.

OPT allows eligible international graduates to apply their education in professional settings. For an electrical engineering graduate, that may involve learning how utilities assess equipment performance, maintain system reliability, or integrate new technologies into existing infrastructure.

I am concerned that the proposed OPT fees could make these training opportunities less accessible, particularly when universities must decide whether they can afford to support individual graduates.

The consequences deserve attention. Energy infrastructure projects often require specialized technical expertise, and workforce constraints can affect project schedules and maintenance planning.

The proposed fees also raise a question of proportionality. Why should an educational institution's financial capacity determine whether an otherwise eligible graduate can pursue legitimate training?

I recognize that DHS must prevent immigration fraud. However, financial requirements should be evaluated against their actual enforcement benefits.

I request withdrawal of the proposed fee provisions under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), along with an assessment of potential consequences for energy workforce development and infrastructure reliability.

A targeted compliance system could address fraudulent arrangements without creating the same broad financial obstacles for legitimate practical training.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees harm training opportunities and explicitly requests withdrawal of the proposed fee provisions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Housing is already too expensive in many American communities. We should be looking for ways to build homes more efficiently, not overlooking policies that could make construction workforce development more difficult.

Modern construction requires more than physical labor. Projects depend on civil engineers, structural designers, building information modeling specialists, and professionals who understand energy efficiency and construction management.

These skills take time to develop. Graduates need practical experience working with building codes, project schedules, technical drawings, and real construction problems.

OPT provides one avenue for eligible international graduates to obtain that experience after studying at American universities.

The proposed OPT fees could discourage some institutions from supporting these graduates, potentially reducing the available pool of entry-level technical professionals.

I am not claiming that OPT fees alone would cause housing prices to rise. Land costs, interest rates, zoning, materials, and many other factors play major roles.

But when housing affordability is already a serious concern, potential workforce constraints deserve careful analysis.

Has DHS examined whether the proposed fees could affect construction-related professional training? Has it considered the possible consequences for smaller engineering and design firms?

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fee provisions under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) and evaluate their potential impact on construction workforce development.

A policy intended to protect American economic interests should account for its possible effects on the cost and availability of housing.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees constrain the workforce and asks DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
When people discuss technology jobs, they often focus on large companies and new products. Less attention is given to the engineers and researchers developing technologies that help people with disabilities live more independently.

Assistive technology includes communication devices, accessible software, mobility equipment, adaptive interfaces, and other tools that support daily activities.

Developing these products requires specialized knowledge across engineering, computer science, rehabilitation technology, and human-centered design.

For graduates entering these fields, practical training is especially valuable. Working with real users, testing accessibility features, and understanding the limitations of existing devices are essential parts of professional development.

OPT can provide eligible international graduates with opportunities to develop those skills in American companies and research organizations.

The proposed fees could make that pathway more difficult, especially for graduates seeking training in smaller organizations with limited resources.

This matters because assistive technology development does not always attract the same investment as larger commercial technology markets. Smaller teams may already face challenges finding people with the right combination of technical knowledge and accessibility expertise.

I do not suggest that every accessibility project depends on OPT. However, the potential effects on specialized fields serving vulnerable populations should not be ignored.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) and consider targeted compliance measures instead.

The Department should also assess whether these fees could disproportionately affect practical training opportunities in smaller, socially important technology sectors.

Accessibility should remain part of the discussion when evaluating policies that influence the availability of specialized technical talent.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees make the OPT pathway more difficult, especially for smaller organizations.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
A supply chain problem rarely stays in one place.

A delay at a warehouse can affect a distributor. A delayed distributor shipment can affect a retailer. Eventually, the customer may be the one waiting for a product.

That is why supply chain efficiency matters to American businesses.

Logistics today relies heavily on inventory analysts, industrial engineers, transportation planners, and information systems specialists. These professionals help companies improve forecasting, reduce errors, and coordinate shipments.

OPT gives eligible international graduates an opportunity to apply university training in these operational environments.

I am concerned that substantial OPT fees could discourage educational institutions from supporting otherwise qualified graduates.

For smaller logistics companies and distributors, recruiting employees with strong analytical and technical skills can already be difficult. Reduced access to trained candidates could create additional operational challenges.

The issue is not whether international graduates should receive preferential treatment. They should not.

The question is whether a broad financial barrier is an effective way to address immigration compliance concerns.

A large payment does not verify that a training position is genuine. It does not establish that an employer is following the law.

I request withdrawal of the proposed fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2).

DHS should instead consider employer verification and targeted investigations while evaluating the possible effects of its proposal on logistics workforce development.

American businesses benefit from reliable supply chains. Policies that could affect the availability of trained operational professionals deserve careful economic review.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees create operational challenges and requests withdrawal of the proposed fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed OPT fee requirements raise an important concern for nonprofit organizations and community-serving institutions that operate with limited financial resources.

Nonprofits provide services in education, environmental protection, community development, research, and other areas of public benefit. Many depend on employees with specialized professional skills but cannot offer the salaries or recruitment resources available to large corporations.

Eligible international graduates may obtain degree-related practical training through OPT in qualifying professional environments, including nonprofit organizations.

Such training can benefit both the graduate and the organization. A data analysis graduate, for example, may gain experience evaluating program outcomes, while a nonprofit improves its ability to measure whether services are reaching the intended population.

The proposed fee requirements could reduce access to these opportunities if educational institutions become unwilling or unable to support OPT recommendations.

The financial effects may be particularly difficult for smaller institutions to absorb. Unlike large organizations, community nonprofits often operate under restricted grants and budgets committed to specific services.

My concern is that the proposed policy may create an indirect disadvantage for legitimate training opportunities associated with resource-constrained organizations.

The related payment requirements under § 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and (iii) also warrant scrutiny. Financial capacity is not equivalent to compliance, and the ability to pay should not substitute for verification of legitimate training arrangements.

I request that DHS withdraw these provisions and consider a regulatory approach based on documented compliance risks.

Any economic assessment should include the potential effects on smaller nonprofit employers and the communities they serve.

A system designed to prevent misuse should distinguish actual violations from legitimate educational training, regardless of an institution's financial resources.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees harm nonprofits and reduce access to valuable practical training opportunities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international student pursuing a master’s degree in mechanical engineering at Texas A&M University, College Station. I came here to learn, work on challenging engineering problems, and hopefully contribute something useful through my work.

For students like me, OPT is a chance to take what we learn in classrooms and research labs and apply it to real technologies. I want to work on problems such as improving cooling systems for powerful computers and making energy systems more efficient. Doing that takes practical experience and opportunities to work alongside experienced engineers.

Fees this high could close that door, even for students who have followed every rule and worked hard throughout their degrees. Universities may be unable to pay, and most students cannot afford such amounts either.

The loss would extend beyond our individual careers. When graduates cannot contribute their skills, promising research can lose people who could help develop it into useful technology. Some will take their ideas and training elsewhere. Others may never get the opportunity to pursue them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed increase in fees associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT).

OPT is more than just a work opportunity for international students. It is a program that creates meaningful benefits for students, American businesses, and the United States as a whole. International students gain valuable professional experience, employers benefit from a diverse and skilled workforce, and the country benefits from the knowledge, talent, and contributions these individuals bring.

However, imposing substantially higher fees would place an unfair financial burden on students who have already made significant sacrifices to pursue their education in the United States. For many, these additional costs could turn an important educational and professional opportunity into something financially out of reach. A program intended to create opportunities should not become another barrier to those seeking to contribute.

The consequences would extend far beyond individual students. American employers could lose access to qualified candidates, while the United States could miss out on the economic contributions, fresh perspectives, and innovative ideas that international graduates offer. A policy that makes OPT less accessible ultimately harms everyone involved.

I firmly believe that OPT should continue to serve its original purpose of connecting education with practical experience while creating benefits for all parties. Making the program prohibitively expensive would weaken that purpose rather than strengthen it.

I respectfully but strongly urge the agency to reconsider the proposed fee increase and protect the accessibility of OPT. International students should be encouraged to contribute their skills and talents, not discouraged by excessive financial barriers.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the proposed OPT fee increases, arguing they harm students and employers.

comments.commentText:
To whom it may concern,

I'm writing as a member of the public about one concern with this proposal: the cost to the U.S. economy.

I understand why DHS wants to protect the integrity of OPT, and I don't object to that goal. My worry is that a $70,000 fee for a first OPT recommendation, plus $30,000 for each one after that, would make U.S. schools much less attractive to international students, and the country would feel that loss well beyond OPT itself.

International students are a big part of the economy. NAFSA estimates they contributed $43.8 billion and supported 378,175 U.S. jobs in the 2023-24 academic year. Much of that money comes from tuition and everyday spending in college towns, and it exists because students expect to be able to gain U.S. work experience after they graduate. If OPT becomes too expensive for schools to offer, many students will simply study in other countries.

DHS's own analysis points the same way. It estimates the rule's primary annualized cost at $4.1 billion, with a range of $32 million to $8.2 billion, and it acknowledges that deterred students could mean lost enrollment. But the notice doesn't make clear how those losses are weighed against the fraud it hopes to reduce.

Because the downside could be large and the benefit is hard to measure, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal and look at narrower ways to deal with fraud that don't put the whole program at risk.

Thank you for taking the time to read this.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees will harm the U.S. economy and asks DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern:
As a concerned U.S. citizen and resident invested in the long-term economic prosperity and technological security of our nation, I am writing to express serious concerns regarding and opposition to the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Proposed Rule on Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100).
While regulatory modernizations and cost-recovery mechanisms are standard federal practices, this proposal, as structured, fails to balance administrative costs against the broader, indispensable benefits that OPT brings to the American economy, higher education system, and strategic innovation capabilities.
1. Threat to America’s Global Competitiveness in Critical Technologies
The Optional Practical Training program is not merely a non-immigrant benefit; it is one of the United States’ most effective instruments for retaining global, high-caliber talent in critical STEM disciplines. At a time when global competitors—such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and the European Union—are actively lowering barriers and expanding post-graduation pathways to capture international researchers and engineers, imposing additional fiscal barriers on OPT participants runs counter to our national interest. Diminishing the attractiveness of the U.S. as a primary destination for premier innovators directly compromises American leadership in artificial intelligence, semiconductors, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing.
2. Adverse Repercussions on American Higher Education and Domestic Students
International students contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to local economies and higher education institutions across all 50 states. These students typically pay full tuition, which directly cross-subsidizes operational costs, STEM laboratory equipment, and financial aid packages for domestic American students. Cumulative administrative and financial hurdles erode the United States' competitive advantage in higher education, threatening university research budgets and ultimately shifting financial pressure onto domestic tuition-paying families.
3. Disproportionate Burden on American Startups and Small Businesses
While large multinational corporations possess the legal and financial resources to absorb regulatory fee increases, early-stage American startups, small enterprises, and academic labs rely heavily on cost-efficient access to recent graduates. By increasing the financial friction of hiring through OPT, this rule inadvertently penalizes the very entrepreneurial sector that drives domestic job growth and commercial innovation.
4. Failure of Economic Justification and Concerns of Duplicate Fees under the APA
Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), agency rulemaking must not be arbitrary, capricious, or unsupported by substantive economic modeling. OPT applicants already pay substantial fees to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) for Form I-765 adjudication, in addition to upfront Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) fees. ICE has not sufficiently demonstrated that the proposed fee corresponds to an actual, distinct, and quantifiable administrative burden not already covered by existing federal fee structures. Without an auditable cost-accounting basis, this rule risks creating redundant bureaucratic extraction.
Conclusion
The U.S. government should be strengthening policies that attract, retain, and integrate top-tier talent into the domestic economy to safeguard American technological supremacy and fuel job creation. Imposing additional fees on the OPT pipeline creates immediate economic disincentives for minimal agency recovery.
I respectfully urge the Department and ICE to withdraw this proposed rule or conduct a comprehensive, independent economic impact assessment that thoroughly evaluates the secondary downstream costs to American industry and academic institutions.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly expresses opposition to the proposed rule, arguing it harms U.S. competitiveness and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement:
As an American taxpayer and professional concerned with our national fiscal health and economic resilience, I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed fee imposition on the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100).
Rather than serving public interest, this rule represents a counterproductive regulatory drag that undermines domestic tax revenue, strains American employers, and relies on an unsubstantiated fee structure.
1. Negative Net Fiscal Impact on Federal and State Tax Revenues
Participants in the OPT program work legally, contribute immediately to payroll taxes (FICA), federal and state income taxes, and inject substantial consumer spending into local communities—all while being ineligible for most public entitlement benefits. Artificially suppressing participation through compounding regulatory fees directly shrinks this tax-contributing workforce. The short-term regulatory revenue collected by ICE will be vastly outweighed by the long-term loss in broad-based tax revenues for both federal and local governments.
2. Misunderstanding of Domestic Job Creation and Innovation Multipliers
Extensive independent economic research confirms that high-skilled practical training programs do not displace American workers; rather, they serve as economic multipliers. STEM graduates participating in OPT provide the technical foundation that allows American firms to scale, secure patents, and subsequently create multiple downstream non-technical support, management, and operational jobs for U.S. citizens. Erecting financial roadblocks at the entry gate stifles business expansion, directly threatening job creation for domestic workers.
3. Inflationary Pressures on Crucial American Industries
American healthcare, engineering, and manufacturing sectors are already navigating chronic shortages of specialized technical personnel. Additional administrative and financial friction on OPT participation will exacerbate these shortages, creating unnecessary upward wage pressure in technical overhead and compounding broader inflationary strains across supply chains and critical domestic projects.
4. Administrative Redundancy and Lack of Cost Accounting Integrity
A core tenet of responsible governance is regulatory efficiency. Students participating in OPT already pay substantial fees to USCIS for employment authorization documents (Form I-765) and bear administrative overhead through their universities' SEVP reporting. ICE has failed to demonstrate a distinct, non-duplicative administrative service that warrants a separate fee assessment. Imposing multi-agency tolls on a single educational-to-practical transition pipeline creates bureaucratic inefficiency and fails the standard of reasoned decision-making required under the Administrative Procedure Act.
Conclusion
A forward-looking U.S. policy must prioritize economic growth, domestic innovation, and fiscal pragmatism. Disincentivizing global graduates trained inside American institutions from contributing to our domestic economy is economically self-defeating. I strongly urge ICE to withdraw this proposed rule.
Respectfully submitted,
An American Taxpayer and Resident
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees will harm tax revenues, employers, and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees because they would undermine U.S. competitiveness: discouraging international enrollment, straining university finances, weakening research, and restricting employers’ access to U.S.-trained talent. DHS’s own analysis estimates $41.05 billion in costs over ten years without quantifying comparable benefits. DHS should withdraw the proposal.

1. DHS’s own estimates show substantial economic costs.

Table 10 estimates $41.05 billion in undiscounted monetized costs over ten years, with a primary annualized cost of $4.11 billion at a 3% discount rate. The accounting statement does not monetize the anticipated benefits. These are DHS’s estimates, not opponents’ projections. Unquantified benefits may exist, but DHS should demonstrate why they justify these costs and why targeted enforcement would be insufficient. Fee revenue is a transfer to the government, not automatically a net gain for the American economy. (public-inspection.federalregister.gov, public-inspection.federalregister.gov)

2. Universities face both direct financial burdens and lost enrollment.

At $70,000 per initial OPT participant, 100 participants would generate $7 million in fees; 1,000 would generate $70 million. These are illustrative calculations. Schools must either absorb the expense, pass it to students or employers, or restrict participation. Each option risks reducing resources for education or making American degrees less attractive. (public-inspection.federalregister.gov, public-inspection.federalregister.gov)

Students compare educational quality, total costs, and opportunities to apply their training. Making practical training prohibitively expensive could redirect enrollment abroad. Tuition-dependent universities could face serious budget shortfalls, while financially vulnerable institutions could experience deeper distress. Because facilities and instructional programs have fixed costs, lost revenue could lead to staff reductions, fewer courses, or higher tuition for American students.

3. Reduced enrollment threatens American jobs beyond universities.

NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in 2024–2025. Its methodology adjusts for U.S.-based financial support. (nafsa.org)

For scale, a hypothetical 10% decline in that contribution would equal $4.29 billion annually. This is an illustration, not a forecast. Nevertheless, it shows why enrollment effects matter: international students support housing, food services, transportation, and university employment. DHS should evaluate these potential losses when assessing whether the proposal protects American workers.

4. America cannot immediately replace its international research pipeline.

NSF reports that temporary visa holders earned 42% of U.S. science and engineering master’s degrees and 38% of doctoral degrees in 2024. Their shares reached 61% of computer and information sciences doctorates and 54% of engineering doctorates. These figures measure degree recipients, not OPT participation, but establish the scale of international talent in advanced American education. (ncses.nsf.gov)

Discouraging these students could weaken laboratories, delay research, and reduce opportunities for American students working alongside them. Expanding domestic STEM education is essential, but developing specialized researchers takes years. Restricting international talent does not instantly produce equally trained domestic replacements.

5. Employers could lose competitiveness rather than simply hire more Americans.

Specialized vacancies require particular skills and experience. An available worker is not necessarily an immediate substitute for a graduate trained in semiconductor design, scientific computing, or another technical specialty.

For illustration, a startup financing initial OPT fees for ten graduates would face $700,000 in additional expenses before salaries and benefits. It might reduce hiring, delay products, or move work abroad. None of these responses guarantees additional American employment. Delayed technical projects can also delay manufacturing, sales, and operational jobs.

NSF reports that approximately 73% of temporary visa holders earning U.S. science and engineering doctorates in 2017–2019 remained in the country in 2023. Although this is not an OPT-specific statistic, it demonstrates that retaining U.S.-trained talent produces lasting domestic benefits. (ncses.nsf.gov)

DHS should withdraw these fees and prioritize targeted fraud investigations, genuine training verification, and enforcement against exploitation. Ability to pay is not evidence of compliance.

Protecting American workers requires strong universities, productive research, and competitive employers. This proposal risks damaging all three while transferring the benefits of American training to competing economies.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the OPT fees harm U.S. competitiveness, impose massive costs, and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

Subject: Strong Support for DHS Proposal to Increase OPT Fees

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to express my strong support for the Department of Homeland Security's proposal to increase Optional Practical Training (OPT) application fees. I believe the proposed fee adjustment is warranted, reasonable, and necessary to ensure the long-term sustainability, integrity, and efficiency of the immigration benefits system.

The OPT program provides significant value to international students by allowing them to gain practical work experience in the United States, enhance their professional skills, and improve their future career opportunities. Given the substantial benefits offered through the program, it is reasonable to expect applicants to bear a greater share of the administrative costs associated with processing and adjudicating these applications.

USCIS operates primarily on a fee-funded basis and must maintain sufficient resources to process applications accurately, securely, and efficiently. As application volumes continue to increase, fee adjustments are an appropriate mechanism to ensure that the agency has the staffing, technology, fraud detection capabilities, and customer service resources needed to administer the program effectively.

A higher OPT fee can also strengthen program integrity. Additional funding can support enhanced verification measures, compliance monitoring, case review processes, and anti-fraud initiatives. Maintaining confidence in the OPT program requires robust oversight to ensure that benefits are granted only to eligible applicants and that the program is used consistent with its intended educational and workforce development purposes.

Furthermore, the proposed increase remains modest when compared to the substantial economic and professional benefits that OPT participants often receive. Many beneficiaries secure employment with competitive salaries, gain valuable U.S. work experience, and improve their prospects for future employment-based immigration opportunities. In that context, the proposed fee increase represents a reasonable investment rather than an undue burden.

It is also important to recognize that failure to adequately fund USCIS operations can result in longer processing times, increased backlogs, and reduced service quality. A properly funded agency benefits applicants, employers, educational institutions, and the broader U.S. economy by ensuring predictable and timely adjudications.

For these reasons, I strongly support DHS's proposal to increase OPT fees and encourage the Department to finalize and implement the fee adjustment. Ensuring that USCIS has the resources necessary to administer immigration benefits effectively is in the best interests of applicants, employers, educational institutions, and the integrity of the U.S. immigration system as a whole.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this proposal.

Respectfully,
Sanjay Rao

I am writing as a United States citizen to express my strong support for the Department of Homeland Security's proposal to increase fees associated with the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program.

My support for this proposal is based not only on principles of sound administration and cost recovery, but also on my personal experience in today's labor market. I recently applied for an information technology position with Delta Dental that closely matched my education, professional experience, and technical skill set. Despite being qualified for the role, I was not selected. The position was ultimately filled by an individual participating in the OPT program.

While employers have the legal right to hire eligible workers, experiences such as mine highlight the importance of ensuring that programs like OPT are administered responsibly and that the full costs of these programs are borne by their users rather than being subsidized through insufficient fees. When a program directly affects labor market competition, it is especially important that it operate with strong oversight, proper funding, and rigorous compliance measures.

OPT participants receive significant benefits through the opportunity to gain valuable work experience in the United States and, in many cases, establish pathways to long-term employment. Given these substantial advantages, it is reasonable to expect beneficiaries to contribute more toward the administrative costs of the program. A fee increase helps ensure that USCIS has adequate resources to review applications thoroughly, conduct program oversight, prevent fraud, and maintain the integrity of the immigration system.

As a U.S. citizen seeking employment in the technology sector, I believe it is important that immigration programs are administered in a manner that is transparent, accountable, and self-sustaining. The proposed fee increase is a sensible step toward achieving these goals. It promotes fiscal responsibility, strengthens public confidence in the system, and helps ensure that the OPT program is supported by those who directly benefit from it.

I respectfully encourage DHS to finalize and implement the proposed OPT fee increase. Adequate funding is essential to maintaining effective oversight and preserving the integrity of programs that have a direct impact on employment opportunities in the United States.

In my view, OPT participants and the employers who benefit from their labor should bear the full administrative costs associated with the program. U.S. citizens and lawful taxpayers should not be expected to indirectly subsidize immigration benefit programs through below-cost fees. Ensuring full cost recovery through higher OPT fees is a fair and appropriate policy that aligns with the principles of fiscal responsibility and user-funded government services.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this proposal.

As Director of International Services at a large, research-intensive University, I write to strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing exceptionally high fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT).These fees would fundamentally undermine a program that has long served as an important bridge between higher education in the United States and the American workforce.

My university enrolls approximately 4,000 international students annually. Approximately two-thirds of these students use OPT, representing roughly 2,667 students based on our current enrollment. This level of participation demonstrates that OPT is not a marginal benefit affecting a small number of graduates. It is a significant component of the educational and professional pathway for our international student population.

Imposing fees at the proposed levels would create a substantial financial barrier for students and employers, discourage international students from choosing U.S. institutions, reduce the availability of qualified candidates for American employers, and weaken the ability of universities to recruit and retain talented faculty and researchers. It would also jeopardize university revenue, local economic activity, research partnerships, and the long-term competitiveness of American higher education.

We urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and pursue proportionate, evidence-based measures to address any demonstrated concerns about fraud or program integrity without effectively placing OPT beyond the reach of qualified international graduates.

The value of U.S. higher education extends beyond the completion of a degree. Students develop advanced knowledge, technical expertise, research capabilities, communication skills, and the ability to solve complex problems. OPT enables eligible F-1 students to apply that preparation in a professional setting related to their academic field.

Through OPT, graduates can contribute to employers while gaining practical experience that complements their academic education. Employers, in turn, can evaluate and benefit from the knowledge and skills developed through U.S. degree programs.

This relationship is particularly important in fields where specialized education must be complemented by practical experience. Examples include engineering, computer science, data science, biotechnology, public health, advanced manufacturing, business analytics, and other science, technology, engineering, and mathematics disciplines. Practical experience also matters in research-intensive fields, where graduates contribute to laboratories, research projects, technology development, and the translation of academic discoveries into real-world applications.

The United States Needs Innovators, Researchers, and Highly Educated Talent
The United States benefits when talented people from around the world choose to study at American universities and contribute their knowledge to the U.S. economy. International students bring diverse perspectives, specialized expertise, research experience, and global connections that benefit classrooms, laboratories, employers, and communities.

The ability to attract talented students is especially important in a global environment where countries compete to recruit individuals with advanced technical and scientific skills. International students make substantial investments in U.S. tuition, housing, transportation, and other expenses. Many also contribute directly to research and technological development during their academic programs.

OPT helps preserve the connection between that investment in education and the opportunity to contribute to the American workforce. It gives U.S. employers access to graduates who have already received advanced education in the United States and whose skills may align closely with employers' needs.

If the purpose of the proposed rule is to improve program integrity, DHS should consider whether the extraordinary fees are reasonably related to that objective, whether less burdensome alternatives are available, and whether the rule's costs and consequences have been adequately evaluated. A fee structure that effectively forecloses a longstanding program for most eligible graduates would be an unnecessarily blunt instrument.

This rule, if implemented, will greatly reduce international student enrollment in the U.S. It is not in the best best of the U.S., it's employers or higher education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I urge DHS to withdraw this fee structure and preserve reasonable access to legitimate, degree-related practical training.

My principal concern is that these fees would make access to practical training depend on financial resources rather than educational merit, professional qualifications, or compliance with immigration requirements. Although the proposal places payment responsibility on educational institutions, it acknowledges that those institutions may pass the financial burden to students or employers. Shifting responsibility for payment does not eliminate the burden. I am concerned that institutions could decline to recommend otherwise qualified students, employers could withdraw legitimate training opportunities, and students could lose access to practical experience despite meeting all other eligibility requirements.

I support protecting American workers, preventing fraud, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, the ability to pay a substantial fee is not evidence of compliance, and the inability to pay is not evidence of misconduct. DHS should demonstrate why these particular amounts would effectively distinguish legitimate educational training from abuse. A reduction in participation should not, by itself, be treated as evidence that fraud has been prevented.

The proposal states that the fees would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury and would not be retained by ICE or specifically earmarked for immigration enforcement activities. I therefore ask DHS to explain how these fees would improve oversight beyond creating a financial deterrent. The agency should evaluate less burdensome alternatives, including targeted compliance reviews, verification of degree-related training, employer accountability, and enforcement of applicable worker protections. Measures directed at demonstrated misconduct would be preferable to a financial barrier affecting compliant participants.

I am also concerned about the proposed effective date of 60 days after publication of a final rule. DHS should meaningfully consider students who have already committed to educational programs, incurred substantial expenses, or accepted future training opportunities under the existing framework. Describing a requirement as prospective does not resolve its potential impact on decisions made years earlier. I request explicit protections for currently enrolled students and existing OPT participants, including those who would need a later recommendation or extension.

Before proceeding, DHS should assess the potential consequences for universities, teaching hospitals, veterinary services, scientific research, small employers, and underserved communities. The analysis should examine whether these fees could discourage legitimate clinical training, interrupt research, reduce educational opportunities, or limit access to essential services. It should also consider whether smaller institutions and modestly funded training programs would face disproportionate barriers compared with organizations possessing greater financial resources.

DHS should also evaluate whether shifting substantial costs to students could increase debt or dependence on employers willing to finance participation. A policy intended to protect workers should be examined carefully for the possibility that it could make participants more financially vulnerable.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure. Any alternative should be supported by transparent evidence, proportionate to its stated objectives, and designed to address demonstrated problems without making legitimate training financially unattainable. At a minimum, DHS should evaluate substantially lower fees, meaningful exemptions or waivers, and transition protections for students with existing educational commitments.

Protecting American workers and preserving immigration integrity are important goals. They should be pursued through effective oversight and evidence-based enforcement, not by making lawful, education-related practical training accessible only to those with exceptional financial resources.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the fee structure.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (FR Doc. 2026-20660). DHS's statement that the rule would not affect health or safety.

1. The health and safety finding has no analysis behind it
The NPRM says the rule "exceeds the $100 million expenditure threshold in the first year" and provides a UMRA statement. UMRA section 202(a)(2) requires that statement to assess the mandate's effect on health and safety. The NPRM's answer is one sentence: "DHS does not believe that this rule would have impacts on health or safety." DHS gives no data, no reasoning, and no sign that it asked the Department of Health and Human Services.

2. DHS's own scenario removes OPT for most health graduates
In its low participation scenario, DHS assumes schools will pay the $70,000 fee "for only F-1 nonimmigrant students eligible for the 24-month STEM OPT extension," and that "non-STEM OPT is no longer recommended." The STEM definition in footnote 49 covers the CIP two-digit series for engineering, biological sciences, mathematics and physical sciences, "or a related field." Most health professions degrees, including nursing and pharmacy practice degrees, sit in a different series (CIP 51) and are not on the STEM list. In that scenario, international graduates of those programs lose post-completion OPT. That is a direct effect on the health workforce, and the NPRM does not mention it.

3. The labor evidence is about computer jobs
The NPRM's labor-market case rests on computer occupations. The proclamation DHS quotes says computer science unemployment is "more than double the unemployment rates of recent biology and art history graduates." DHS cites nothing showing that OPT workers in nursing, pharmacy, public health or clinical research displace U.S. workers or depress wages. It also assumes "employers may find alternative workers." For clinical roles, that is a factual question about staffing, and DHS did not ask it. Where a hospital or clinic cannot fill a licensed position, the cost is measured in patient access, not only in payroll.

4. The refund rule fits licensed fields badly
Many health occupations require a state license, and graduates often sit for the licensing exam after the program ends. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1), the $70,000 fee "will not be refunded under any circumstances once the F-1 student has been granted the employment authorization document." If a graduate's license is delayed, the school loses the full fee even though no patient care was ever provided. A school pricing that risk will drop health students first. DHS did not consider this.

5. Biomedical research takes the STEM path, at full price
Biological sciences graduates do qualify for STEM OPT. That means $70,000 plus $30,000 for each graduate who moves into biotech, drug development, biostatistics or clinical trial work. The NPRM names "technology and critical infrastructure" as the high-risk sectors where abuse is "more likely." It cites no OPT fraud case in biomedical research or patient care. A flat fee charges these fields the same as the sectors DHS says concern it.

6. What DHS should have done
DHS has SEVIS data by program and employer. It could have reported how many OPT and STEM OPT participants hold health professions or biomedical degrees, and how many work for hospitals, clinics, health systems or clinical research sites. It could also have checked whether those employers sit in federally designated Health Professional Shortage Areas. It did none of this before concluding there is no health effect.

7. Requests
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS re-proposes any OPT fee, it should:
(a) complete the UMRA section 202(a)(2) health and safety assessment, in consultation with HHS, and publish it for comment;
(b) publish SEVIS counts of OPT and STEM OPT participants by CIP series and by health care employer type;
(c) exempt graduates of health professions programs and OPT employment with licensed health care providers, or at minimum allow a refund when a required license is not issued; and
(d) explain why a flat fee is needed in fields where DHS cites no fraud and no labor surplus.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule, citing a lack of health and safety analysis and workforce impacts.

I am writing as a PhD student at Yale University studying microbiology to express my opposition to the proposed rule under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, concerning fees associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT). I urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. Although I am not an international student myself, I work closely with many international members of the scientific community, and their contributions are essential to my research, my laboratory, and my development as a scientist. I believe this proposal would have consequences that extend far beyond the international students directly affected. It would change the environment in which American graduate students are trained, make it harder for universities to retain talented researchers, and potentially weaken the United States' position as a global leader in scientific research.
As a microbiology PhD student, I understand that research is rarely an individual effort. Much of what we accomplish depends on the knowledge, technical skills, and perspectives of the people around us. In my laboratory, I work with international researchers who bring different academic backgrounds, specialized expertise, and valuable scientific perspectives. They contribute to experimental design, troubleshoot difficult experiments, share protocols, discuss unexpected results, and help one another develop new approaches to scientific questions. These interactions are not incidental to our work; they are fundamental to how research progresses. In microbiology, experiments can be technically demanding and time-consuming, and the ability to learn from someone with experience in a particular method or biological system can make a substantial difference to the progress of a project. Losing a trained laboratory member is not simply a matter of replacing one employee with another. It can mean losing years of accumulated knowledge, disrupting ongoing experiments, delaying publications, and forcing other members of the laboratory to spend significant time rebuilding expertise that was already present.
The proposed rule is particularly concerning because of the financial barriers it would introduce. Specifically, Section V.A. of the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566, 64576–64577 (Oct. 8, 2026), establishes a proposed $70,000 fee for an institution's initial OPT recommendation for an F-1 student and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations under the specified conditions. The proposed regulatory provisions are 8 C.F.R. §§ 214.2(f)(11) and 214.13(i). These amounts are extraordinarily high in the context of academic research, where laboratories operate under limited grant funding and carefully planned budgets. Universities must already balance the costs of personnel, equipment, reagents, facilities, and research infrastructure. An additional financial burden of this magnitude could influence whether an institution is willing or able to support an otherwise qualified international researcher. Even if a university wants to retain a student who has spent several years contributing to its research program, the financial implications could make that decision considerably more difficult. I am concerned that decisions about retaining talented researchers could increasingly be driven by financial considerations rather than scientific ability, research contributions, or institutional need.
This would also directly affect students like me who are not international students. My own graduate education depends on having access to a strong, collaborative research environment. I benefit from working alongside international colleagues because they challenge my thinking, introduce me to different approaches, and help me develop technical and scientific skills that I will carry throughout my career. If these researchers are unable to remain in the United States after completing their degrees, American students will lose valuable opportunities for mentorship, collaboration, and professional development. This is an important point that deserves greater consideration: policies that restrict international academic workers do not only affect international students. They also affect the American researchers who learn from them, collaborate with them, and depend on their expertise. As someone hoping to build a career in American science, I want to work in an environment that attracts talented researchers from around the world rather than one that makes it increasingly difficult for them to remain.
I am also concerned about the practical consequences for ongoing research collaborations. Scientific projects often take several years to complete, and much of the knowledge required to carry them forward exists within the people working on them. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yun-De Liu
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation.

I am an international graduate student pursuing an advanced degree in a STEM field at a U.S. university. My academic and professional experiences have shown me the importance of practical training opportunities in connecting higher education with industry innovation. I chose to pursue graduate education in the United States because of its world-class academic environment, research opportunities, and commitment to technological advancement.

I recognize the importance of preventing immigration fraud, protecting American workers, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, I am deeply concerned that the proposed fees would impose disproportionate burdens on legitimate students, educational institutions, and employers without adequately distinguishing lawful participation from fraudulent activity.

First, the proposed fees would undermine the accessibility and educational purpose of OPT.

Practical training is an important extension of academic education, enabling students to apply specialized knowledge in real-world settings. A $70,000 initial fee could make such opportunities financially inaccessible, regardless of a student's academic qualifications, professional potential, or compliance with immigration requirements. This financial barrier would disproportionately affect students with limited financial resources and could discourage talented individuals from pursuing advanced education in the United States.

Second, the proposed rule could weaken American technological competitiveness and innovation.

International graduates contribute specialized knowledge and skills to American research institutions and companies working in artificial intelligence, advanced computing, semiconductor technologies, and other strategically important industries. Practical training opportunities allow American employers to benefit from talent educated within the United States. Imposing substantial financial barriers could encourage highly skilled graduates to pursue opportunities in other countries, potentially reducing America's ability to attract and retain international talent and weakening its long-term leadership in science and technology.

Third, placing the payment obligation on universities does not eliminate the financial burden on students and employers.

Although the proposed rule formally assigns payment responsibility to educational institutions, it explicitly allows institutions to pass these costs on to students or employers. Universities may also choose not to recommend otherwise qualified students because of the substantial financial obligation. Consequently, access to practical training could become increasingly dependent on financial resources rather than academic merit, professional qualifications, or legitimate educational objectives. This outcome would be particularly concerning for students who have already invested significant time and resources in their education based on the existing regulatory framework.

Fourth, more targeted alternatives could address fraud without disproportionately burdening legitimate participants.

I support stronger measures to prevent fraudulent employment arrangements and ensure that practical training remains directly related to students' academic fields. However, substantial fees imposed broadly on all participants are not necessarily an effective means of identifying or preventing fraud. I encourage DHS to consider alternative measures, including enhanced employer verification, risk-based compliance reviews, improved reporting mechanisms, and stronger enforcement against fraudulent institutions and employment arrangements. These approaches could strengthen program integrity while preserving legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

Furthermore, I urge DHS to carefully evaluate the broader economic and educational consequences of the proposed fee structure, including its effects on university enrollment, international student recruitment, employer participation, and the competitiveness of the American research and technology ecosystem.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure and preserve accessible practical training opportunities for qualified international students. At a minimum, DHS should conduct a more comprehensive assessment of the proposal's impact on current students, educational institutions, employers, and American technological competitiveness before adopting such substantial fees.

Maintaining a fair, predictable, and accessible practical training framework is essential to ensuring that the United States remains a leading destination for education, research, and innovation.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they impose disproportionate financial burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Michael VanJaarsveld
comments.commentText:
End the OPT Program immediately - it harms American youth and steals their opportunities.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to end the Optional Practical Training program. The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees are an acknowledgment that the current system is broken, but they are not enough. OPT is a government-created work authorization that places foreign students into American jobs and training opportunities at the direct expense of American youth. This is not a minor policy issue. It is a national emergency for the career futures of young Americans who did everything the system asked of them.

Recent data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York show unemployment among recent college graduates at approximately 5.2 percent and underemployment among employed recent graduates at 42.5 percent. These are Americans who studied, earned degrees, and took on student debt under the promise that education would open doors. Instead, many are sending out hundreds of resumes, facing rejection, or working in jobs that do not require their degrees. At the same time, hundreds of thousands of foreign students receive OPT work authorization each year and are placed into the same entry-level and early-career roles that American graduates need. Employers are not required to demonstrate that they first tried to hire qualified Americans. This is policy-driven displacement of American workers.

OPT functions as a theft of training and opportunity from American kids. It gives foreign students preferential access to practical experience, skill-building, and job networks in the United States without the caps, labor market tests, or recruitment protections that should apply when temporary foreign labor is authorized. STEM extensions make the problem worse by extending this advantage for years. The result is fewer first jobs, lower starting wages in some fields, and diminished career trajectories for American graduates. Allowing this to continue while young Americans struggle is indefensible.

The proposed fees correctly raise the cost of using OPT as a volume labor channel and should be finalized if the program is not immediately ended. But fees alone leave the structural preference in place. The only appropriate response is to terminate the program.

I therefore recommend that DHS:
- End the Optional Practical Training program as quickly as possible, with no new recommendations accepted after a short transition period.
- In the interim, finalize the $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees and impose a mandatory labor market test requiring documented good-faith recruitment of American applicants before any OPT hire.
- Immediately end the STEM OPT extension.
- Prioritize policies that expand training, apprenticeships, and entry-level opportunities for American citizens rather than foreign students.

American youth should not have their futures subordinated to a government program that hands their job and training opportunities to non-citizens. Ending OPT is the necessary step to protect their chance to build careers, support families, and pursue the American Dream. I urge the Department to act decisively in the national interest of American workers.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that OPT harms American youth and urges DHS to end the program entirely.

I strongly support this proposal. The OPT program has been widely abused, and it is time to take a serious look at how it is being used.

Over the years, some colleges, particularly low-quality institutions, appear to have turned international student admissions into an immigration business rather than focusing on providing a meaningful education. They recruit students from developing countries, charge them substantial tuition fees, and sell the promise of access to the U.S. job market and a potential path to immigration rather than offering genuine educational value. A college should be an institution for education, not a backdoor into the U.S. immigration system.

Having worked in the IT industry for more than 16 years, I am also deeply concerned about the impact these practices have on American workers. We are already seeing intense competition for IT jobs, companies laying off American employees, and qualified U.S. professionals struggling to find employment. The situation is becoming even more challenging for recent American college graduates. With AI transforming the job market and companies increasingly automating tasks and reducing entry-level hiring, many young Americans are struggling to find their first jobs and get their careers started. At a time when our own graduates are facing such challenges, it makes little sense to overlook the impact of programs that bring additional competition into an already difficult job market.

At the same time, employers have access to a large pool of foreign workers who may be willing to accept lower compensation or work longer hours, including evenings, weekends, and holidays, sometimes because their immigration status makes them more dependent on their employers.

This creates an uneven playing field and raises legitimate questions about whether these programs are actually addressing labor shortages or simply providing employers with access to a cheaper workforce.
