comments.title: Comment Submitted by SHOUMIK DEBNATH
comments.commentText:
I am an international Ph.D. student in Electrical Engineering at Colorado State University, conducting research in integrated photonics, semiconductor technologies, and optical communications. I am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed $70,000 fee for an institution's initial OPT recommendation and an additional $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions.

OPT provides an essential bridge between advanced academic education and professional employment. International STEM graduates contribute to American universities through research, teaching, innovation, and technological development. After graduation, OPT allows them to apply their specialized knowledge in industries and research institutions, particularly in strategically important fields such as semiconductors, photonics, telecommunications, artificial intelligence hardware, and advanced manufacturing.

The proposed fees could create significant unintended consequences. A combined $100,000 institutional expense could discourage universities from supporting international graduates and make employers less willing to recruit them. Smaller technology companies, startups, and research organizations may be particularly unable to absorb such substantial additional costs. Consequently, qualified graduates could face reduced employment opportunities not because of their academic qualifications or professional abilities, but because of the financial burden associated with their immigration status.

Furthermore, these fees could undermine America's ability to attract and retain global STEM talent. International doctoral students invest years in advanced education and contribute directly to the American research ecosystem. Creating substantial financial barriers between graduation and professional employment could encourage talented researchers and engineers to pursue opportunities in countries with more accessible post-study employment pathways. This could negatively affect American research institutions, technological innovation, and long-term industrial competitiveness.

I recognize the government's responsibility to maintain the integrity of immigration programs. However, regulatory fees should be proportionate, transparent, and supported by demonstrable administrative costs.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider the proposed fee structure, conduct a comprehensive economic impact assessment, establish fees based on actual administrative expenses, and consider appropriate exemptions or alternative arrangements for STEM graduates and research-intensive institutions.

I chose to pursue doctoral education in the United States because of its world-class research environment and opportunities to translate scientific knowledge into practical innovations. Like many international students, I hope to contribute meaningfully to American research and technological advancement.

International students are not simply participants in the American education system; they are researchers, engineers, educators, and contributors to the nation's innovation ecosystem. Policies governing their transition into professional employment should recognize these contributions rather than inadvertently create substantial financial barriers.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider this proposal and pursue a balanced approach that protects the integrity of immigration programs while preserving America's ability to attract and retain highly skilled international STEM graduates.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Wen Jin
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Wen Jin, and I'm a faculty of physics at the Benedictine University.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Increasing OPT fees would place an additional financial burden on students who have spent years contributing to American universities through research and teaching.

OPT provides an essential bridge between education and employment. For international students pursuing careers in scientific research, this opportunity is especially important because finding suitable research positions often requires time and flexibility.

Higher OPT fees could discourage talented international students from choosing the United States for their education and careers. This would ultimately hurt American universities, scientific research, and the country's ability to attract and retain highly skilled talent.

Sincerely,
Wen Jin

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Justin Lampley
comments.commentText:
The proposed $70,000 OPT and $30,000 STEM OPT fee proposal is arbitrary, illogical, and will make the United States a much less attractive destination for talented international students worldwide. If there is evidence of fraud or abuse within the OPT program, then there are surely other more targeted strategies DHS can implement to address that fraud that they (DHS) refuse to consider. This fee will simply price out all F1 visa students of work authorization as no reasonable person (or university) would pay such an outrageous fee simply to work in their field of study in the US.

The argument of 'protecting American workers' is tiresome and has become a default response from the current administration and DHS to counter any immigration or temporary work programs in the US. There's no evidence behind it; it's simply a tired talking point. Students on OPT are not stealing or undercutting wages. They are filling jobs that would otherwise go unfilled and trying to obtain work experience in their field of study. Some F1 students do stay in the US after changing visa status, but many get valuable work experience in the US then return home to pursue their career.

If the US is to compete in STEM industries (including AI) then we need to be an attractive destination for the best and the brightest from around the world to study and work. The OPT program is a major reason talented international students choose to pursue Undergraduate and Graduate study in the United States. This fee would simply price them out of obtaining work authorization, and they will find other countries to study that are more welcoming to international students.

Of course fraud of any kind should be investigated, but blowing up the OPT program (which this fee would do) because of isolated cases of abuse is irresponsible and shortsighted. This will dry up the pipeline of talented international students which have played a crucial role in making the US a leader in STEM field (including medicine and AI) research.

It seems DHS wants to deter talented students from even considering the US as a study destination. That is sad, and will make the United States worse off in the coming years and decades.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees — DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01

Reference: 91 FR 64566, October 8, 2026; Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)

I am an international PhD student in engineering who has dedicated years to pursuing advanced education, conducting research, and gaining professional experience in the United States. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2).

1. Disproportionate Financial Burden on Universities and Students (Sections IV.C and VII.A.4)

In Section IV.C (91 FR 64575), DHS explicitly acknowledges that educational institutions may pass the financial burden of these fees onto international students, other students, or employers. This raises a serious concern: even though universities are officially responsible for paying the fees, students could ultimately bear the costs.

Furthermore, DHS estimates in Section VII.A.4 (91 FR 64583, Table 3) that the proposed fees could generate between $8.4 billion and $16.5 billion annually, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. These figures demonstrate the extraordinary financial scale of the proposal.

Many universities, particularly smaller institutions and publicly funded research universities, may be unable to absorb these costs. As a result, qualified students could lose access to practical training simply because their institutions cannot afford the fees.

2. Financial Ability Does Not Establish Academic Merit or Prevent Fraud (Sections IV.A and IV.

In Section IV.A (91 FR 64570–64571), DHS describes fraudulent employment arrangements, including shell companies and nonexistent workplaces. I recognize the seriousness of these concerns and support stronger enforcement against such activities.

However, Section IV.C (91 FR 64574) suggests that requiring substantial fees would encourage institutions to recommend only highly qualified students. Financial capacity is not an appropriate measure of academic achievement, professional qualifications, or compliance with immigration regulations.

A student who has maintained lawful status, successfully completed an advanced degree, and secured legitimate training should not be denied an opportunity solely because their university cannot pay $70,000.

DHS should instead prioritize targeted employer verification, compliance investigations, and enforcement against fraudulent entities rather than imposing financial barriers on all students.

3. Negative Consequences for Research and STEM Education (Sections VI and VII.A.5)

In Section VI (91 FR 64578), DHS recognizes that the proposed fees could affect institutions' existing budgets and suggests that universities could mitigate those impacts by transferring the costs to students or employers.

This approach does not eliminate the financial burden; it simply transfers it to another party.

For international graduate students in engineering and other STEM fields, practical training provides an opportunity to apply years of specialized education and research to real-world challenges. These experiences can benefit American businesses, infrastructure development, and technological innovation.

The proposed fees could discourage universities from supporting OPT participation, limit access to professional training, and make the United States less attractive to talented international researchers.

4. Opposition to Repeated Fees at Higher Educational Levels (Section V.A)

In Section V.A (91 FR 64577), DHS specifically requests public comments on an alternative that would impose an additional $70,000 initial OPT fee whenever a student advances to a higher educational level.

I strongly oppose this alternative. Students who continue from bachelor's to master's or doctoral programs are investing additional years in education and developing specialized expertise. Repeatedly imposing such substantial fees would create an additional financial barrier to advanced education and professional development.

**Requested Action**

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2), reject the alternative of repeating the $70,000 fee at higher educational levels, and consider more targeted, evidence-based approaches to preventing OPT fraud.

Protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of immigration programs are legitimate and important objectives. However, these goals should be achieved through effective enforcement and oversight, not by imposing disproportionate financial barriers on legitimate international students, educational institutions, and employers.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, citing excessive financial burdens on students and universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by David Herrera
comments.commentText:
RE: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Proposed Rule "Optional Practical Training Fees"

I write as an individual who would be directly affected by this proposal. I am currently in the United States on a J-1 exchange visitor visa and plan to pursue a STEM master's degree on F-1 status beginning in 2027, with the goal of using post-completion Optional Practical Training (OPT) and the 24-month STEM OPT extension to work in my field of study, geospatial data and data science.

The proposed fees — $70,000 for a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, paid by the school before a Designated School Official may enter the recommendation — would in practice end that path:

1. The affordable programs available to me cost roughly $15,000–$21,000 in total tuition. No school charging that can absorb $70,000 to $100,000 per student. The Department acknowledges schools "may" pass the cost to students; for students like me, the cost will land on the student, and I cannot pay $100,000 on top of tuition. The practical result is that schools will decline to recommend OPT for students at affordable programs, or students like me will be priced out of OPT entirely.

2. The fee is detached from any cost of administering OPT. A charge roughly 140 times the current I-765 filing fee does not fund a service; it prices out participation, and it falls hardest on students at the least expensive schools.

3. The 24-month STEM OPT extension exists to keep STEM graduates working in the United States. A $30,000 fee on the extension defeats that purpose: schools and employers will not pay it for entry-level analysts, so STEM graduates will take their skills elsewhere.

4. I oppose the alternative the Department seeks comment on — charging the $70,000 initial fee again each time a student moves to a higher degree level. That would compound the harm above for students who pursue a master's after a bachelor's degree.

I respectfully ask the Department to withdraw the proposed fees. If fees are considered at all, they should be tied to actual administrative costs and set at a level that does not make OPT unavailable at affordable institutions.

Respectfully submitted,
David Herrera, prospective F-1 STEM graduate student
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees are prohibitively expensive and will price international students out of participating in OPT.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am not in favor of the proposed $70,000 fee for recommending OPT. While it is important to stop fraud in OPT and the student visa system, the reasoning in the notice is deeply flawed. It is comparing apples and oranges.

First, this would represent an increase of more than 14,700% over the current OPT application fee.

Any substantial fee increase should be decided by Congress after hearings and debate. If there are flaws in the OPT and student visa programs, those issues should be addressed by Congress. This exorbitant fee would discourage a vast majority of legitimate international students seeking practical training from applying for OPT, and it could have an even broader negative effect on international students choosing to study in the United States.

Several times in the notice, the justification for the fee increase is that DHS does not have the resources to monitor fraud. However, these students are graduates of U.S. undergraduate and graduate programs, and they are highly qualified individuals who are interested in furthering their academic qualifications. They are not students coming to the United States solely to seek employment.

The SEVP database already contains OPT employer information and could be used to identify suspicious employers. For example, the database includes the employer’s name, address, supervisor’s name, email, telephone number, and the job duties being performed by the student. The notice does not explain why this tool is not being used, or cannot be used, to identify employers and students who are out of compliance or committing fraud.

An ICE news release from October 21, 2020 stated: “ICE has a system of checks in place to mitigate fraud and is committed to protecting national security by ensuring that students, visitors, and schools comply with U.S. immigration laws,” and noted that ICE was actively targeting individuals who try to exploit the student visa system. That suggests ICE does have the ability to address fraud. In addition, the fee collected would go to the general fund, not directly to DHS, so DHS staffing would remain unchanged. It appears the purpose of the new $70,000 fee is simply to discourage colleges from recommending OPT and students from pursuing it.

ICE and DHS have also received major increases in funding in recent years. ICE has seen its budget increase more than threefold, jumping from about $10 billion in FY 2025 to over $85 billion total available resources following major federal spending bills. The Big Beautiful Bill (2025), increased the DHS budget by 75 billion dollars. Secure America Act (2026), added nearly $39 billion more in multi-year funding. Yet the notice continues to claim that the agencies do not have the resources to monitor fraud in the OPT program.

The argument also ignores the scale and importance of international students. In 2024–25, there were about 1.18 million international students in the United States, making up about 6% of total college enrollment. More than 57% of international students pursue STEM fields, which drive the vast majority of extended OPT utilization. Math and Computer science (25.9%), engineering (21.7%), and business/management remain the most common majors. It is only natural that OPT and STEM OPT participation would rise as well. Historical data shows that about 70% of OPT participants graduated with a master’s degree or higher.

International students contribute significantly to the U.S. economy. the US Department of Commerce estimates, international students contribute the equivalent of $55 Billion to the US economy and support over 355,000 jobs. They contribute an average of $50,000 per year to the US economy. They support jobs, pay substantial tuition and living expenses, and strengthen U.S. colleges and communities. Requiring the vast majority of students who follow the rules to pay an exorbitant fee because of the misconduct of a few will likely reduce the number of students coming to the United States for higher education.A 10% dip in the number of students attending US colleges will have a 35,000 US job loss.

This proposed $70,000 fee is wrong and misguided. In a highly competitive global environment, it could seriously harm U.S. higher education, jobs, and the economy. It should not be implemented.
Thank you!
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee is exorbitant, harmful to international students, and should not be enacted.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the newly proposed fees for both OPT recommendation and subsequent recommendation. Combating fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives. However, the ability to pay is not a measure of compliance, and individual instances of fraud do not, by themselves, establish that imposing substantial fees on every recommendation is a reasonable response.

DHS acknowledges that it cannot reliably predict the decline in participation. Its primary estimate places the proposal’s ten-year costs at $35.1 billion, discounted at 3 percent. If schools reduce OPT recommendations, lawful students’ access to practical training and employers’ access to talent would also be restricted. Yet one fewer OPT participant does not necessarily translate into one additional job for a U.S. worker; that outcome depends on whether the relevant skills and positions are interchangeable.

In National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States (1974), the Supreme Court distinguished regulatory fees from taxes and emphasized the limits of congressional authorization. In DHS v. Regents of the University of California (2020), the Court required adequate consideration of reliance interests and relevant alternatives when reversing policy. Although the former case did not address OPT fees, it provides an important analogy.

DHS should explain its statutory authority to impose these fees, substantiate the amounts, and evaluate alternatives such as risk-based audits. If the final rule lacks an adequate justification, it could exceed statutory authority or be **arbitrary** and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. The proposal should therefore be withdrawn or redesigned.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an international PhD student in a STEM field at a U.S. research university. I write to oppose this proposed rule, in particular the $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i), and the alternative of reapplying the $70,000 fee at each degree level.

1. The fee would effectively close OPT as a path into U.S. academic research.
For international students who earn a PhD in the U.S., starting a postdoctoral appointment on F-1 OPT or STEM OPT is very common. J-1 and H-1B are alternatives, but OPT is usually preferred: the student applies for it directly, without needing the employer to file a job-specific petition with labor certification and fees, and it avoids the two-year home-residence requirement that can attach to J-1 status. The entry-level NIH Kirschstein-NRSA postdoctoral stipend for FY 2026 is $63,480. The proposed $70,000 fee exceeds a full year of a postdoc's pay. The school must pay before recommending OPT and may pass the cost to the student or employer, but academic labs pay postdocs from research grants with fixed budgets, and early-career scholars cannot pay it themselves. In practice, universities will stop recommending OPT or labs will stop hiring international graduates as postdocs.

2. The fee is not tailored to the fraud DHS describes.
The rule cites shell employers and "visa mills." Universities, national laboratories and nonprofit research institutes are not shell companies, and STEM OPT employers must already enroll in E-Verify and sign a Form I-983 training plan. A flat fee on every student penalizes legitimate employers and students alike; fraud is better addressed by enforcement against the bad actors DHS has already identified. The rule also states the fees go to the Treasury's general fund and will not be retained by ICE, so the money would not fund fraud prevention. A charge tied neither to the cost of administering OPT nor to the problem it claims to solve works as a barrier, not an integrity measure.

3. International researchers are central to U.S. science.
According to the NSF Survey of Earned Doctorates, temporary visa holders earned 54% of U.S. engineering doctorates and 61% of computer and information science doctorates in 2024. NSF also found that 73% of temporary visa holders who earned science and engineering doctorates in 2017-19 still lived in the U.S. in 2023. These are researchers trained in U.S. labs, often on U.S. research funding, and most stay to contribute here. Since 2000, immigrants have won 40% of the Nobel Prizes awarded to Americans in chemistry, medicine and physics combined (45% in physics alone), according to the National Foundation for American Policy. Much of that leadership was built by people who came as students and stayed.

4. Talented students have other choices.
International students do not come to the U.S. because we lack opportunities at home. We come because U.S. universities have been the best place to do science, and because the path from PhD to postdoc to faculty or industry research has been open. That openness is already eroding. In a 2025 Nature poll, three-quarters of U.S.-based researchers who responded said they were considering leaving the country, including 548 of 690 postdocs. Other countries are recruiting them: the European Union launched a 500-million-euro "Choose Europe for Science" package for 2025-2027 to attract researchers from around the world. Established scientists are leaving too: in July 2026, Omar Yaghi, who came to the U.S. as a teenager and shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, left UC Berkeley to lead a new institute at Tsinghua University in Beijing. A $70,000 fee at the very start of an academic career would add to this pressure, telling the next generation of scientists to go elsewhere, and U.S. research will bear the cost.

5. Requests
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS proceeds, it should at minimum:
- exempt OPT employment at institutions of higher education, their affiliated nonprofits, and nonprofit or governmental research organizations, consistent with how Congress treats these employers under the H-1B cap (8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(5));
- reject the alternative of reapplying the $70,000 fee at each degree level, which would fall hardest on PhD students who have earned several U.S. degrees;
- analyze the rule's effect on university research and postdoctoral hiring before finalizing it.

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Erin Heffernan
comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to submit a comment with respect to the Proposed Rule on optional Practical Training Fees (ICEB-2026-0100).

I have 14 years of experience working in the international education sector, most recently with nearly 5 years of experience in graduate admissions for a U.S. university. Although I write in my personal capacity, and not for my employer, my past work experience and expertise in this field inform my view on this proposed rule.

A 2024 survey by Shorelight and the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education showed that 79% of students responded to the question “If OPT were no longer available, would you still choose to study in the U.S.” with either “No” or “Not Sure” (Shorelight, https://shorelight.widen.net/s/8djqz7kpqc/sl_25-opt-in-focus-report_lr) This new rule would make OPT effectively nonexistent, with the $70,000 fee surpassing the tuition money that many universities bring in from a student in a year, therefore putting the program out of reach for universities and, by extension, students. A 79% decrease in international students would be catastrophic for U.S. higher education and for the U.S. student experience. It would also put hundreds of thousands of U.S. jobs at risk as I will outline below.

My journey toward working in higher education started when I was an undergraduate student myself. A study abroad experience followed by subsequent friendships I formed with international students when I returned to the U.S. helped me to build my own skills and interest in intercultural competence and communication. I dedicated my career to making the world a more open and welcoming place through cultural exchange and educational programs. Over the years, in my work, I have seen the power of exchange programs, including the F-1 Visa program, to bring talented students to the U.S., giving them an opportunity to learn from U.S. educators and peers, as well as the opportunities for educators and peers to learn from them.

The interactions and friendships formed between U.S. citizens (including students, faculty, staff, and community members) and international students are powerful and often enduring long after international students have graduated and even left the U.S. They return to their countries with a positive perception of the U.S., in addition to personal connections, with these programs contributing invaluably to U.S. soft power around the world at relatively little cost to U.S. taxpayers.

In fact, international students increase opportunities for U.S. students. In addition to offering connections and resources that help U.S. students develop their own intercultural competencies, international student enrollment supports a greater diversity of programs available to U.S. students. There are many graduate and undergraduate programs across the country that would not be able to maintain faculty and staffing levels without international student tuition dollars in play. According to NAFSA: Association of International Educators, “1.1 million international students at U.S. colleges and universities contributed $43.8 billion to the U.S. economy during the 2023-2024 academic year and supported more than 378,000 jobs” (NAFSA: Association of International Educators, https://www.nafsa.org/about/about-nafsa/international-students-contribute-record-breaking-level-spending-and-378000-jobs)

The rule purports to “to protect the interests of U.S. workers,” but does not account for the tremendous harm that would be done to institutions that employ the 378,000 individuals whose jobs are created or supported by international students, including mine. With fewer international students in the U.S., this would lead to colleges and universities cutting stuff, and does not even include indirect loss of income to businesses in college towns and cities where international students and students working through OPT live and work, including the landlords they pay rent to, restaurants and stores they frequent, and online businesses that they order from. The proposed rule does not contain an analysis of the harm to U.S. jobs and businesses and DHS needs to address that concern before implementing the rule.

It also does not account for the ways in which this loss of international students would make things more expensive for U.S. students, who would not have tuition-paying international students to shoulder the expenses required by colleges and universities, who would likely raise tuition for remaining students.

In summary, this proposed rule will substantially decrease the numbers of international students in the U.S., by up to 79%. This will cause harm to U.S. students, U.S. universities, U.S. university faculty and staff, and businesses supported by international students.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the extreme fee would make OPT nonexistent and harm U.S. higher education and jobs.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. Charging schools $70,000 per student for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including STEM OPT, would weaken the American economy, strain American universities, and hand our competitors talent the U.S. has already paid to train.

I work as a scientist in the biotech sector and help hire research staff. U.S.-trained international graduates are a real part of the talent pool that keeps our research moving.

It throws away an investment America has already made. International students are educated at American universities, often in labs funded by American research dollars. OPT is how that training becomes work here, in U.S. labs, startups, hospitals, and factories. A six-figure price tag on that step means the U.S. trains scientists and engineers and then sends them to Canada, the UK, Australia, Germany, and China, all of which are actively recruiting the same graduates.

It hurts the American students it claims to protect. International tuition helps fund domestic students’ seats, financial aid, and graduate programs. DHS itself acknowledges that schools may pass the cost on to international students, to all students, or to employers. Either way, the burden lands on Americans. Lower international enrollment means lost tuition revenue, and American families, taxpayers, and the college towns that depend on these institutions absorb that loss.

It is the wrong tool for protecting workers. If the concern is that OPT undercuts American wages, the answer is wage and training standards, not a flat fee. STEM OPT already requires employers to provide a formal training plan and pay comparable to similarly situated U.S. workers. A flat fee does not distinguish a well-paid PhD researcher from a low-wage placement. It simply prices out smaller schools, students without family wealth, and startups and small businesses that cannot absorb $70,000 to $100,000 per hire. That leaves the largest companies as the only ones able to compete for this talent.
It is the wrong tool for fighting fraud. If SEVP has found abuse, the right response is targeted enforcement against the specific schools and employers involved. A blanket fee punishes thousands of legitimate institutions for the conduct of a few. And DHS would not even keep the fee revenue to fund enforcement.

The analysis contradicts itself. The rule’s claimed benefits depend on substantially reducing OPT participation: fewer participants to monitor, and more jobs for U.S. workers. Yet DHS’s economic analysis assumes schools will largely keep recommending OPT. Both cannot be true. Suppose the fee shrinks the pipeline. Then the U.S. suffers the losses to innovation, growth, and university finances that DHS waves off as too speculative to weigh. Suppose instead that it doesn’t shrink the pipeline. Then the rule delivers none of its stated benefits while imposing billions of dollars in annual costs, as DHS’s own estimates acknowledge. A rule built on contradictory assumptions should not be finalized.

It weakens U.S. competitiveness where it matters most. Leadership in AI, semiconductors, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing depends on STEM talent, and international students make up a large share of U.S. STEM graduate programs. Many American companies, and the jobs they created, were founded by people who first came here as students. Pushing these graduates out just as they are ready to contribute hurts American competitiveness and national security.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fee. If DHS has specific integrity concerns, it should address them through targeted enforcement, wage and training-plan compliance, and school oversight. Those measures protect American workers without dismantling a program that keeps American-trained talent working for America.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees. DHS has not provided a convincing economic justification for either the fee amount or its consequences.

DHS estimates that the proposal would collect approximately $12.4 billion annually. However, DHS itself classifies these payments as transfers, not new economic benefits. It also acknowledges that ICE cannot retain the money and that it will not be specifically allocated to OPT oversight or immigration enforcement.

If the purpose is preventing fraud, why charge such enormous fees without directing the revenue toward fraud investigations?

More importantly, where is the cost-benefit justification? A recent analysis by the Institute for Progress (October 2026) estimates that the proposed fees could reduce annual U.S. GDP by approximately $362 billion after ten years under its central model. This is almost 29 times DHS's projected annual fee collections, although these are different economic measures and the GDP estimate concerns the longer-term impact.

DHS estimates only $4.1 billion in annualized economic costs under its primary scenario. But the agency assumes that the lost economic value of an OPT opportunity is no greater than the unpaid fee, instead of independently estimating the economic contribution of these workers. How can DHS conclude that the fees are reasonable when it has not properly quantified what the United States could lose?

Collecting money for the Treasury does not automatically make the country richer. If the fees discourage productive workers, reduce university enrollment, and damage American businesses, the U.S. could lose far more than the government collects.

I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal until it can provide a credible cost-benefit analysis that includes long-term economic losses.

As an international PhD student at an American university, I am especially concerned that DHS has underestimated how much this proposal could damage American higher education.

International students provide important revenue for universities. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy in 2024–2025, excluding people already on OPT.

For comparison, DHS expects to collect $12.4 billion annually in OPT fees. A hypothetical 30% reduction in the current economic contributions of enrolled international students would mean a loss of approximately $12.9 billion annually, already exceeding the projected fee collections. This is an illustration, not a prediction, but it shows how quickly the economic losses could become substantial.

And large enrollment declines are a real concern. A September 2026 economic study by Michael Clemens estimates that restrictions of this scale could reduce international bachelor's enrollment by 3–31% and master's enrollment by 5–58%, depending on who bears the cost. The study estimates that universities could lose hundreds of millions to over $4 billion annually in net margins.

The Institute for Progress further estimates that the proposed fees could result in approximately 46,000 fewer American students enrolling in bachelor's and master's programs each year, because universities would have less revenue to support their education.

This is not simply a problem for international students. It could mean fewer courses, less financial aid, fewer academic programs, and reduced educational opportunities for Americans.

For graduate research, the problem is even more serious. International PhD students are not simply paying tuition. They conduct research, teach courses, and contribute years of specialized work to American universities. Losing them would also damage research productivity.

DHS assumes universities can pay $70,000 for initial OPT and another $30,000 for an extension. But Clemens estimates that universities earn roughly $13,700 in annual net margins from an international master's student. Why would universities pay $100,000 for an OPT opportunity when that amount is several times the net revenue they receive from educating the student?

I ask DHS to properly account for lost tuition revenue, reduced domestic enrollment, and research productivity before imposing a policy that could seriously weaken American universities.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees will damage higher education, reduce enrollment, and cause severe economic harm.

comments.commentText: I get that this rule is to protect U.S workers and prevent fraud, but I think the fees are to high. I think the costs should be more reasonable and fair. The government needs to make sure this rule doesn't create any unnecessary problems from the people affected by it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
DHS has not provided enough evidence that OPT fraud is widespread enough to justify these fees.

DHS cites an investigation involving more than 10,000 OPT students working for highly suspect employers. However, working for a suspicious employer is not proof that the student committed fraud.

How many of these cases were confirmed? How many resulted in convictions? What proportion of all OPT participants actually engaged in fraud?

ICE reported 194,554 OPT authorizations and 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024. DHS should be able to explain the scale of confirmed fraud relative to the legitimate OPT population. Instead, the proposal relies on selected cases and investigations without establishing a reliable program-wide fraud rate.

DHS also claims that OPT fraud harms American workers. What is the measured economic damage? How many American jobs were actually lost because of confirmed OPT fraud?

Charging $70,000 does not distinguish fraudulent students from legitimate ones. It distinguishes those who can afford the fee from those who cannot.

If DHS has evidence of fraudulent employers or universities, why not investigate them directly? Why should legitimate students and American institutions pay for misconduct they did not commit?

I ask DHS to publish reliable data on the prevalence and economic impact of OPT fraud, and explain why targeted enforcement would not be more effective.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees are unjustified, penalize legitimate students, and asks DHS to reconsider.

I am an international engineering student pursuing an undergraduate degree in the United States. I oppose the proposed OPT fee increases because they would create significant barriers for international graduates seeking to contribute their education and technical skills to the U.S. workforce.

International students make substantial financial investments in American universities and contribute to the U.S. economy through tuition, research, internships, and local spending. OPT provides an important pathway for graduates to apply their education through practical work experience. A proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT application and $30,000 for a subsequent application could discourage universities from recommending eligible students, even when those students have legitimate employment opportunities. Although universities would technically pay these fees, the financial burden could ultimately reduce access to OPT and discourage prospective students from choosing American institutions.

This proposal could also undermine U.S. competitiveness in critical STEM industries, including semiconductor manufacturing, advanced materials, and engineering. These industries require specialized technical knowledge that takes years of education and practical training to develop. International graduates who have studied and trained in the United States represent an opportunity for American employers to recruit talent already familiar with U.S. educational and research environments. Making post-graduation employment pathways financially inaccessible risks pushing that talent toward countries with more accessible post-study work opportunities.

I recognize the importance of preventing fraud and maintaining the integrity of OPT. However, targeted employer verification, compliance monitoring, and enforcement against fraudulent institutions would address these concerns more directly than imposing extraordinarily high fees on universities for eligible students.

I urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure and pursue proportionate alternatives that preserve legitimate opportunities for international STEM graduates to contribute to the U.S. economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Peyman J.bin
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100). While the Department aims to address program fraud and protect domestic labor, imposing exorbitant financial barriers fundamentally misapprehends the educational necessity of OPT and severely threatens U.S. economic and technological leadership.

First, these prohibitive fees will drastically diminish the global competitiveness of the U.S. higher education system. Experiential learning is an indispensable component of modern education. By pricing educational institutions and international students out of practical training, the U.S. will deter the world's most brilliant minds, driving them to competing nations with more accessible post-graduate training frameworks. This resulting "brain drain" translates directly to billions of dollars in lost tuition, diminished local economic spending, and a critical deficit in future innovation.

Second, the premise that OPT participants inherently displace U.S. workers ignores substantial economic data. Highly skilled international students complement the domestic workforce and act as catalysts for job creation. Studies consistently show that international students and highly skilled immigrants found startups, secure research funding, and drive technological advancements that generate proportional, high-paying employment opportunities for U.S. citizens.

Third, a diverse and competitive academic environment elevates the rigor of U.S. institutions. The presence of top-tier global talent in U.S. research and labor markets pushes domestic students to maintain cutting-edge proficiency. Insulating the domestic pipeline by removing international peers from this ecosystem will inadvertently stagnate U.S. innovation and lower the overall skill ceiling of the emerging workforce.

Finally, while ensuring fair labor practices is a shared priority, creating arbitrary financial barriers to experiential learning contradicts the spirit of equal access and merit-based advancement. Rather than effectively targeting fraudulent “visa mills” or bad actors, a blanket $70,000 fee penalizes legitimate students and SEVP-certified institutions.

I urge the Department to withdraw this proposed fee structure and instead pursue targeted compliance and enforcement measures that do not jeopardize the United States' position as the premier destination for global talent.

May God bless the United States of America.

Respectfully,
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they harm U.S. economic competitiveness and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As an international PhD student at an American university, I strongly oppose this proposal, especially its impact on students who are already studying in the United States.

The U.S. has already invested enormous resources in educating and training international students. In 2024 alone, the federal government funded $64.6 billion in university research, according to the National Science Foundation. International graduate students participate in this research, receiving specialized training while contributing to American scientific progress.

Many of these students spend five or more years completing their PhDs. By the time they graduate, they have developed specialized skills, research experience, and knowledge that American universities and companies can use.

According to NSF's 2026 report, approximately 73% of international science and engineering PhD graduates from 2017–2019 were still in the U.S. in 2023, around five years after graduation. Approximately 68% of an earlier cohort remained after ten years.

This means the U.S. has historically been able to retain much of the talent it trained. These graduates continue contributing through employment, research, innovation, and taxes.

However, the proposed $70,000 OPT fee could make it impossible for many students who are about to graduate to work in the U.S. What is the point of spending years training highly skilled researchers and then creating a financial barrier that drives them away just when they are ready to contribute?

DHS proposes only a 60-day transition period. But what about students who started their degrees three, four, or five years ago? Neither they nor their universities could have reasonably planned for a $70,000 fee when they began their education. How is 60 days sufficient to address years of educational and financial commitments?

There is also a long-term concern. Even if international students continue coming to the U.S. for education, making it difficult for them to stay afterward means they will take much of their American training and expertise back to their home countries or elsewhere.

Of course, international scientific cooperation has value. But why would the U.S. deliberately give up the opportunity to retain researchers it has already trained, especially when other countries would benefit from employing them?

OPT provides a way for the U.S. to receive a more direct return on its investment in international education. Graduates can apply their knowledge in American companies and research institutions, contribute to the economy, and help train the next generation of workers.

I don't understand how encouraging these graduates to leave would benefit the United States. It seems like an unnecessary waste of American educational resources and research investment.

I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal. At the very least, students who have already enrolled in American universities under the existing OPT rules should not be subjected to these enormous new fees.

Sources:
NSF, The State of U.S. Science and Engineering 2026: https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsbsep20261/stem-talent-education-training-and-workforce-2

NSF, Higher Education R&D Expenditures FY 2024: https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsf26305

I am an international student. I am now studying for a master's degree in computer science, and I will graduate in May 2027. I am writing to share how the proposed OPT fees would affect me and many students like me.

$100,000 is simply too much. My total cost to finish my master's degree is about $80,000, including tuition and two years of living expenses. This fee would increase my total cost of studying by 130%. If this rule had existed before, I would not have applied to universities in the US at all. I chose to study CS in the US because the job opportunities here are much better than in other countries, and the tech industry here is the best in the world. But if the OPT permission is this expensive, Europe and Singapore would be a better choice.

As far as I know, many younger Chinese students I know have already given up on applying to US universities because of the uncertain visa policies. They are now looking at Hong Kong and Singapore instead, where the visa and policy support is better. Many of them are excellent students, and most of them already have offers from top tech companies.

In my group — people who go back to school after working for about 5 years, mainly to make a breakthrough in their careers — most of us are very sensitive about budget. We have to give up our full-time jobs, pay a large amount of money for school, and take the risk of a career break. So our goals are very clear, and budget is very important. This fee would be a very important factor in our decision. I believe most people like us would simply give up the US option, because with our work experience, we can also go to work in Europe directly through employer sponsorship. Studying abroad is not a must for us. The balance is very delicate, and this fee would break that balance directly.

Not only people with career goals would give up the US. PhD students would too. To be honest, a PhD salary is only barely enough to live on, with the high cost of living. I know many PhD students need to work through summer internships, using CPT or pre-completion OPT. If both of these are restricted too, PhD students can only stay in school and do research. This is negative for both industry and research, because papers also need to be used in the real world to have value. Not being able to connect with industry is a very big disadvantage. And students who can get into US PhD programs usually have other good choices too.

One more point is the uncertainty itself. Students make their plans many years in advance. A new cost like this changes the rules after students have already started their programs. Also, even if the fee is charged to schools, schools may pass the cost to students, or become less willing to support OPT. In the end, the US would lose both tuition income and talented students to other countries.

There is also the total amount. One student may need more than one OPT recommendation — for example, pre-completion OPT, post-completion OPT, and then STEM OPT. The cost would then be $70,000 plus $30,000 plus $30,000, which is $130,000 in total. That is almost two times my whole cost of a master's degree. And OPT itself does not guarantee a job. Students would have to take this very large cost and risk first, with no promise of any result.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and not put these fees in place. Thank you for reading my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is too high and will drive international students to study in other countries.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tanya Maldonado
comments.commentText:
Re: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed OPT Fee Structure – DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
I am writing to express my strong support for maintaining and protecting Optional Practical Training (OPT) opportunities for international students pursuing higher education in the US. I am deeply concerned about the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for each F-1 international student recommended for OPT. While I recognize the government's responsibility to maintain the integrity of the immigration system and address potential misuse, I believe this proposed fee structure creates significant financial barriers, places an unreasonable burden on educational institutions, and undermines the educational and workforce-development benefits that OPT provides.
OPT is an essential bridge between academic learning and professional development. Students spend years investing in their education, developing specialized knowledge, and preparing for careers. Practical training allows them to apply classroom instruction to real-world situations, strengthen technical and professional skills, learn workplace expectations, and gain meaningful experience that cannot be fully replicated in a classroom.
Restricting access to OPT through excessive institutional fees risks creating a disconnect between academic achievement and meaningful career preparation. Students should have a reasonable opportunity to demonstrate what they have learned and develop the professional competencies necessary to succeed.
The proposed $70,000 initial fee per student creates an extraordinary financial burden for educational institutions, particularly smaller colleges, community-based institutions, and schools with limited operating budgets. Institutions could experience a financial impact that disrupts budgets, limits educational resources, and forces difficult decisions about which students they can afford to support.
A student who has successfully completed a degree and meets all eligibility requirements should not lose access to an essential career-development opportunity because their educational institution cannot absorb an extraordinary federal fee. The proposed fee also creates inequity among educational institutions. Larger, well-funded universities may have greater financial flexibility, while smaller institutions and schools will be unable to participate.
International students participating in OPT bring specialized knowledge and valuable skills to American businesses, nonprofit organizations, healthcare systems, educational institutions, and other community services. OPT participants contribute to projects, help organizations address workforce needs, and bring fresh perspectives to complex challenges. Consider the contributions of international graduates working in healthcare, technology, education, business, and scientific research. Their practical experience strengthens organizations while allowing them to apply their academic preparation in ways that benefit the broader public. In smaller communities, where employers may have difficulty attracting individuals with specialized skills, international graduates can help fill important workforce gaps.
I recognize that the federal government has a responsibility to prevent fraud, ensure compliance, and protect the interests of American workers. However, measures intended to address these concerns should be proportionate, targeted, and designed to preserve legitimate educational and professional opportunities.
A $70,000 initial fee per student is not a reasonable or sustainable mechanism for ensuring program integrity. It places the financial responsibility on educational institutions regardless of the individual student's circumstances, the quality of the educational program, or the legitimacy of the proposed employment experience.
There are more balanced approaches available, including strengthened institutional oversight, improved reporting requirements, verification of employment related to a student's field of study, and reasonable administrative fees that reflect actual oversight costs. These measures could help address legitimate government concerns without effectively pricing students and educational institutions out of the program.
The proposed fee structure threatens to turn an educational opportunity into a privilege available only to institutions with substantial financial resources and students whose employers or schools can absorb extraordinary costs.
I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. Thank you for considering this public comment and for recognizing the importance of maintaining accessible, meaningful practical training opportunities for eligible international students.
Respectfully,
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed exorbitant OPT fees create financial barriers and undermine workforce benefits.

I strongly oppose the proposed fee increase for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

OPT was designed to be a mutually beneficial program for international students, U.S. employers, and the country as a whole. It allows students to apply their education in real-world settings, helps employers access talented and highly educated individuals, and contributes to the American economy and innovation.

Significantly increasing the cost of OPT would undermine the very purpose of this program. For many international students who have already invested enormous amounts of money, time, and effort into their education in the United States, additional financial burdens could make OPT simply unaffordable. Raising fees to such an extent would effectively destroy the accessibility and value of OPT.

This would not only hurt international students. Employers would lose access to valuable talent, and the United States would risk losing skilled individuals who could otherwise contribute to its economy, research, and technological advancement. Ultimately, students, employers, and the country would all suffer.

OPT should remain an opportunity that benefits everyone, not become a privilege available only to those who can afford increasingly high fees.

I sincerely urge the agency to reconsider this proposal and preserve OPT as an accessible and mutually beneficial program. I strongly oppose this fee increase.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I urge DHS to withdraw the [proposed OPT fee rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/08/2026-20660/optional-practical-training-fees), including the fees in section V.A. Requiring schools to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions, would create a severe barrier to legitimate practical training. Protecting American workers and preventing fraud are valid goals, but these fees would penalize compliant students and institutions while putting America's long-term economic competitiveness at risk.

The financial burden would reach students regardless of who formally pays. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass costs to students or employers. If students pay, access would depend heavily on family wealth and borrowing capacity. If schools absorb the fees, they could restrict recommendations, raise tuition, or divert resources from teaching, research, and student services. An institution recommending 100 students for initial OPT would face $7 million in fees. A student's eligibility and academic merit should not become secondary to the size of a university's budget.

Students already enrolled deserve particular consideration. They committed years of study, tuition, and living expenses under a framework that allowed eligible students to apply for practical training. The opportunity to seek relevant training can reasonably influence educational and financial decisions. Applying a prohibitive new condition to future recommendations for these students could strand investments they cannot recover. Section V.C should give greater weight to these reliance interests.

The policy could also harm U.S. higher education exports. Students comparing countries consider the complete educational experience, including opportunities to apply classroom learning. Restricting that experience could discourage future enrollment. [NAFSA's analysis](https://www.nafsa.org/policy-and-advocacy/policy-resources/nafsa-international-student-economic-value-tool-v2) estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024-2025. These figures cover international students as a whole and show the economic activity at risk. Lower enrollment could hurt university budgets and businesses in college communities.

The longer-term cost is lost talent and innovation. America benefits when people trained in its universities can apply their skills in its laboratories and businesses. Making practical training unaffordable could encourage graduates to take those skills to competing economies. [NBER research](https://www.nber.org/papers/w30797) finds that immigrants represented 16% of inventors but accounted for 23% of patents in its sample. Although that study examines immigrants broadly, it illustrates why restricting skilled graduates' opportunities can carry consequences beyond an individual job opening. The United States risks educating talented people and then making it harder to benefit from their work.

Protecting U.S. workers requires evidence about job creation and displacement. Skilled colleagues can help teams develop products, expand operations, and support additional jobs. Some positions may go unfilled, projects may be delayed, and employers may move work elsewhere when needed talent is unavailable. Section VII.A should assess these potential outcomes. Small businesses, startups, and research organizations could be especially disadvantaged if they are asked to reimburse costs that larger employers can more readily absorb.

A large payment is also a poor substitute for verifying compliance. Ability to pay does not establish that training is legitimate, just as inability to pay does not establish fraud. DHS should target misconduct through employer verification, risk-based audits, checks that work relates to the student's degree, and meaningful penalties for fraudulent actors. If additional oversight funding is necessary, DHS should explain its costs and evaluate proportionate fees. A broad financial barrier could exclude honest participants while leaving the underlying methods of fraud insufficiently addressed.

Before imposing these fees, DHS should provide persuasive evidence that the amounts are necessary, assess effects on enrollment and research, and compare less burdensome alternatives. Fee revenue transferred to the government should not be confused with newly created economic value. The analysis must account for lost training, forgone earnings, reduced educational exports, and losses in innovation and business growth.

I respectfully request withdrawal of the $70,000 and $30,000 fees and preservation of accessible OPT for eligible students. Strong enforcement and worker protections can coexist with practical training that strengthens American universities, businesses, and long-term prosperity.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule, arguing it creates severe financial barriers.

comments.commentText: I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule regarding substantial new fee structures for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations. As a PhD student in Petroleum Engineering developing artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twin technologies for the U.S. energy sector, I know firsthand that this proposal will inflict significant long-term damage on American innovation and global competitiveness. Navigating legal immigration into the United States is already a complex, arduous process. International students often face administrative delays and policy shifts completely beyond their control. Yet, we come to the United States with a shared commitment: to pursue rigorous education, build vital professional networks, and contribute our skills directly to the advancement of the U.S. economy. My own research focuses on creating AI-driven digital twin models capable of predicting hydraulic fracturing outcomes before a campaign takes place. Recognizing the transformative potential of this work, America’s leading oil and gas servicing firm recruited me for an internship to address a complex problem they had struggled to solve for years. Through this collaboration, a single dedicated PhD researcher provided a high-impact, cost-effective solution to modernize data intelligence and automation in energy production, work that is now drawing direct interest from major U.S. energy operators and actively supporting America’s energy security and sustainability. Investing four to five painstaking years in advanced academic research only to be blocked from applying that work in real-world environments diminishes the value of the research itself. OPT is not a commodity to be purchased; it is a mutually beneficial partnership. American industry gains immediate access to specialized, U.S.-trained technical solutions, while students gain the practical experience necessary to maximize their research impact. Imposing astronomical fees creates an insurmountable barrier for hardworking, talented researchers. It reframes post-graduation training from a collaborative economic engine into a pay-to-stay system, effectively pricing out the very talent American universities cultivate. Critics may suggest that industry partners should simply sponsor high-value researchers directly on work visas rather than relying on OPT. However, this argument overlooks the structural realities of U.S. immigration law. Work visas such as the H-1B are subject to rigid annual lotteries and start-date restrictions that make immediate post-graduation hiring legally impossible without a transitional bridge. OPT provides the necessary timeline for international talent to transition research into commercial applications while participating in visa selection cycles. Penalizing or pricing out OPT cuts off the talent pipeline before direct sponsorship can even become a legal possibility. America’s strength has historically resided in its diversity and its willingness to welcome the brightest minds from around the world to help propel the nation forward. Shutting out international researchers, particularly in critical STEM fields, harms domestic industry far more than any fee revenue could justify. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider this proposed rule from a holistic perspective and maintain accessible pathways for foreign talent to contribute to the nation’s future.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Beatrice Spolidoro
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am a Registered Architect, WELL Accredited Professional, and the Principal and CEO of Fisher ARCHitecture LLC, a small architecture firm in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, licensed in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Maryland. I also teach at Carnegie Mellon University’s School of Architecture. I oppose the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees (Sections IV.C and V.A).

My own path shows what temporary training programs are for. I came to the United States on a J-1 visa. It gave me twelve months to show an employer that I was worth investing in. I worked hard, earned that employer’s confidence, built a career here, and now run a firm that employs people and serves clients in three states. Programs like the J-1 and OPT work because merit is proven through work, and employers who value it can then choose to keep that talent here. DHS states that the fee will lead schools to recommend only “the most promising students” (Section IV.C). But a school’s willingness to pay $70,000 does not measure promise. The way to measure it is the one OPT already provides: a period of real, supervised work.

The fee does not reach the fraud DHS describes (Sections IV.A and IV.C). The rule’s evidence concerns employers: shell companies, staged worksites, and residential addresses with no employees. Yet the fee is triggered by a school’s recommendation and is not tied to any employer. A fraudulent employer pays nothing. A legitimate student at an accredited university loses access to OPT when the school cannot justify $70,000. DHS identifies roughly 10,000 students with highly suspect employers, out of more than 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. A fee charged to every participant is not a proportionate response to a problem concentrated among a small share of employers.

The fee does not fund the oversight DHS says it lacks (Section IV.C). DHS states that its compliance resources have not kept pace with the program, but the proposed fees would go to the general Treasury, not to SEVP or ICE. The rule would reduce participation without adding any capacity to find fraud among those who remain.

Impact on small firms and the architecture profession (Section VII.B.6). The small-entity analysis looks at schools but not at small employers like mine. Architecture graduates must complete supervised professional experience through NCARB’s Architectural Experience Program before they can be licensed. For international graduates of U.S. architecture programs, OPT is how they earn that experience. Architecture schools will not pay $70,000 per student to recommend graduates for entry-level design positions. As a result, the rule would effectively close OPT to the profession, even though DHS has made no finding that architecture graduates or firms are involved in fraud. Small firms like mine would lose access to talented designers whom U.S. universities have already educated.

Recommendations.

Withdraw the fee. Alternatively, reduce it to the actual cost of oversight and direct the revenue to SEVP compliance.
Target employers, not schools and students. Extend the Form I-983 training plan, E-Verify, and employer attestations to post-completion OPT, and require verification that the business and worksite exist before employment begins. DHS considered this option in Section IV.C and rejected it because of the administrative effort involved. Effort aimed at the actual source of fraud is a better trade than a flat fee charged to legitimate participants.
At minimum, exempt small employers and licensure-track professions with structured, supervised experience requirements, and include small employers in the Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis.

Conclusion. I support DHS prosecuting OPT fraud. But this rule charges the wrong party, adds no enforcement capacity, and would remove the very mechanism through which people like me proved their worth and went on to contribute to the U.S. economy. I urge DHS to withdraw the fee and adopt employer-focused safeguards.

Beatrice (Bea) Spolidoro, RA, WELL AP
Principal and CEO, Fisher ARCHitecture LLC, Pittsburgh, PA

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Strong Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees – Docket ICEB-2026-0100

I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorization. While preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives, these excessive fees would discourage talented international students from pursuing education in the United States, impose unrealistic financial burdens on universities, and undermine America's long-term economic competitiveness.

1. Unrealistic Financial Burden on Universities

The proposal assumes that American educational institutions will be willing and financially capable of paying $70,000 per student for OPT authorization. This assumption is fundamentally unrealistic.

Many American universities charge less than $70,000 in total tuition for an entire degree program. Expecting institutions to pay an additional $70,000 simply to recommend a student for practical training creates an unreasonable financial burden. Universities have little direct financial incentive to fund graduates' employment authorization after completing their education.

Consequently, many universities may stop recommending students for OPT altogether, regardless of their qualifications or potential contributions. Allowing institutions to pass these fees to students or employers does not resolve the problem; it merely transfers an unaffordable financial burden to another party.

2. Contradiction With President Trump's Vision of Attracting Global Talent

In a June 2024 interview, President Donald Trump suggested that international students graduating from American colleges should receive a Green Card along with their diploma. His remarks reflected an important principle: America benefits when it attracts, educates, and retains talented individuals from around the world.

The proposed OPT fees move in precisely the opposite direction.

Rather than encouraging highly educated graduates to contribute to America's economy, these restrictions would effectively force many talented individuals to leave after graduation.

The United States invests tremendous resources in building world-class universities and research institutions. Educating international students only to drive them toward competing countries after graduation would be economically counterproductive.

3. Threat to America's Leadership in Technology and Artificial Intelligence

America's leadership in technology, artificial intelligence, engineering, healthcare, and scientific research has been strengthened by generations of skilled immigrants and international graduates.

Foreign-born researchers, engineers, entrepreneurs, and technology professionals have helped build successful American companies, advance innovation, create employment opportunities, and strengthen the nation's global economic position.

At a time when countries are competing aggressively for leadership in artificial intelligence, semiconductor technology, advanced manufacturing, and scientific innovation, the United States should be attracting more exceptional talent, not creating barriers that push it away.

Countries such as Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom actively compete to attract international graduates. These proposed fees would make America substantially less competitive as a destination for higher education and skilled professionals.

America risks educating the next generation of innovators only to see their knowledge, skills, and entrepreneurial potential benefit competing economies.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee and instead adopt targeted, evidence-based measures to prevent fraud.

Protecting American workers and attracting global talent are not mutually exclusive goals. Skilled immigrants and international graduates have played an important role in making the United States a global leader in technology, innovation, and economic development.

President Trump's 2024 remarks recognized the value of retaining talented graduates educated in America. Policies should build upon that vision rather than undermine it.

America's greatest competitive advantage has always been its ability to attract the world's brightest minds. We should encourage these individuals to study, innovate, build businesses, and create jobs in the United States—not impose financial barriers that drive them toward competing nations.

I strongly urge DHS to reconsider this proposal in the interest of American economic growth, educational excellence, technological leadership, and long-term national competitiveness.

In our modern global society, diverse classrooms and campuses are incredible assets. They teach the next generation how to collaborate across cultures and solve complex global issues. International students bring immense talent, intelligence, and diverse perspectives to U.S. universities and the broader workforce.
