comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $100,000 fee associated with employing international graduates under Optional Practical Training (OPT). As an international graduate who has personally experienced the opportunities a U.S. education provides, I believe this proposal creates an unreasonable financial barrier that undermines OPT and makes the United States less attractive to international students.

International students make enormous financial investments in American education, paying tuition, housing, and living expenses, often without access to the same financial aid as domestic students. Many come here because of educational, technological, and professional opportunities unavailable in their home countries.

I came to the United States from Venezuela to pursue a degree in Computer Science. Around 2019, when I was finishing high school, Computer Science was not yet an established or widely accessible career path in Venezuela as it was in the United States. The educational opportunities, exposure to emerging technologies, and professional environment I wanted were simply not available to me at home. Studying in the United States opened doors that otherwise would not have been accessible.

However, obtaining a degree was only part of that opportunity. Being able to work in the United States after graduation through OPT allowed me to apply what I learned in a real professional environment. Working for a U.S. company gave me hands-on experience with technologies and systems, helped me develop professional skills, and showed me how academic knowledge translates into real-world applications. This experience was transformative for my career. Without the opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation, my decision to leave my home country and make such a substantial financial investment in a U.S. education would have been very different.

International education also has a broader purpose. Students come to the United States to acquire knowledge, skills, and professional experience that they can eventually bring back to their countries of origin. The goal is not necessarily to remain in the United States permanently, but to learn, gain exposure to advanced technologies and professional environments, and use that experience to contribute to the development of their home countries. A university education provides theoretical knowledge, but practical experience teaches students how to apply it. Restricting OPT limits this essential learning opportunity and the potential benefits those skills could bring to other countries.

For STEM graduates especially, OPT provides an essential bridge between education and employment. A $100,000 fee would discourage employers from hiring recent international graduates. From an employer’s perspective, it would be extremely difficult to justify an additional $100,000 expense for a temporary employee when equally qualified domestic candidates are available without that cost. Most employers would simply choose not to hire OPT students.

Universities are unlikely to absorb this expense, and recently graduated students cannot reasonably be expected to pay it. They have already invested thousands of dollars in their education and are only beginning their professional careers.

This proposal also risks discouraging future international students from choosing American universities. Why would someone invest years and substantial amounts of money in a U.S. education if they cannot realistically obtain the practical experience that makes that education valuable? Students will increasingly consider countries where post-graduation opportunities are more accessible.

The United States benefits from attracting international students who contribute to education, research, innovation, and the economy. I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and preserve a realistic pathway for international graduates to apply their education and contribute to the workforce.

It makes little sense to encourage international students to invest in an American education while creating financial barriers that prevent them from applying that education in the American workplace. OPT is not an unreasonable privilege; it is an opportunity to put an American education into practice, develop valuable skills, and contribute to both the United States and the wider world.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The OPT program gives corporations a substantial financial incentive to favor foreign workers over qualified American graduates. Hiring eligible OPT workers gives employers an immediate payroll tax advantage through exemptions from Social Security, Medicare, and federal unemployment taxes. Because these workers' immigration status depends on continued employment and sponsorship, they are also a captive workforce, allowing companies to suppress wages, reduce recruitment and retention costs, and demand longer hours under the implicit threat of jeopardizing their status.

This proposed rule is a long-overdue correction, but these fees don't begin to capture the full cost to Americans. That cost includes lost jobs, wage suppression, reduced career mobility, and the displacement of domestic graduates from entry-level positions. The fees should be substantially higher to reflect the actual economic and societal costs of the program.

The disadvantage starts at the beginning of Americans' careers. Foreign graduates who secure these first jobs gain professional experience, industry connections, mentorship, and references that help them advance. Those advantages compound over time, while American graduates face delayed entry into their fields, lost opportunities to build experience and professional connections, and a later start to career advancement. Even when they eventually secure positions, they are already competing against people who have had a head start building the networks and experience needed to advance.

Universities also monetize OPT by using post-graduation work authorization to attract international students willing to pay substantial tuition, effectively turning degree programs into visa pipelines at the expense of domestic graduates.

This system also undermines American students and weakens the domestic talent pipeline from within. I speak from experience as the only American student in my PhD group at a publicly funded research university. The entire group was Chinese, not Chinese American. They were decent people, but actively encouraged me to leave lectures so they could conduct them in Chinese. I was being sidelined in my own academic program while academia simultaneously claims Americans lack the interest or skills to pursue these fields.

Finally, OPT participants benefit from publicly funded infrastructure while employers avoid certain payroll contributions supporting Social Security and Medicare. Taxpayers subsidize a system in which corporations and universities capture the financial benefits while American graduates bear the competitive costs.

Corporations and universities profiting from imported foreign labor should bear its full costs rather than shifting them onto American taxpayers and domestic graduates. The proposed fees are a start, not an adequate accounting of what this system costs the country.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for every later OPT recommendation. I support action against fraud, false employment, and employer abuse, but this proposal should be withdrawn because it creates a financial screen rather than an evidence-based anti-fraud measure.

DHS documents real fraud, including shell companies and false worksites. But it does not demonstrate that a $70,000 school-paid fee for every otherwise eligible student will identify fraudulent employers, improve compliance, reduce wage suppression, or protect U.S. workers better than targeted investigations. DHS acknowledges that it cannot confidently predict the effect on participation and relies on assumptions that affected parties will “collectively cost share.” 91 FR 64574–75, 64582–89. DHS should provide data and a transparent methodology showing a causal connection between this fee and the claimed outcomes.

The amount is not cost-based. DHS selected it by comparison to H-1B fees, not by showing that OPT oversight costs $70,000 per student. It estimates $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion annually in fee transfers, yet states that the money would go to the U.S. Treasury and ICE cannot retain or use it. 91 FR 64575–76, 64583–84. The fee therefore does not fund additional site visits, investigations, adjudicators, or student support. DHS should not impose it without an itemized cost basis, explanation of legal authority, public enforcement plan, and measurable outcomes.

DHS acknowledges schools may pass the cost to F-1 students, all students, or employers. This makes access dependent on the resources of a school, employer, or student—not solely on OPT eligibility and fraud risk. Initial OPT may be recommended before a student secures employment, but the fee must be paid first. 91 FR 64569, 64575. DHS’s low-participation scenario assumes schools may fund only STEM-eligible students because $70,000 buys one year of non-STEM OPT, while $100,000 can buy up to three years of STEM OPT. 91 FR 64583–84. This would exclude otherwise eligible students in fields such as music, the arts, education, and public-interest work.

The proposal urges schools to choose only the “most promising” students but does not define “genuine educational value” or provide objective, uniform standards. 91 FR 64574–75. DHS should not force schools to create subjective rationing systems without clear criteria, written reasons, review procedures, and safeguards against inconsistent or discriminatory effects.

DHS also understates the administrative burden. It estimates 30 minutes each for a DSO and administrator per payment while admitting it cannot estimate the costs of new budgeting, accounting, audit, tracking, and recordkeeping systems. 91 FR 64585, 64590. Refunds are discretionary and nonappealable before an EAD is issued, with none available after issuance. DHS must address lost, delayed, misdelivered, defective, or government-delayed EADs and lost usable OPT time.

DHS should withdraw this proposal. If additional safeguards are needed, it should issue a new proposal based on targeted employer investigations, data verification, risk-based site visits, objective federal standards, a full equity analysis, and clear refund protections. Any future fee should be modest, cost-justified, transparently appropriated, and tied to measurable enforcement goals.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: The exorbitant fees would effectively place OPT beyond the reach of most international students and educational institutions, substantially reduce international student enrollment, undermine the educational purposes of practical training, and harm U.S. innovation, research, economic competitiveness, and American workers. Citing economic studies projecting significant declines in OPT participation and substantial losses to universities and the broader economy, I challenge DHS’s assessment of the proposal’s consequences. I also question DHS’s statutory authority to impose charges that bear no demonstrated relationship to program administration or enforcement costs, arguing that the assessments function more like deterrent taxes on lawful activity than legitimate regulatory fees. I further identify significant ambiguities concerning when and how often the fees would apply, potentially resulting in cumulative institutional liabilities exceeding $100,000 per student. Rather than imposing sweeping financial barriers, NAFSA urges DHS to strengthen existing oversight mechanisms, use SEVIS data more effectively, and pursue targeted, evidence-based enforcement measures to address demonstrated fraud and compliance concerns while preserving OPT’s educational and economic benefits.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees harm students, institutions, and the economy, and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sadie Siegel
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,I am submitting this comment to express my serious opposition to this proposed rule. American institutions of higher education are considered among the best in the world, attracting talent and genius from across the globe. Since our inception as a nation, we have celebrated this diversity of ideas and unification under shared values, rather than ties of blood and heritage that dominated nationality in the old world. American institutions thrive in a large part because of our constant integration of talent from abroad, bringing the cutting edge science, techniques, and new perspectives of thought to our universities and research institutions. These international scholars make our institutions what they are, and encourage competition to bring all scholars and researchers to a higher standard of performance. I've seen this effect first-hand through the incredible work that international students and researchers perform at my institution. During their scholarly program and/or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make enormous contributions to breakthroughs in medicine, agriculture, and energy, across the private and public sector. These breakthroughs fuel innovation in technology that help create a better nation and better world, ready to withstand the challenges of a growing population with finite resources. We must encourage and support this exchange of ideas and development of international scholars in our country, otherwise we risk losing all that development of knowledge (developed in US institutions) to other universities and companies in other countries, forcing us to actually lose the investment in international workers' skills. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. By imposing these punitive fees for international workers, all we succeed in is forcing talent out of our country, into the hands of our political and scientific competitors. To keep America and our institutions strong, we must support our international coworkers and advocate for their rights in their workplace. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. Already we are seeing so much intellectual talent--domestic and international alike--flee to other nations where they can more easily do their research without fear of sudden funding cut-backs; we need to do all we can to retain this talent and keep the standard for work high, not dependent on citizenship or nationality. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. I ask you to rescind this proposed rule, for the benefit of America's future in science.Sadie Siegelsadiersiegel@berkeley.eduBerkeley, California 94704-3219

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Cameron  Galloway
comments.commentText:
ID ICEB-2026-0100-0001
Subject: Public Comment Opposing Proposed SEVP Fee Increases for F-1 OPT Students

To Whom It May Concern,

My name is Cameron Galloway, and I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed rule that would introduce extremely high fees for international students participating in the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program.

My girlfriend is an immigrant student, and I have seen firsthand how much hard work, time, and money go into pursuing an education in the United States. International students already face significant financial challenges, and I believe this proposal would make things even harder for them.

I oppose this proposal for several reasons:

1. Unfair Financial Burden on Students

Even though the fees would technically be charged to schools, those costs could eventually be passed on to students. Fees of $70,000 to $100,000 would be impossible for most international students to afford. Many students have already spent years paying for their education and should not have to face another enormous financial barrier just to gain work experience.

2. Negative Impact on Universities

Universities would also struggle to afford these fees. Some schools may be forced to reduce or eliminate their international student programs. This would hurt universities financially and reduce opportunities for students from around the world to study in the United States.

3. Unreasonable Fees

The proposed fees seem extremely high compared to the actual administrative work involved in processing OPT applications. Government fees should be reasonable and based on the actual cost of providing a service, not set so high that students are prevented from participating.

4. Harm to the U.S. Economy

International students contribute a lot to the United States through their education, work, and skills. OPT gives students the opportunity to gain valuable experience and contribute to American businesses. Making the program unaffordable could push talented students to pursue their education and careers in other countries instead.

I believe international students should be given a fair opportunity to complete their education and gain professional experience in the United States without facing unreasonable financial barriers.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule and reconsider the impact these fees would have on international students, universities, and the U.S. economy.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

Cameron Galloway
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they place an unfair financial burden on students and universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
*Punish fraud, not talent. Protect America's future, not just its borders.*

As someone involved in American higher education and academic research, I am deeply concerned about the potential consequences of this proposal and strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees.

Preventing illegal employment and OPT abuse is essential to protecting American workers and national interests. However, imposing outrageous fees on legitimate OPT participants is an absurd, shortsighted, and frankly stupid approach.

Consider someone who has devoted nearly three decades of their life to education, left their homeland, and dedicated themselves to advancing science, engineering, or human progress. After passing competitive admissions processes and legally earning advanced degrees from American universities, including master's degrees and PhDs, their opportunity to apply their knowledge in American industries could be blocked by an enormous and unreasonable fee.

Ironically, those who respect and comply with American laws would bear the greatest burden, while individuals or employers already willing to circumvent those laws might simply continue operating outside the legal system.

Are we really proposing a system in which respecting American law becomes a disadvantage, while those willing to violate it simply ignore the restrictions?How many talented individuals would still choose America if this were the outcome awaiting them?

Apart from individuals, there will be other consequences:

1.This proposal could seriously harm America's national interests.

America has spent decades attracting and educating talented people from around the world. Imagine a highly qualified engineer, scientist, or medical researcher who could improve infrastructure, develop advanced technologies, or even save lives, but is forced to leave because they or their institution cannot afford an enormous OPT fee.

*Who exactly is America protecting by preventing qualified people from contributing to America?*

Instead of allowing these individuals to contribute to American society, we risk sending American-educated professionals to competing countries, wasting educational resources and weakening America's long-term competitiveness.

America should not invest in developing talent only to drive it away when it is ready to contribute.

2. This proposal demonstrates poor governance and undermines America's credibility.

*A government that cannot distinguish legitimate participants from those abusing the system should improve its enforcement capabilities, not make everyone pay for its shortcomings.*

If OPT fraud is the problem, investigate fraudulent employers, strengthen verification procedures, and punish actual violators. Punishing everyone because some participants break the rules is not effective regulation. It is a failure of governance.

The same principle applies to gun regulation: preventing criminal misuse should not mean indiscriminately restricting responsible, law-abiding individuals. Effective governance requires targeted enforcement, not broad restrictions that disproportionately burden those who follow the law.

Moreover, enormous fees primarily distinguish those who can afford to pay from those who cannot, rather than distinguishing qualified professionals from fraudulent participants. America should reward talent, hard work, and integrity, not merely financial privilege.

America's strength has always come from freedom, opportunity, innovation, and the ability to attract exceptional people. Driving away qualified talent through unreasonable policies risks damaging international confidence in America and weakening its long-term competitiveness.

I strongly urge to withdraw the proposed OPT fees and instead adopt targeted, evidence-based enforcement measures. We need effective enforcement, not collective punishment. We need policies that protect American workers without sacrificing American progress.

A policy that drives away talent, undermines American innovation, and punishes law-abiding participants for the misconduct of others is not protecting America. It is weakening America.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees, arguing they burden legal and talented individuals.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by imma Lin
comments.commentText:
As a graduate student at a U.S. university, I am writing to express my serious concern about the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 for initial applications and $30,000 for extensions. I strongly oppose this proposal.

Graduate education takes years of hard work, dedication, and often considerable personal sacrifice. For many international students, studying in the United States means building a life far from home, learning to navigate a different academic environment, and investing years in the hope that their education will open doors to meaningful work. OPT is an important part of that journey. It gives students a chance to put what they have learned into practice, gain professional experience, and contribute to the communities in which they have studied and lived.

I find it difficult to understand how fees this high could be justified. Most universities simply cannot afford them. And if institutions cannot pay, students will lose these opportunities regardless of how hard they have worked or what they might contribute. Years of education and research could suddenly lead to a dead end, for reasons that have little to do with a student's abilities or qualifications.

I am particularly worried about the impact on graduate students and early-career researchers. Universities depend on international scholars in countless ways, from laboratory research and teaching to collaborative projects that take years to develop. Many of these students hope to continue their work after graduation, sometimes in fields where salaries are modest but the social value of their contributions is substantial. What happens to these research communities when talented graduates can no longer afford to stay and apply their skills?

There is also a larger question about what kind of academic environment the United States wants to sustain. International students bring different experiences, perspectives, and ideas into classrooms and research communities. They make universities more intellectually vibrant. If studying here comes with the knowledge that opportunities after graduation may be effectively closed off by overwhelming fees, many prospective students may understandably choose to go elsewhere.

What troubles me most is how much uncertainty this proposal would introduce into students' lives. Graduate students already navigate demanding academic work, financial pressures, and uncertain career prospects. Adding another enormous financial barrier would make an already difficult path even harder. I worry about the people who have spent years working toward their degrees, only to discover that the opportunity to use their education is now beyond reach.

I recognize the importance of maintaining an accountable immigration system. But I cannot see how imposing fees of this magnitude would serve students, universities, or the broader public. The potential damage to research, education, and the lives of individual students deserves serious consideration.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue a more reasonable approach that preserves access to practical training while addressing legitimate administrative and compliance concerns.

Thank you for taking the time to consider my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees because they are too high and harm students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my opposition to Optional Practical Training Fees Docket (ICEB-2026-0100)

The US Department of Homeland Security has not properly investigated, evaluated, or suggested possible alternatives that would meet the goals of this proposed regulation much more efficiently with less burden to the American people, disruption to international students, bureaucracy to higher educational institutions.

In addition, as mentioned in the proposed regulation “Notably, the proposed OPT fees collected under this rule would be deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302. ICE would not maintain or use the funding collected under these OPT fee provisions promulgated pursuant to INA 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184, because the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected. While the OPT fees would be deposited into the Treasury of the United States and not specifically earmarked for ICE SEVP or immigration enforcement activities, the collection of these fees remain essential in addressing the vulnerabilities of the OPT program for the reasons explained in this section. It is also conceivable that funds collected could later be effectively appropriated by Congress to various government agencies to further enhance the integrity of the immigration system. However, the deterrent nature of the OPT fee remains regardless of whether these funds are appropriated by Congress to government agencies for this purpose.”
-The above quotation proves that the Optional Practical Training Fee is actually a tax and not a fee by the definition of tax
-The funds cannot be earmarked for resolving any of the supposed harms that DHS claims, so the collection of funds are pointless.

Since DHS has pointed out that “the deterrent nature of the OPT fee remains regardless of whether these funds are appropriated by Congress to government agencies for this purpose” but has not properly investigated alternatives that meet the same deterrent goal with less burden on the American people, international students, the government, and academic institutions:
-DHS could propose regulations that would limit the number of OPT recommendation I-20s that a school could issue
-DHS could require a physical fitness test as part of its USCIS biometric screening that an individual must pass before being considered for OPT which would deter people who would not pass the test
-DHS could require rock, paper, scissors competition as part of USCIS biometric screening, I realize this is silly, but it has the same result as the current proposal . . . to deter OPT participants
-DHS through USCIS could propose a lottery or citizenship quota/limits on the granting of OPT

DHS has not adequately explored other options if its goal is to deter individuals from applying for OPT.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly expresses opposition to the OPT fees and argues they cause unnecessary disruption and burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule “Optional Practical Training Fees” (Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01) and ask DHS to withdraw it.

The rule would charge schools $70,000 for a student’s first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one. DHS’s own analysis estimates that this would move $8.7 to $16.9 billion a year from schools to the federal government, and the notice says the money would go to the general Treasury and would not be earmarked for ICE or SEVP. A charge of that size and destination does not read as fraud prevention.

I understand the concern about fraudulent employers and visa mills. But much of the fraud DHS describes involves shell companies and phantom worksites, and those are best addressed through employer verification and targeted investigation. A flat fee on every school for every student penalizes honest students and the many schools that follow the rules. DHS also finds that the rule would significantly affect a substantial number of small entities. Many colleges could not pay this, and those that pass it on would price out students with the least money.

OPT lets international graduates apply what they learned and brings skilled new colleagues to U.S. employers and campuses.

I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal and instead pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
Optional practical training is an established component of the F-1 student program that allows eligible international students to obtain practical experience directly related to their fields of study. It connects classroom education with professional practice, supports American employers and research institutions, and contributes to the United States' ability to attract and retain international talent. The proposed fees would fundamentally undermine these objectives by making OPT financially inaccessible to most students and institutions.
Although DHS characterizes the proposed charges as fees intended to deter fraud, strengthen immigration integrity, and protect U.S. workers, the amounts bear no demonstrated relationship to the costs of administering OPT or the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) or investigating noncompliance. Instead, they would operate as substantial financial barriers to participation in a longstanding regulatory program. Available economic research indicates that the resulting reductions in OPT participation, international student enrollment, and skilled-worker retention could impose significant costs on American higher education, employers, and the broader economy.
The proposed fee will be detrimental to universities as a whole and their communities.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees create massive financial barriers that undermine the OPT program and economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
Recent economic research provides substantial reason to question DHS's assessment of the proposed rule's effects.
In September 2026, Michael A. Clemens published Taxes on International Students: Demand and Supply Response for Post-Graduation Foreign Workers on Optional Practical Training, IZA Discussion Paper No. 18933. The study examines how a $100,000 charge on OPT would affect student demand, university decisions, and employer hiring.
Clemens estimates that such a charge would reduce OPT participation substantially under different assumptions about who ultimately bears the cost. Under central scenarios in which universities bear the charge, OPT starts could decline by approximately 80 percent. The study also estimates that reduced international enrollment could cost universities hundreds of millions to more than $4 billion annually in net margins. These are model-based projections, subject to uncertainty, but they demonstrate the potential magnitude of the proposal's effects.
The Institute for Progress (IFP) similarly projects substantial reductions in OPT participation and international student enrollment. Its modeling estimates that the proposal could ultimately reduce annual U.S. gross domestic product by approximately $362 billion after ten years, with significant consequences for the domestic STEM workforce. IFP also estimates that the resulting reductions in university revenue and capacity could mean approximately 46,000 fewer American students enrolling annually in bachelor's and master's programs. The resultant decline in enrollment and negative impact on the economy stand in opposition to the goal of protecting U.S. workers.
Although these are estimates, they do raise important questions that DHS must address in assessing the proposal's economic effects. In particular, DHS should examine how students, institutions, and employers would respond to fees that in all but the most limited circumstances would exceed the financial resources available for the underlying training opportunity.
The consequences would extend beyond current F-1 students considering OPT. Prospective international students evaluate the availability of practical training, including OPT, when deciding whether to pursue an American degree. A substantial reduction in access to OPT would therefore affect enrollment decisions made years before a student becomes eligible for employment authorization.
According to research by IDP Education in August 2025, international students will adjust their educational plans based on policy changes such as access to post-study work experiences. In this research, 66 percent of the student survey respondents would go elsewhere or consider going elsewhere if post-graduation work opportunities were not available.
Assigning formal responsibility for payment to the educational institution does not eliminate the economic burden on students. Institutions may be unable or unwilling to absorb the charge, while attempts to recover it through direct reimbursement by or advance collection from the student, tuition, special charges, or employer contributions would create additional barriers. Inequitable treatment will arise between rural and urban institutions as well as well-resourced and lesser-resourced institutions. Students without substantial financial resources or access to employers willing to contribute would be particularly disadvantaged.
DHS should conduct a comprehensive assessment of these behavioral responses, including effects on prospective enrollment, student retention, institutional finances, and the distribution of optional practical training opportunities across institutions and academic disciplines.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee harms students, universities, and GDP.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
OPT is an important part of the educational experience for many international students. Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10), eligible students may apply to engage in OPT that includes pre-completion training, post-completion training, and, for eligible graduates in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields, a 24-month extension of post-completion OPT.
These opportunities serve related but distinct educational purposes to classroom instruction. Pre-completion OPT allows students to apply academic knowledge while pursuing their degrees. Post-completion OPT provides practical experience to continue training and apply what was learned in the classroom following graduation. The STEM extension allows eligible graduates to obtain additional structured training under employer training plans and reporting requirements.
The proposed fees would apply to any OPT recommendations, including pre-completion OPT, rather than exclusively to post-graduation employment, so even students seeking relatively brief summer training opportunities could face the same initial $70,000 institutional fee as students seeking a full year of post-completion OPT.
This structure creates an especially severe disincentive for optional short-term internships. A student seeking three months of pre-completion OPT could trigger a $70,000 fee, followed by another $30,000 fee when seeking post-completion OPT. Since the proposal directs schools to pay these fees, schools will likely respond by declining to recommend otherwise eligible students for training, regardless of the educational value of the experience. It is not realistic to expect any party, higher education institutions, students, or employers, to absorb these exorbitant fees.
DHS should explain how these consequences are consistent with the educational purposes of OPT and why existing oversight mechanisms are inadequate to address the agency's stated concerns.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees create severe disincentives and burdens for students and schools.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tianyi Xiang
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

Dear DHS Officials:

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i). My experience as an international doctoral student illustrates how these fees could interrupt specialized training and discourage U.S.-trained researchers from contributing to the United States.

I am a PhD candidate in Pharmaceutics at the University of Minnesota, where I also earned my master’s degree. My research focuses on understanding and improving pharmaceutical tablet manufacturing, including how to prevent material from sticking to manufacturing equipment and how to produce tablets with reliable mechanical strength. I have published peer-reviewed research and received academic fellowships and research awards.

My doctoral training has also included research internships at Eli Lilly and Merck. One internship was supported through the National Science Foundation’s INTERN program. These experiences have allowed me to apply academic research to practical pharmaceutical development problems while learning from scientists working in the U.S. pharmaceutical industry. I submit this comment in my personal capacity and do not speak for these organizations.

As I approach graduation, OPT represents an important opportunity to continue training in my field and apply the specialized knowledge I have developed through years of graduate education. Pharmaceutical research requires experience with complex materials, manufacturing processes, and analytical methods. Developing these skills takes sustained training, and the transition from doctoral research to supervised professional practice is an important part of that development.

Although the proposal requires educational institutions to pay these fees, students’ access to OPT would depend on whether their institutions could afford and agree to make those payments. I cannot assume that my university would be able to pay tens of thousands of dollars for my recommendation. My concern is that qualified students could lose access to practical training because of an institution’s budget rather than any deficiency in their education, proposed training, or compliance with immigration requirements.

The uncertainty also affects planning. Students make decisions about graduate education and research careers over many years. A substantial new financial barrier near graduation could disrupt those plans after students and their universities have already devoted considerable time and resources to their education. Employers seeking to train graduates in specialized fields could also face uncertainty about whether those graduates would be able to participate.

I support efforts to prevent fraud and ensure that OPT provides legitimate training related to a student’s degree. I respectfully ask DHS to pursue targeted oversight and enforcement rather than fees that could prevent otherwise eligible students from participating.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. If DHS proceeds with changes, I ask it to consider substantially lower fees supported by documented administrative costs, meaningful exemptions or waivers, and transition protections for currently enrolled students, including their subsequent STEM OPT training.

I hope to continue contributing to pharmaceutical research and the development of reliable medicines in the United States. Please consider the effects of this proposal on students like me and on the universities and research organizations that have helped train us.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Tianyi Xiang
PhD Candidate in Pharmaceutics
University of Minnesota
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they would interrupt specialized training.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 10 of 10: Reliance and transition.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposal and its treatment of existing students' reliance interests. Section V.C proposes a 60-day implementation period. Section VI places substantial weight on the fact that OPT is temporary and not guaranteed. Neither point establishes that people can readily undo educational and financial decisions made over several years.

Acknowledging reliance does not require promising employment, permanent residence, or approval of every application. It requires examining the real disruption when an otherwise eligible person encounters a new financial barrier after enrolling, paying tuition, and progressing toward a degree. Schools and employers also need time to revise budgets and training plans.

It is deeply unfair to treat those sunk commitments as insignificant simply because practical training was never an unconditional entitlement. DHS should analyze current cohorts separately and explain why less disruptive alternatives would not meet legitimate oversight goals.

My primary request is withdrawal of the proposed fees. If DHS nevertheless proceeds, it should at least protect students already enrolled before implementation and provide a substantially longer, clearly defined transition. That fallback does not reduce my strong opposition to the proposal itself.

Reference: NPRM, sections V.C and VI.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and requests their withdrawal due to unfair reliance interests.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
Ambiguity surrounding the subsequent $30,000 fee further illustrates the proposal's deficiencies.
A. DHS must clarify whether the $30,000 OPT fee applies only to the first subsequent OPT recommendation or to every subsequent recommendation.
Under the proposal, the initial $70,000 fee would be triggered by the first OPT recommendation for a particular student by a DSO at a particular SEVP-certified school following the final rule's effective date. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1).
Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2) then provides that a school that has paid the initial $70,000 fee for a particular student must pay $30,000 before "a subsequent recommendation" for that student for whom it has already paid the initial $70,000 fee.
But proposed 8 CFR 214.12(i)(3) then says that “any subsequent DSO recommendations for OPT issued for any F-1 student who has previously participated in OPT, and for which the $70,000 OPT fee has been paid, will be subject to the subsequent OPT fee of $30,000 per alien.”
Using the singular “a subsequent recommendation” and the plural “any subsequent DSO recommendations” in the same paragraph (i) creates ambiguity and uncertainty as to whether DHS intends a single $30,000 payment for the first subsequent OPT recommendation or $30,000 payments for each subsequent recommendation.
Two interpretations are possible.
Under the first interpretation, a particular school would pay $70,000 for the student's initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for the first subsequent recommendation, with no further fee for additional OPT recommendations for that student at that school. Total liability would be limited to $100,000. This interpretation appears consistent with a notice distributed on October 8, 2026 by SEVP to DSOs, which describes a $70,000 initial charge and a $30,000 charge for the “second year” of practicaltraining, with no additional fees in subsequent years. DHS also uses a $100,000 total in portions of its economic analysis included in the proposed rule.
Under the second interpretation, the school would pay $70,000 for the initial recommendation and an additional $30,000 each time it subsequently recommends OPT for the same student. Total liability could therefore exceed $100,000. Statements in the proposed rule preamble support this second interpretation. The preamble summary describes the subsequent fee as applicable to "any subsequent OPT." Elsewhere in the preamble DHS expressly describes the proposed charge as applying "each time there is a subsequent OPT recommendation for that student." These statements are difficult to reconcile with a single second-payment interpretation.
The distinction is illustrated by the following examples.
Example. Consider a Master of Engineering student who seeks three months of pre-completion OPT for a summer internship, followed by nine months of post-completion OPT and a subsequent 24-month STEM OPT extension.
•
This student's school would first pay $70,000 before recommending the pre-completion OPT. It would then pay $30,000 before recommending post-completion OPT.
•
If DHS intends a maximum of one subsequent fee, the school would owe no additional amount when recommending the STEM extension, and total liability would be $100,000.
•
If DHS intends to assess the fee for each subsequent recommendation, the STEM extension would trigger another $30,000 payment, bringing total liability to $130,000.
Example. The same ambiguity could also affect students pursuing post-completion OPT following successively higher degrees at the same school, for example, a student who obtains a bachelor’s degree, then a master’s degree, and then a doctoral degree at the same school, each followed by a period of post-completion OPT permitted.
•
Under the first interpretation ($100,000 limit), the school would have to pay a total of $100,000 for the three OPT recommendations ($70,000 for the first, $30,000 for the second, and $0 for the third).
•
Under the second interpretation, though, the school would have to pay a total of $130,000 ($70,000 for the first, $30,000 for the second, and $30,000 for the third).
DHS must clarify this in any final regulatory wording.
comments.reason: Comment highlights major ambiguities and deficiencies in the proposed OPT fee structure.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
International students and graduates contribute substantially to the nation's scientific and technological capacity. OPT provides an important bridge between American higher education and the U.S. workforce, enabling employers to recruit individuals already educated at U.S. institutions.
The Institute of International Education (IIE)’s Fall 2025 International Student Enrollment Snapshot Survey posits institutions will continue to place significant value on the OPT program, with 76 percent of institutions responding it was important for recruiting international students, and 92 percent reporting that, without OPT, many international students would likely choose to study in other countries.
Research from Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology illustrates the importance of international educational pathways to American innovation. Its September 2026 report, How Global Talent Pathways Shape U.S. STEM Award Achievement, examines 550 recipients of major STEM awards between 2014 and 2024. Of the 471 awardees who had studied, worked, or lived in the United States, 47 percent were foreign-born. Among foreign-born U.S. awardees whose initial educational or professional activity could be identified, approximately two-thirds first came to the United States as students.
Although these findings do not establish that OPT itself caused these achievements, they demonstrate the importance of maintaining educational and early-career pathways through which international talent contributes to American science and technology.
The OPT Observatory, developed by IFP using detailed SEVIS microdata obtained through the Freedom of Information Act, provides further evidence of the importance and breadth of these pathways. Its data document international student participation across institutions, degree levels, academic fields, and employment sectors. These data, together with DHS's own SEVIS by the Numbers reports, provide a substantial empirical foundation for examining the proposal's effects on different student populations and institutions. DHS should use these resources to evaluate whether the proposal would disproportionately affect STEM graduates, smaller institutions, rural institutions, regional universities, and employers that lack the financial resources to support excessively large fees.
The effects would also extend to American workers. International students attending U.S. colleges and universities contribute tuition revenue that supports academic programs, faculty positions, research infrastructure, and educational opportunities for domestic students. International graduates also contribute specialized skills to businesses, laboratories, and research teams. Reducing these contributions could undermine, rather than advance, the interests of U.S. workers.
A key finding of The 2026 US Talent Report, Benchmarking America’s STEM Pipeline Amid the Great Talent Competition, produced by the Hoover Institution and the Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence at Stanford University and written by Emerson Johnston and Amy Zegart, is that “[i]nternational talent powers American research and industry after graduation. International graduates constitute majorities of postdoctoral researchers in several STEM fields, work in STEM at higher rates than US-born graduates with comparable degrees, and have founded or co-founded a large share of the country’s leading AI firms.” (Ibid, page 7).
The report also found that while the United States has abruptly changing policies that create uncertainty about opportunities after graduation, “Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, Germany, and Singapore have moved in the opposite direction, offering skilled migrants clearer criteria, faster decisions, or more direct routes to permanent residence.” (Ibid, page 159). Considering competition among countries, the researchers state, “America is no longer competing only on the quality of its universities and laboratories. It is competing on the predictability of the path that follows them.” (Ibid, page 159).
This change in demand is evidenced in the most recent Global Enrolment Benchmark survey (January to March 2026 Intake) that indicates sharp declines in international enrollments in the U.S. and Canada while many European and Asian institutions reported growth. Restrictive government policies and visa restrictions were cited as the biggest negative impact for those institutions experiencing enrollment declines.
Imposing charges of this magnitude would create a substantial competitive disadvantage for American institutions and employers, particularly when other countries offer more accessible post-study work opportunities.
comments.reason: The commenter emphasizes the value of OPT and international talent, arguing against changes that harm pathways.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
DHS identifies fraud prevention, immigration system integrity, protection of U.S. workers, and the costs of OPT investigations as principal justifications for the proposal. These are legitimate areas of governmental concern. They do not, however, establish that fees of $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary, appropriate, or authorized.
The proposal does not adequately demonstrate why these particular amounts are required. Nor does it establish that charging educational institutions extraordinary amounts for making otherwise permissible OPT recommendations is a proportionate response to identified compliance problems.
The distinction between a regulatory fee and a revenue-raising or deterrent charge is particularly important. Congress has established statutory frameworks governing immigration-related fees, including 8 U.S.C. 1356(m) and 8 U.S.C. 1372. DHS must identify statutory authority supporting the charges it proposes and explain how that authority permits fees designed to discourage participation rather than recover the costs of providing governmental services or administering a program.
General authority to administer and enforce immigration laws does not, without further explanation, resolve whether DHS may impose charges of this magnitude for the purpose of changing institutional, student, and employer behavior.
DHS should provide a transparent accounting of the governmental costs that the proposed fees are intended to recover, including the extent to which those costs are attributable to individual OPT recommendations. It should also distinguish administrative cost recovery from any intended deterrent effect.
If the objective is to encourage greater institutional review of OPT recommendations, DHS should explain why targeted documentation requirements, enhanced compliance reviews, and enforcement against identified violations would be insufficient. If the objective is to deter fraudulent employment arrangements, DHS should demonstrate how imposing the same substantial charges on compliant institutions and students would more effectively accomplish that purpose than targeted investigations and enforcement.
The proposal also warrants closer examination under the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (5 U.S.C. 601-612, as amended) and the principles governing reasoned agency decision-making. Its effects on small educational institutions, students, employers, and other affected entities cannot be adequately evaluated without accounting for the likelihood that institutions will decline to make OPT recommendations rather than incur the proposed fees.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed OPT fees are disproportionate, lack statutory justification, and are excessively high.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
DHS says in the proposed rule preamble that its authority to impose the proposed OPT fees rests on "multiple, independent, and mutually reinforcing statutory sources." However, the authorities identified concern DHS's general responsibility to administer immigration laws, regulate nonimmigrant status and employment, and oversee educational institutions certified by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) and tracked in SEVIS. [DHS states in the preamble, “The Secretary has authority under Section 102 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA) (Pub. L. 107-296, 116 Stat. 2135), 6 U.S.C. 112,and section 103(a)(1) and (3) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1), (3), to administer and enforce the immigration and naturalization laws of the United States, to include the issuance of regulations that he deems necessary. Section 214(a) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), authorizes the Secretary to prescribe the time and conditions of admission of any alien as a nonimmigrant.”] None of these provisions expressly authorizes DHS to impose the extraordinary charges contemplated by this proposal. DHS's reliance on these provisions raises substantial questions about whether it is attempting to exercise taxing authority that Congress has not delegated.
DHS's proposal to deposit OPT “fees” into the general Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302, rather than retain or earmark them for SEVP administration or immigration enforcement, raises further questions not only about their characterization as regulatory fees. DHS acknowledges that ICE would not receive the revenue and that any subsequent appropriation for immigration enforcement would depend on congressional action. And so there is no assurance that the substantial amounts DHS seeks to collect from educational institutions would be used to address the very program vulnerabilities DHS invokes to justify the charges. DHS dismisses this concern by asserting that the charges would retain their deterrent effect regardless of whether Congress ever appropriates the revenue for immigration enforcement. Although depositing revenue into the general Treasury does not itself invalidate a regulatory fee, the absence of any dedicated use for the funds, coupled with the lack of a demonstrated relationship between the amounts charged and the costs of administering or enforcing OPT requirements, strengthens the argument that these assessments function primarily as deterrent taxes on lawful activity rather than fees to recover costs for governmental services. DHS has not identified clear statutory authority to impose charges of this nature.
DHS identifies deterring fraud and other misconduct involving OPT as a principal justification for the proposed fees yet offers no systematic evidence establishing the prevalence of such misconduct, relying instead on anecdotal accounts. Rather than targeting demonstrated abuses, the proposal would arbitrarily impose substantial charges on all institutions and students seeking to participate in a longstanding, lawful immigration benefit, regardless of any evidence of wrongdoing. In this respect, the proposed charges more closely resemble an arbitrary excise tax designed to discourage otherwise lawful activity than a regulatory fee intended to recover the costs of administering or enforcing the program.
The power to issue regulations necessary to administer a statutory program cannot be interpreted as authority to impose taxes or high fees on participation in that program. Broad regulatory discretion is not a substitute for the clear congressional delegation required to exercise Congress's taxing power.
DHS also relies on INA section 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), which authorizes the Secretary to generally prescribe the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission, as well as other provisions granting DHS the authority to implement programs. But the authority to prescribe conditions governing optional practical training does not necessarily include authority to tax institutions or charge them exorbitant fees for making otherwise lawful OPT recommendations.
As mentioned above, the proposed charges exhibit characteristics that support their treatment as taxes rather than ordinary regulatory fees. They would apply to otherwise lawful activity, would not depend on a finding of misconduct (as would a fine), and do not correspond to the governmental cost of processing an OPT recommendation or administering the associated regulatory requirements. DHS instead emphasizes their intended deterrent effects, which, although ostensibly targeting bad behavior, will instead indiscriminately deter all use of the OPT benefit.
comments.reason: The commenter argues DHS lacks statutory authority to impose such high OPT fees, effectively acting as an undelegated tax.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
DHS tangentially references section 641 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, 8 U.S.C. 1372, which authorizes the collection of information concerning nonimmigrant students and exchange visitors and provides a statutory framework for SEVIS. This statute contains specific provisions at 8 U.S.C. 1372(e) addressing fees associated with the student and exchange visitor monitoring program. Those provisions demonstrate that Congress knows how to authorize fees for the administration of this program and to define their purposes. DHS does not explain how the proposed OPT charges, which are designed in substantial part to deter participation and address broader immigration policy concerns, fall within that specific statutory fee framework. Nor does DHS establish that the proposed amounts are related to the costs Congress authorized the agency to recover. The existence of express, purpose-limited fee authority weighs against interpreting more general immigration provisions as granting an additional, unrestricted power to impose exorbitant monetary assessments.
Absent a persuasive statutory justification, the proposed charges would exceed DHS's delegated authority. Therefore, DHS should withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees exceed DHS's statutory authority and requests that the proposal be withdrawn.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my opposition to Optional Practical Training Fees Docket (ICEB-2026-0100)

The proposed regulation is inadequate and contradicts regulation that it is not attempting to change.

Historically, SEVP has taken the position that institutions may not charge students a separate fee for processing OPT recommendation I-20s (or other SEVIS authorizations), as eligible students are entitled to those immigration benefits and schools certify to SEVP that they possess the personnel, facilities, and financial resources necessary to administer SEVIS and meet regulatory obligations. This proposal appears carefully drafted to avoid directly addressing whether institutions could recover the new OPT fee through a student-specific charge. In addition, SEVP has continually emphasized that I-20s are the property of DHS and not the institution and that school DSOs are in the position of reporting information. Through issuance of the OPT recommendation I-20 the DSO is reporting certain objective information such as the student is completing their studies, the student met the 1 year of studies requirement, the student submitted for I-983.

SEVP field representatives continue to remind schools that they “cannot hold I-20s hostage” to require students to pay bills or fees and MUST issue OPT recommendation I-20s to students who meet the criteria. This proposed regulation does not change those portions of current regulation.

Lastly, this proposed regulation does not change the standards for which a student is entitled to the OPT other than including a receipt for the school payment. Nor does the proposed regulation include any mention of institutions granting OPT recommendation I-20s based on merit. The only addition would be submission of receipt for payment of the “OPT fee”.

Thus, DHS is unable to provide any documentation of merit as the standards for “selection” of who is eligible for OPT recommend I-20 is not changed.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states opposition to the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
B. DHS must clarify whether the payment history of a particular school for a particular student persists after a break in study when the student returns in the future to pursue additional study at the same school.
Example. It is possible that a student pursues OPT following completion of a degree at one school, returns home for more than a temporary absence (or otherwise has a lawful break in the continuity of F-1 status as in a change of status to H-1B), and then returns to the same school to pursue another degree at a higher educational level. For example, a student completes a bachelor’s degree at a school, does 12 months of post-completion OPT, returns home to work in that country (let us say for two years in this example), and then returns to the same school to pursue a master’s degree, finishes the master’s degree, and then plans for a period of 12 months of post-completion OPT following the master’s.
•
In this case, the school would have paid a $70,000 fee before making the OPT recommendation following the bachelor’s degree.
•
If the payment history persists, the school would pay a $30,000 fee before making the OPT recommendation following the master’s degree.
•
If the payment history does not persist following a lawful break in F status, the school would have to pay another $70,000 fee for the same student.
DHS must clarify this in any final regulatory wording.
C. DHS Must Clarify How the Rule Would Work When OPT is Recommended by Different Schools.
There is also ambiguity as to whether payment history and obligation is school-specific or follows the student across institutions, although the regulatory wording is best interpreted as OPT fee payment liability being school-specific. For example, consider this scenario under that interpretation:
•
Student at School A wants to apply for 12 months of OPT eligibility as post-completion OPT, following completion of the master’s degree.
o
Before recommending the post-completion OPT, the DSO at School A must ensure that School A has paid the $70,000 amount, since this is the first OPT being recommended for that student by that school.
•
After completing the 12 months of OPT based on the master’s degree earned at School A, student transfers to School B for a PhD in engineering.
•
Student wants to apply for 12 months of OPT eligibility as post-completion OPT, following completion of the PhD degree at School B.
o
Before recommending the post-completion OPT, the DSO at School B must ensure that School B has paid the $70,000 amount, since this is the first OPT being recommended for that student by that school (i.e., a different school).
•
Student wants to apply for STEM OPT
o
Before recommending the STEM OPT, the DSO at School B must ensure that School B has paid the $30,000 amount.
In the event that DHS proceeds with any form of this proposed rule, DHS must clarify these fee payment ambiguities in the regulatory wording. The proposal's financial analysis cannot be considered reliable unless DHS clearly identifies the circumstances triggering each fee and models the resulting liabilities. An analysis based on a fee maximum would understate costs if institutions could incur additional charges.
comments.reason: The comment asks for administrative clarification on fee application rules without expressing support or opposition.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
DHS can address legitimate concerns about fraud, program integrity, and worker protections without imposing financial barriers that would effectively eliminate OPT opportunities for large numbers of otherwise eligible students.
The existing regulatory framework and SEVIS already provide DHS with substantial tools and information to identify potential fraud and noncompliance in OPT. DSOs must determine student eligibility and enter OPT recommendations in SEVIS, while students must report changes in employment and other required information. For STEM OPT, additional safeguards include employer participation in E-Verify, individualized Form I-983 training plans, employer attestations, periodic student evaluations, reportingobligations, and DHS authority to conduct employer site visits. SEVIS maintains information on students' academic programs, immigration status, OPT authorization periods, and reported employment, enabling DHS to identify potentially suspicious patterns across students, employers, and institutions. These existing data and oversight mechanisms provide a substantial foundation for targeted, risk-based compliance reviews and enforcement against actual misconduct, without imposing extraordinary fees on institutions making otherwise lawful OPT recommendations.
Potential alternatives include improved use of SEVIS data to identify unusual employment patterns, risk-based compliance reviews, clearer institutional reporting requirements, enhanced enforcement against fraudulent employers or institutions, and additional guidance concerning DSO responsibilities. Any proposed administrative fees should be supported by a documented cost analysis and proportionate to the governmental services or regulatory activities involved.
DHS should also meaningfully evaluate the effects of the proposal on students already enrolled in U.S. institutions who made educational and financial decisions in reliance on the availability of OPT. Even prospective application of the proposed fees would substantially disrupt the expectations of these students and their institutions.
The economic studies and administrative data identified in these comments provide a basis for a more comprehensive assessment of the proposal's costs and alternatives. DHS should incorporate these resources into its analysis, address their findings, and provide the public with an adequate opportunity to evaluate any substantially revised proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees create financial barriers that eliminate OPT opportunities and suggests alternatives.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
The proposed OPT fees that function as a tax would impose extraordinary costs on American educational institutions and threaten an established pathway through which international students gain practical experience and contribute to the U.S. economy. DHS has not adequately demonstrated that the proposed amounts are necessary to achieve its stated objectives, that the fees are supported by the statutory authorities cited, or that their likely consequences for students, institutions, employers, and American workers have been fully evaluated. Existing regulatory mechanisms already provide for school certification, DSO oversight, student and school reporting, employer obligations under STEM OPT, and investigations of suspected violations. DHS should instead better assess whether these mechanisms can be strengthened through more targeted measures. The ambiguity surrounding the subsequent $30,000 fee further illustrates the proposal's deficiencies.
For these reasons, we urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that address identifiable compliance concerns while preserving the educational and economic benefits of OPT.
