comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
DHS docket # CEB-2026-0100

This is a deeply flawed proposal, and I urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety.

It is hard to find data to confirm the level of fraud in OPT as news reports quote DHS sources to provide their numbers, and DHS doesn’t say where these numbers come from. We have no way to verify their accuracy. Sharing a YouTube clip where someone makes a comment or states a number doesn’t make it true. Is there fraud in OPT? Yes, probably. But when imposing something as drastic as an $100,000 fee it’s important to ask how much fraud is really there to be found. DHS really needs to justify a change of this magnitude.

One recent article from The National Law Review from May 2026 (https://natlawreview.com/article/opt-under-scrutiny-what-increased-ice-enforcement-means-employers) says that ICE claims the number is potentially around 10,000 cases. No time frame is given for this number: is it per year, or over the last couple of years? Decades? It is unclear. According to DHS’s own data, as cited by the Center for Immigration Studies (https://cis.org/Jacobs/DHSs-Crackdown-OPT-Fraud-Will-Not-Fix-Programs-Biggest-Problems), 505,590 international students participated in OPT and STEM OPT in FY 2024.

Imagining for a moment that the number of cases quoted is 10,000 cases per year, this gives a fraud rate of 1.9%. That means that 98.1% of OPT students are NOT fraudulent.

Therefore, 98% of OPT holders are working legitimately. They pay taxes, consume food and entertainment, pay rent to landlords etc. They contribute to our communities and to the US economy. This ridiculous plan to penalize everyone for 1.9% of wrongdoers seems like a great example of cutting your nose to spite your face and will do nothing but hurt American businesses and communities.

The same article from The National Law Review referenced above indicates that the fraud on the part of employers (note: not universities) was uncovered by DHS investigations. DHS already reviews every single OPT and STEM OPT application for fraud, and clearly occasionally finds something. The current processes work. Students must report employment through SEVIS, so mechanisms to detect fraud already exist: DHS is successfully using them already.

Also, by DHS’s own admission, the funds raised through these fees will not actually go to fraud prevention but to a miscellaneous fund at the US Treasury. By confirming that they will not actually receive the funds raised, DHS is confirming that they don’t need the money to fight fraud. The logic doesn’t hold together at all: “we need funds to fight fraud, but we wont actually use the funds to fight fraud”. Saying funds raised will be used for one thing and then not actually using them for that thing: isn’t that committing fraud?

If DHS is so convinced that the OPT process is comprehensively fraudulent, surely it would make more sense to punish the employers who hire fraudulently, not universities? If DHS was serious about looking for more fraud there would be investment in site visits, increased reporting requirements, additional and updated processes etc. Not a ridiculous fee. Financial payments don’t verify anything. Any fraud that takes place is at the employer level per DHS own data. It is not perpetuated by universities or DSOs, so how will making a university pay an exorbitant fee prevent fraud from taking place?

This fee will not possibly achieve its stated goal of stopping fraud. It is a deeply flawed proposal and should be entirely withdrawn.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee is drastically high and urges DHS to withdraw it in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed rule under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, which would impose a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. As an international student at the University of Southern California (USC), I find this proposal deeply unfair, economically damaging, and contradictory to the values that make American higher education exceptional. International students make enormous financial, academic, and personal sacrifices to study in the United States. We pay substantial tuition, contribute to local economies, support American businesses, and invest years pursuing an American education. We choose institutions like USC for their academic excellence and opportunities to apply our education professionally. Imposing a $70,000 fee would make OPT inaccessible for countless hardworking, law-abiding students. First, this proposal punishes legitimate students for the misconduct of a minority. DHS cites fraud and abuse as justification. Fraud should be prosecuted, but imposing enormous financial burdens on every international student fails to distinguish between fraudulent participants and those who follow immigration rules and earn legitimate degrees. A student's wealth or their university's willingness to pay $70,000 does not determine academic merit, professional qualifications, or immigration compliance. This proposal risks transforming OPT into a privilege reserved for the wealthy. Second, the proposal disregards students already enrolled in American universities. Many of us committed to studying in the United States years before this proposal appeared. Our families invested significantly in tuition, housing, and living expenses with an understanding of the opportunities available, including OPT. Although the rule would apply prospectively, it would still affect enrolled students without an OPT recommendation. We cannot simply reverse years of financial commitments or educational decisions. The proposal inadequately addresses these legitimate reliance interests. Third, this rule threatens America's competitiveness in attracting global talent. Universities like USC attract ambitious students, researchers, and innovators worldwide. If post-graduation training becomes financially inaccessible, talented students will increasingly consider other countries. American universities could experience declining international enrollment, reduced tuition revenue, and diminished contributions to research and innovation. Local economies would also suffer. Fourth, the proposal could harm American employers, particularly startups, small businesses, and nonprofit organizations. OPT allows employers to recruit graduates educated at American institutions who possess valuable skills. Requiring a $70,000 payment, potentially passed to employers or students, creates an enormous barrier to accessing this talent. Professional opportunities should depend on qualifications and merit rather than financial capacity. Fifth, these fees are disproportionate and lack a convincing connection to fraud prevention. Making OPT prohibitively expensive does not necessarily make it more secure. Financial barriers cannot replace employer verification, targeted investigations, compliance audits, and enforcement against fraudulent organizations. The proposal acknowledges that collected fees would enter the U.S. Treasury rather than be specifically allocated to OPT enforcement. DHS should prioritize stronger employer verification, penalties for fraudulent organizations, and investigations of suspicious employment arrangements instead of imposing billions of dollars in financial burdens. Finally, the proposal risks creating an inequitable system. A talented international graduate from a modest financial background deserves the same opportunity to gain practical experience as someone from a wealthy family. Financial capacity should never replace academic achievement, professional qualifications, or lawful compliance. I support protecting American workers and strengthening immigration integrity. However, these objectives should be pursued through proportionate, evidence-based policies rather than sweeping financial restrictions. As a USC student, I see international students contributing to classrooms, campus organizations, research, local businesses, and the broader Los Angeles community. We came to the United States to learn, develop our skills, and contribute meaningfully. Policies like this undermine the opportunities that attracted us here. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and pursue targeted reforms addressing genuine fraud without unfairly penalizing law-abiding students. The United States should continue attracting global talent, not discourage it through financial barriers that undermine its educational excellence. Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

I am a postdoctoral researcher in theoretical physics working in the United States under F-1 post-completion OPT, and I expect to apply for a STEM OPT extension in 2027. I came to the United States for scientific training and research and made long-term educational and professional decisions based on the existing F-1 and OPT framework.

My principal concern is that the proposed fee is not well targeted to the fraud and program-integrity problems DHS identifies.

DHS states that the fee is intended in substantial part to deter participation, and the collected funds would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury rather than retained by ICE specifically to increase OPT enforcement. A fee of $70,000 therefore does not appear closely connected to the administrative cost of reviewing an individual student's participation.

If fraud is the concern, more targeted approaches are available: increased audits of employers or institutions presenting compliance risks, expanded site visits, stronger enforcement of existing STEM OPT training-plan requirements, or fees reasonably connected to the cost of additional oversight. These measures would address misconduct more directly without imposing the same extraordinary cost on legitimate participants.

The proposal may also have unintended consequences for U.S. scientific research. Many STEM graduates work in universities, research institutes, nonprofit organizations, start-ups, and laboratories that do not have the resources of large corporations. A cost of tens of thousands of dollars per researcher could make continued employment impossible even when the training arrangement is legitimate and scientifically valuable.

DHS itself acknowledges substantial uncertainty about how institutions, students, and employers will respond to these fees. That uncertainty is important. Before imposing fees large enough to change whether institutions participate in OPT at all, DHS should more fully evaluate their effects on universities, scientific research, small employers, and the ability of the United States to attract and retain international STEM talent.

I am also particularly concerned about current F-1 students and OPT participants. People already in the United States have spent years pursuing degrees, conducting research, paying tuition and living expenses, and planning careers under the existing OPT framework. For a person already participating in post-completion OPT, introducing a fee of this magnitude before a planned STEM extension changes the economic conditions of a decision that was made years earlier.

If DHS nevertheless proceeds with a new fee, I strongly urge it to grandfather students who are already in F-1 status, and particularly those who are already participating in post-completion OPT and later seek a STEM OPT extension.

I support reasonable enforcement measures to protect the integrity of OPT. But those measures should target actual misconduct and compliance risk rather than use an exceptionally large uniform financial barrier as a proxy for enforcement.

I therefore respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fee structure. Alternatively, DHS should adopt substantially lower, cost-justified fees, more targeted enforcement mechanisms, and meaningful grandfathering protections for current F-1 students and OPT participants.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 graduate student at a university in California, and I write to oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal.

I came to the United States to study, and like many international students, I have invested years of work and substantial tuition in my education. OPT is the reason many of us can apply what we learned and contribute to the American economy after graduation. A $70,000 fee, more than 130 times the current $520 application cost, would destroy that path. DHS itself acknowledges that schools may pass this cost on to students or stop recommending students for OPT altogether. For students who followed every rule and studied seriously, this proposal replaces a clear, lawful path with deep uncertainty about whether we will be allowed to work in our field at all. That loss of security is itself a serious harm.

The fee would also harm American interests. International graduates do not only fill jobs, they create them. A high school classmate of mine came to the United States to study and later founded a startup in Silicon Valley. That company has generated at least $300 million in revenue in the United States and created more than 80 new jobs. Those positions were senior technical and creative roles, new jobs created by a new company, not jobs taken from American workers. If OPT had been priced out of reach, that company, its revenue, and those jobs might never have existed here.

This pattern is not unusual. Research by the Niskanen Center and the National Foundation for American Policy has found that OPT does not displace American workers, and international students and their families contribute tens of billions of dollars to the United States economy each year. OPT also fills shortages in high demand STEM fields. A fee of this size would push talented graduates to Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and other countries that welcome them, and the United States would lose the companies, jobs, and tax revenue they would have created here.

Finally, the fee bears no relation to the cost of administering the program. The current OPT application fee is $520. A $70,000 charge is not cost recovery. It is a barrier designed to shrink the program, and it falls hardest on students and schools, not on any party responsible for fraud.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and preserve OPT as a lawful, affordable path for international students who study and contribute in the United States.

Respectfully submitted,
An F-1 graduate student in California

The OPT program serves as a pathway for international students to find a permanent place in advancing the STEM-relevant capabilities of the U.S., whether this occurs through academic institutions, national laboratories, and especially industry, which STEM-majors often pursue. Adding any hindrance into the OPT program will deter international students from staying within the U.S., thereby exporting U.S.-educated talent.
International student enrollment in higher (graduate) education programs at U.S. institutions relies largely on confidence on the part of the student and the institution itself. An available (and attainable) OPT program boosts confidence in students to seek education in foreign institutions, as a possibility to continue working in a nation at the frontier of scientific research and innovation supports their commitment to starting a new life abroad. Similarly, U.S. institutions take the prospective future of their students into account, ensuring they find positions that progress their careers after graduation. The proposed fees on OPT programs discourage both international students from applying and U.S. institutions from making offers. Scaling back enrollments due to a lack of confidence will immediately affect international students and further spread to the broader graduate body. This will ultimately limit opportunities for national students to obtain higher education in this country, thereby eroding our country’s lead in STEM innovation.
Alongside the decreased growth and integration of talent within U.S. academia and industry, paying the proposed fees raises multiple concerns. The cost of OPT fees paid by universities would largely fall onto research grants and tuition paid by undergraduate students. This results in less funding for the research itself, as well as raising cost of college education for Americans. Both aspects stretch well beyond the realm of international students within the U.S. by choking the funding supporting current research and depleting the pipeline of domestic talent pertinent to the future of this country.
For these reasons, I urge DHS to reject the proposed fees on OPT in DHS Docket No. ICEB–2026–0100. U.S. research and innovation rely heavily on attracting, educating, and retaining talented students from around the world. Any hindrance placed on the OPT program risks losing our position as a leader in science and engineering on the global stage.

comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I submit this comment as a member of the public. DHS's interest in OPT program integrity is legitimate, and fraud should be addressed. I respectfully ask DHS to reconsider the design of this proposal, which may not achieve that goal and may carry costs the notice does not fully weigh.

1. Fit between problem and remedy. The notice describes fraud mainly through enforcement press releases and individual prosecutions. A uniform $70,000/$30,000 charge falls equally on compliant and noncompliant schools, and the notice does not show how the fee amount relates to any reduction in fraud. DHS considered targeted alternatives, such as extending STEM OPT oversight (site visits, training plans, reporting) to OPT generally, but set them aside as more complex. Agencies must reasonably consider alternatives. Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43, 48 (1983).

2. Costs and benefits. DHS's own analysis estimates primary annualized costs of $4.1 billion (range: $32 million to $8.2 billion) and annualized transfers of about $12.8 billion. The fraud-reduction benefit is not quantified comparably. DHS also assumes limited effects on international enrollment, which is uncertain at this fee level. International students contributed $43.8 billion and supported 378,175 U.S. jobs in 2023–24 (NAFSA).

3. Small institutions. DHS estimates that 56 percent of affected institutions are small entities, yet declines an exemption. The Regulatory Flexibility Act requires consideration of significant alternatives that minimize burden on small entities. 5 U.S.C. § 603(c).

4. Legal authority. The notice relies on INA §§ 103(a) and 214(a), and states that fees would be deposited as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. § 3302, with ICE retaining nothing. Neither INA provision expressly authorizes a fee of this size, and courts now interpret statutes without deference to agency readings. Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024). A charge of this magnitude, unconnected to the cost of a service, may also draw major-questions scrutiny. West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022). The notice sets the OPT fee to align with the H-1B fee, which a federal court set aside in June 2026 (Forbes).

5. Reliance. Students admitted and enrolled have planned degrees around OPT eligibility. Reliance interests must be weighed. DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1, 30–33 (2020).

6. Comment period. A 30-day period is short for a rule with a projected ten-year transfer of roughly $109 billion.

Requested action. DHS should withdraw the proposal or, at minimum: (a) adopt targeted compliance measures instead of a uniform fee; (b) exempt small and public institutions; (c) grandfather currently enrolled students; and (d) extend the comment period to 60 days.

Sources
- DHS, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026): https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/08/2026-20660/optional-practical-training-fees
- NAFSA, International Student Economic Value Tool (2023–24): https://www.nafsa.org/economicvalue
- Forbes, "DHS Immigration Rule Proposes $100,000 In Practical Training Fees" (Oct. 8, 2026): https://www.forbes.com/sites/stuartanderson/2026/10/08/dhs-immigration-rule-proposes-100000-in-practical-training-fees/

comments.commentText:
I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule establishing significant fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations ($70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT, including STEM OPT extensions).

The current OPT program is widely used as a de facto work visa and pathway to H-1B status and eventual permanent residency rather than as genuine practical training tied to a student’s academic program. Many F-1 students, particularly large numbers from India and China, enter the United States on student visas while stating an intent to return home after studies, yet arrive with a clear plan to remain and work long-term. OPT has become a primary vehicle for this strategy: students obtain OPT authorization, often with minimal or non-substantive employment at companies that exist largely to facilitate immigration status, and then use that status to enter the H-1B process and later pursue green cards.

This undermines the integrity of both the F-1 and H-1B programs. It allows individuals who never intended temporary study to bypass the numerical limits, wage protections, and higher scrutiny of the H-1B system. It also disadvantages U.S. workers and well-qualified international students who pursue legitimate training and employment opportunities.

High fees will force educational institutions to be far more selective in recommending students for OPT. Schools will have a strong financial incentive to carefully review each case, verify that the proposed employment is real and related to the student’s field of study, and decline recommendations for students whose primary purpose is immigration rather than genuine practical training. This is a necessary and appropriate step to reduce fraud and abuse.

I urge DHS to finalize the proposed fees without significant reductions or exemptions that would weaken their deterrent effect. The entire OPT-to-H-1B-to-permanent-residence pipeline should be tightened so that only well-qualified students who meet the original temporary-student intent requirements can access OPT. The proposed fees are a meaningful step in that direction and will help protect the integrity of the immigration system and American workers.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fee at 91 FR 64566.

1. This is a program-elimination measure in fee form. A $70,000 charge per student for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT, payable by the SEVP-certified institution before a designated school official may recommend OPT, cannot be absorbed by any institution. The predictable response is not to charge students $70,000; it is to stop recommending OPT. If the intent is to end post-completion OPT, DHS should defend that directly rather than route it through a fee the regulated party cannot pay.

2. Labeling the fee a transfer understates the burden. The regulatory impact analysis treats institutional payments to the Federal Government as transfers rather than costs. But public institutions have no authority to levy a $70,000 per-student surcharge, so the charge cannot be passed through as a price; it lands on the student as a benefit withdrawn. A benefit withdrawn is a cost, and it appears nowhere in the analysis.

3. The fee is not tailored to the harms cited. The rule cites fraud and program integrity, yet the charge is per student and is not tied to employer identity, wage level, or any fraud indicator. A legitimate employer paying a prevailing wage costs the institution the same $70,000 as a fraudulent staffing arrangement. Employer-side fees for serial or related-party filings, expanded site visits, and funded SEVIS audits would target the stated problem without eliminating the benefit for every student.

4. The small-entity analysis does not support the rule. The IRFA invites comment on small-entity impact, so: for community colleges, small liberal arts colleges, and seminaries, $70,000 per student exceeds total tuition revenue per student in many programs. The proposed fee therefore eliminates OPT at exactly the institutions whose students have the fewest alternatives, and the analysis records that outcome as a transfer rather than as the loss it is.

5. Reliance and retroactivity. Students chose programs and took on debt on the documented premise that post-completion OPT exists at the current $470 Form I-765 fee. Any final rule should not apply to students already enrolled.

6. Process. Thirty days, from October 8 to November 9, is not adequate for a change of this magnitude. I ask DHS to extend the comment period by at least 60 days, to publish the fee level at which the program remains viable as against the level at which it is functionally eliminated, and to consider cost-recovery pricing with audit funding instead of a punitive per-student charge.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee acts as a program-elimination measure that harms students and institutions.

Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2)

I am an F-1 student currently on post-completion OPT, and I oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation.

1. The fee is charged to the school, but its effect falls on students. A fee of this size is larger than the full tuition of many legitimate graduate programs. Faced with a $70,000 charge per student, most SEVP-certified schools — especially smaller institutions and programs serving working adult students — will simply stop recommending OPT, or pass the cost to students through higher tuition. Either way, the practical result is the end of OPT access for students at those schools, regardless of their individual merits or compliance history.

2. The fee is not calibrated to the stated purpose. DHS justifies the fee by fraud prevention and program integrity, but SEVP already has site visits, reporting requirements, and DSO oversight, and schools already pay SEVIS-related fees. A flat $70,000 per recommendation is not tied to the actual cost of oversight for an individual student and does not distinguish schools or students with clean compliance records from bad actors. It punishes compliant institutions and students for the misconduct of others.

3. The fee would harm U.S. employers and local economies. OPT allows U.S. businesses — including small businesses in healthcare, technology, and other shortage fields — to employ graduates of U.S. programs who were educated here. If schools stop recommending OPT because of the fee, employers lose access to these workers and communities lose their spending and tax contributions.

4. The subsequent-OPT fee penalizes educational progression. A student who completes a higher degree level and becomes eligible for a new OPT period — a pathway Congress and DHS regulations expressly allow — would trigger a new $30,000 charge to the school. This discourages students from pursuing further U.S. education and discourages schools from enrolling them.

For these reasons, I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees in 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2). If DHS proceeds, it should, at a minimum, set any fee at a level tied to documented oversight costs, exempt or reduce the fee for subsequent OPT following completion of a higher degree level, and provide a longer transition period for students already in F-1 status who planned their education in reliance on the current rules.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international PhD student in computer science at Yale University, working on machine learning for healthcare. I oppose the OPT fees in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) and 214.2(f)(11) and ask DHS to withdraw them. I have attached five short documents with data and sources, summarized below.

1. The fee would cut off graduates the U.S. has already trained. I am in the offer stage for U.S. industry roles developing AI for healthcare. Under the proposal, my school would have to pay $70,000 before recommending me for OPT and another $30,000 for the STEM extension, $100,000 in total. Several of my labmates and friends are in the same position, and some already hold offers that depend on OPT. DHS's own primary estimate is $12.4 billion in fees per year (91 FR 64579). Canada charges about $185 and the U.K. about $4,000 for comparable post-study work permits (Attachment 1). Temporary visa holders earned 61% of U.S. computer science doctorates in 2024, and about 90% of those with definite job commitments took positions in the U.S. Immigrants founded 60% of the U.S. companies on the 2025 Forbes AI 50 (Attachment 3). Losing these graduates would weaken U.S. leadership in AI and biomedicine just as other countries are competing hardest for them.

2. The fee would deter the strongest applicants, not only bad actors. Prospective students I have talked with, including prospective master's students, told me they would study outside the U.S. if this rule takes effect. Surveys and peer-reviewed studies point the same way. In a 2026 survey, 69% of current and former F-1 students said they would not have enrolled under these fees, and past restrictions on post-study work lowered both the number and the quality of applicants (Attachment 2). A fee screens by ability to pay, not by merit.

3. The fee would cost universities a large share of their master's tuition, which already funds departments and research. International students are 59% of U.S. computer science master's students, and 77% of full-time CS master's students pay their own way. Many of them choose the U.S. because of OPT, and the prospective master's students I have spoken with say they would go elsewhere under this fee. When they do not enroll, the university loses their tuition. That tuition supports faculty, courses, and the PhD students and labs that tuition-free PhD programs depend on. First-time international master's enrollment already fell 21% from 2023 to 2024, and one economic analysis estimates that a fee of this kind would cost universities hundreds of millions to over $4 billion a year in lost enrollment margin. Even a $30,000 fee exceeds what universities net on 55% of OPT-bound international master's students (Attachment 4). Labs are hit directly too. A large share of the PhD students in my lab are international, and the lab's work at the intersection of AI and biomedicine depends on them. At Yale, 1,219 students were on OPT in 2024, which implies up to about $85 million a year in fees. Friends in labs at other U.S. universities describe the same dependence. In addition, under SEVP's August 2026 CPT guidance, a PhD student's summer research internship will often require pre-completion OPT, which this rule would price at $70,000 (Attachment 1).

4. The fee does not target the fraud DHS describes. DHS's evidence concerns specific shell employers and document vendors, but the fee applies equally to every student at every school. The money goes to the Treasury, not to oversight (91 FR 64576). The amount has no cost basis, and the economic analysis does not estimate benefits or lost enrollment. Better alternatives exist: extend STEM OPT's training-plan, E-Verify, and site-visit safeguards to all OPT; exempt employment at universities, research nonprofits, government labs, and hospitals; do not charge for pre-completion OPT; and do not charge the $70,000 fee again at each degree level (Attachment 5).

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and pursue targeted integrity measures instead.

Attachments:
1. The Proposed OPT Fees: Size, Mechanics, and Comparison with Peer Countries
2. The Fees Would Deter Highly Qualified International Students, Not Only Bad Actors
3. International Graduates Are Central to U.S. Leadership in AI and Biomedical Research
4. Effects on University Finances and Academic Research Labs, with Yale as an Example
5. The Fee Is Not Tailored to the Problem DHS Identifies: Issues in the Analysis, and Better Alternatives
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they would harm U.S. competitiveness and talent retention.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Andrew Olteanu
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed regulation.

International students contribute significantly to the U.S. economy, not only through tuition payments but also through their living expenses, investments in education, and taxes paid while working.

I am an international aviation student, and I am personally investing approximately **$120,000** in my flight training in the United States. Under the current F-1 and OPT system, I hope to work for approximately two years after graduation, pay taxes, gain professional experience, and eventually return to my home country.

In my case, I am not taking a permanent job away from an American pilot. I am investing in my education, contributing to the American economy, and eventually leaving the workforce, creating opportunities for American pilots to pursue those same positions.

This proposed regulation risks discouraging international students from investing in the United States. The result could be fewer students, less revenue for American universities and flight schools, reduced spending in local communities, and fewer tax contributions.

International students are not stealing American jobs. We are contributing to the economy, investing in American education, and helping support industries such as aviation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

As an international undergraduate student studying in the United States, I find this proposal deeply alarming. OPT is not simply an additional benefit for international students. It is an essential opportunity for students to gain practical work experience, apply the knowledge and skills they have developed through their education, and begin building their professional careers.

The proposed fees would place an extraordinary financial burden on educational institutions. Requiring schools to pay $70,000 for each student's initial OPT recommendation and another $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation could discourage institutions from supporting international students' employment opportunities altogether.

Although the proposed fees would technically be paid by educational institutions rather than directly by students, the consequences would inevitably fall on students. Schools may become unwilling or unable to recommend students for OPT, and students could lose access to employment opportunities despite having completed their degrees and met all applicable eligibility requirements.

This proposal also raises serious concerns about fairness and equal access. International students already make substantial financial investments in American higher education, often paying significantly higher tuition than domestic students. They contribute to university communities, conduct research, participate in campus activities, and bring valuable international perspectives to American institutions. It is unreasonable to create another enormous financial barrier at the very moment when they are trying to transition from education to employment.

If the goal is to prevent fraud and protect American workers, the government should pursue targeted oversight, stronger enforcement against actual violations, and reasonable administrative requirements. An extraordinarily high fee is not a reasonable substitute for effective oversight. It risks restricting legitimate students rather than addressing the specific problems the government claims to be concerned about.

Moreover, this policy could damage the international reputation of American higher education. International students make decisions about where to study based not only on academic quality but also on whether they can realistically pursue professional opportunities after graduation. Making OPT financially inaccessible would send a clear message that international students are welcome to pay tuition but may not be welcome to contribute their skills to the American workforce.

The United States should not undermine the educational and professional opportunities it has historically offered to international students.

I strongly urge ICE and DHS to withdraw this proposed fee structure and pursue reasonable, proportionate alternatives that address fraud without effectively destroying access to OPT for legitimate international students.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed high OPT fees place an unfair financial burden on schools and students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Laura Buhs
comments.commentText:
I am writing in opposition to the proposed rule to establish up to $100,000/student in fees for OPT recommendations. As an international education professional, I am very familiar with the current state and the expected impacts of the proposed rule.

1.The proposed fees will not recover the costs of the OPT application or administration of the program including deterring fraud and investigating noncompliance. The fees will go to general Treasury funds, so there is no plan for them to address the issues DHS identifies. In fact, the authority to collect the tax is in question. DHs has not established a rational connection between the fee and the issues it claims the fee will address.

I object to universities, students, or their employers being taxed at an extremely high rate when the money will not even support OPT or the F-1 program in general. This does not mean OPT will only be used by highly talented and qualified students. It will limit it to those with the ability to pay – unrelated to merit. This will not prevent fraud and abuse.

In addition, there are far more efficient and effective ways for DHS to deter fraud and investigate noncompliance with the information it already has within SEVIS to identify fraud and noncompliance.

2.There is lack of clarity in the regulatory language that must be addressed:
•It is not clear if $30,000 will be charged only for the first OPT recommendation after paying the $70,000 fee or for every OPT recommendation after paying the $70,000 fee.
•It is not clear how the fee will work when OPT is recommended by different schools for the same student.
•It is not clear how the fee will work for a student with a break in F-1 status.

3.The analysis by DHS does not reflect the expected impact on F-1 students, postsecondary institutions, domestic postsecondary students, local and national economies, job growth, or innovation and discovery.
a.The number of OPT applications will drop dramatically as very few institutions and students can absorb the exorbitant fees and F-1 students will be deprived of valuable practical experiences that complement their education and that contribute to the employment market and economy.
b.Postsecondary institutions and their communities will lose the economic and cultural/social benefits of F-1 students who choose not to study in the U.S. because of the lack of OPT. This will cause budgetary issues for institutions which will affect domestic students and the opportunities available to them.
c.Study after study shows that immigrant participation in the labor market contributes to job growth and does not take jobs from U.S. workers. Other actions by the current administration are already impacting the economy and job growth. The OPT fee will further exacerbate this.
d.The U.S. will lose out in the marketplace for top global talent, especially in STEM fields, affecting research and teaching, innovation, and leading in top fields such as AI. If the concern is about not enough U.S. workers in critical fields, I suggest the federal government invest in U.S. public education as a complement to keeping int’l talent for maximum benefit.

4.Finally, a 30-day comment period instead of the normal 60-day period is not sufficient to review the impacts and prepare comments on such a major change.
I urge you to reconsider the proposed regulations and devise methods that will actually deter fraud, improve immigration integrity and protect U.S. workers.

Laura Buhs

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule imposing substantial fees on institutions for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations.

I am a Professor of Public Administration and Director of the Mark O. Hatfield School of Government at Portland State University (PSU), a public urban research university in Oregon. Our School provides education, research, and professional development in public administration, public policy, and related fields, with extensive partnerships involving government agencies and nonprofit organizations.

The proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations would create an extraordinary financial burden on public universities already facing significant budget constraints. At PSU, where we are navigating substantial financial challenges and institutional restructuring, such fees would divert scarce resources from education, research, and student support. If these costs were passed on to students, they would effectively make OPT inaccessible to many.

International students contribute significantly to our academic community by bringing diverse perspectives, professional experiences, and knowledge of governance systems around the world. Their participation enriches classroom discussions, collaborative research, and learning opportunities for domestic students. OPT provides an important bridge between academic learning and professional practice, benefiting both graduates and the organizations they serve.

The proposed rule would also undermine the ability of U.S. universities to attract talented international students, potentially weakening research collaborations, community partnerships, and workforce development.

Furthermore, the proposed fees appear disproportionate to the administrative services involved. DHS should clarify how these amounts were determined, whether they apply per student or institution, and how the revenue would be used. Universities already maintain established procedures for OPT eligibility verification, reporting, and compliance. Any legitimate concerns about program integrity should be addressed through targeted improvements to existing oversight mechanisms rather than extraordinary financial barriers.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and consider its broader consequences for higher education, international student recruitment, and the communities served by public universities.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Masami Nishishiba, Ph.D.
Professor of Public Administration
Director, Mark O. Hatfield School of Government
Portland State University

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully object to the proposed fee structure of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) authorization and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations. I strongly encourage DHS to rescind these fees and maintain affordable access to legitimate practical training that aligns with students' degrees.

I'm a researcher at a public university in the US and work alongside citizens and international colleagues, from interns over grad students to postdocs and beyond. Some of my colleagues are currently able to do groundbreaking and lifesaving science only thanks to the OPT program. These researchers have worked hard to obtain their degrees at US-based universities alongside their citizen peers, all of them have received the world-class education that the US is known for. Keeping OPT an affordable and accessible option means those graduates can put their hard-won knowledge and skills to use directly to the benefit of the US economy and for the US people. Imposing the suggested fees would mean many internationals students will leave the US after graduating, draining precious talent and skills that the US economy desperately needs, as many universities will not be able to pay these fees.

I fully endorse protecting American workers, combating fraud, and upholding immigration system integrity. However, financial capacity to pay high fees does not indicate compliance, nor does inability to pay signal wrongdoing. DHS must justify how these specific fee amounts would effectively differentiate between legitimate educational training and system abuse. A decline in program participation due to high fees cannot be considered proof of successful fraud prevention. I respectfully ask DHS to explain how these fees would effectively combat fraud beyond imposing a large financial burden that inevitably limits legitimate use of the OPT program. The agency should consider less restrictive alternatives, such as focused compliance audits, validation that training relates to degree programs, employer oversight, and enforcement of existing worker protections. Interventions targeting actual misconduct would be more appropriate than imposing financial obstacles that impact law-abiding participants.

I'm concerned about the proposed 60-day implementation timeline. DHS should protect students already enrolled in programs or committed to training under current rules. Prospective application doesn't address impacts on decisions made years earlier. I request explicit protections for current students and existing OPT participants needing future recommendations or extensions.

DHS should assess consequences for universities, hospitals, research institutions, small employers, and underserved communities. The analysis should examine whether these fees could discourage clinical training, disrupt research, or limit essential services, and whether smaller institutions would face disproportionate barriers.

DHS should also consider whether shifting costs to students could increase debt or employer dependence, potentially making participants more financially vulnerable.

I request DHS withdraw this fee structure. Any alternative should be evidence-based, proportionate, and address actual problems without making legitimate training financially unattainable. At minimum, DHS should evaluate substantially lower fees, meaningful waivers, and transition protections.

Protecting American workers and immigration integrity are important goals that should be pursued through effective oversight and evidence-based enforcement, not by restricting lawful educational training to those with exceptional financial resources.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter objects to the proposed OPT fees and argues they will harm the US economy and talent retention.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by University of Idaho
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
The University of Idaho opposes the proposed rule published October 8, 2026, and urges that it be withdrawn in its entirety.
The University of Idaho, in Moscow, is Idaho's public land-grant R1 research university and oldest institution of higher education. With over 50 extension centers, we educate and employ people across Idaho. Fall 2025 enrollment was 12,383, including 709 international students and a record 602 doctoral students. F-1 students are vital to our research, teaching, and operations.
The proposed tax imposes a substantial financial burden
The rule charges $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one. The cost is driven by volume, not risk. Applied to our 2020–2026 records, it would have required U of I to pay $19,690,000 for 335 recommendations. Graduate students account for 76% of that total, so the tax falls hardest where practical training is most integral to the degree. Even the 2024 and 2025 cohorts would each cost about $2 million, before the staff time and systems needed to collect, approve, and refund payments.
No budget line can absorb a nearly $20 million tax. We would have to absorb an unfunded cost, charge students, or limit access to practical training, and limiting access is the only realistic option. Access would turn on who can pay, not on who qualifies. Designated School Officials would be left recommending only students with money, which could be seen as bias.
The rule harms enrollment, Idaho's economy, and domestic students
International enrollment fell by 111 students from 2024 to 2025 amid recent federal policies, and each new restriction deepens that decline. According to NAFSA, Idaho's 3,601 international students contributed $85.5 million to the state economy and supported 586 jobs in 2024/25; U of I generated the largest share, $32.3 million and 264 jobs. Our international undergraduates also pay about $3.4 million a year above resident tuition, revenue that helps keep costs low for Idaho students and sustains the courses they take.
Students weigh post-graduation work heavily when choosing where to study. In one recent survey, 37–69% of international students, and 38–70% of STEM students, said they would not have enrolled with these fees in place. They would choose countries that offer that opportunity.
The rule restricts access to practical training
OPT is part of a student's education: professional experience tied directly to the field of study. The fees would divide equally eligible students into those who can pay and those who cannot, harming students with fewer resources most. U of I also hires 25 to 40 staff, postdocs, and faculty each year who hold OPT work authorization; losing them would interrupt research projects that serve Idaho.
The rule disrupts research and workforce pipelines
Our OPT authorizations from 2020 through 2026 span 76 majors, with roughly 85% in engineering, computer science, agriculture, and the sciences; computer science alone is 17%. These are fields where Idaho employers need more graduates than the domestic workforce supplies. OPT participants complement, rather than replace, American workers. Losing international graduate students would also put U of I's R1 status at risk: R1 requires 70 research doctorates a year, and we award about 80.
International graduates also stay and pay taxes. We estimate each OPT worker pays about $15,000 a year in federal income tax and $4,200 in Idaho income tax. Nationally, OPT workers pay about $3.6 billion a year in federal income tax plus $1.2 billion in payroll taxes. If OPT participation fell about 80%, federal tax losses of roughly $3.8 billion a year would exceed the fees collected.
Additional concerns
We are committed to OPT compliance and have invested in dedicated advising staff, SEVIS reporting, and eligibility reviews. DHS has not explained why ability to pay would deter misconduct better than these safeguards, especially when the revenue goes to the Treasury rather than to OPT oversight. Nor has it justified the amounts, or explained how often the $30,000 fee applies, how refunds work, or how fees apply to transfers and later degrees.
Together with recent limits on practical training, visa processing, and duration of status, the rule compounds the deterrent to studying in the U.S. DHS should analyze these cumulative effects and narrower alternatives, such as targeting employers linked to fraud. The 30-day comment period is too short for a full institutional response; we request an extension.
For these reasons, we urge the Department to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.
Respectfully submitted,
C. Scott Green, President, University of Idaho, 875 Perimeter Drive, Moscow, ID 83843
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees impose an unsustainable financial burden and urges withdrawing the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Bulent Altay

I am an international Ph.D. researcher at Texas A&M University, and I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT applications.

During my doctoral studies, I have contributed to federally supported engineering research at the Texas A&M Transportation Institute, focusing on computational modeling, material failure, and fatigue crack propagation in railroad infrastructure. Optional Practical Training provides an essential opportunity for researchers like me to apply the specialized knowledge developed through American graduate education to real-world engineering challenges. Although the proposed rule places the payment obligation on educational institutions, universities may transfer these costs to students or employers. Neither recent Ph.D. graduates nor most academic research groups and early-career employers can reasonably absorb such expenses. A $70,000 fee would make many otherwise qualified international graduates financially ineligible for employment opportunities, regardless of their academic achievements, technical expertise, or potential contributions.

I am particularly concerned about the long-term consequences for American scientific and technological competitiveness. International graduate researchers contribute to federally funded projects, collaborate with American colleagues, and develop specialized expertise in fields such as advanced manufacturing, materials science, computational mechanics, and infrastructure engineering. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jundong  Song
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. These fees would create an extraordinary financial barrier to legitimate practical training and could undermine the value of an American education for international students.

My objections concern the proposed fee levels, the transition provisions, and the treatment of students who have already invested in U.S. degree programs.

1. The proposed fees would make practical training financially inaccessible.

Requiring universities to pay does not eliminate the economic burden. Universities could refuse to recommend eligible students or pass the costs to students or employers. Access to practical training would then depend heavily on financial resources rather than academic qualifications, compliance with immigration rules, or the educational value of the training.

DHS should provide a transparent justification for these amounts, including their relationship to actual administrative and enforcement costs.

2. Students already enrolled deserve meaningful transition protection.

Current students have committed substantial tuition, time, and effort under rules allowing eligible graduates to apply for OPT. Although employment authorization is not guaranteed, the opportunity to pursue practical training is a meaningful consideration in choosing a U.S. education.

A 60-day transition would not adequately address commitments made over several years. If DHS adopts any new fee, it should exempt students enrolled before the final rule takes effect, including their post-completion OPT and associated STEM OPT extensions.

3. The proposal could harm U.S. employers and universities.

The fees could discourage employers, particularly small businesses, from hiring otherwise qualified graduates. They could also reduce the attractiveness of U.S. universities and encourage students educated here to take their skills elsewhere. DHS should evaluate these consequences explicitly before proceeding.

4. Fraud prevention should focus on misconduct.

Protecting program integrity is a legitimate objective. However, imposing prohibitive fees on all participants would burden compliant students, institutions, and employers alongside those who violate the rules. DHS should assess targeted investigations, institutional oversight, and proportionate, cost-supported fees as alternatives.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal. If the agency proceeds, it should substantially reduce the fees, explain their cost basis, and provide clear protection for students already enrolled and their associated OPT and STEM OPT opportunities.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they create unfair financial barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

These fees would not meaningfully distinguish legitimate students and employers from fraudulent actors. Instead, they would create an enormous financial barrier for law-abiding F-1 students who have already invested heavily in U.S. education and are seeking temporary, degree-related practical training exactly as OPT was designed to provide.

The proposed fees could also discourage international students from choosing U.S. universities, weaken the competitiveness of American higher education, and deprive U.S. employers of graduates trained in this country.

I strongly request that DHS remove these proposed OPT fees and adopt targeted, evidence-based enforcement measures instead. Fraud should be punished directly; compliant students should not be priced out of lawful practical training.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 1 of 10: Student affordability.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw them. Sections IV.C and V.A would make schools pay $70,000 before an initial OPT recommendation and permit the burden to be passed to students. Moving the bill between a school and a student does not make the barrier disappear.

It is deeply troubling to make access to legitimate educational training depend on finding an additional sum of this size. A student's honesty, academic preparation, and the educational value of a placement cannot be measured by family wealth. A school that cannot finance the payment could refuse a qualified student's recommendation even when every substantive requirement is satisfied.

DHS should assess who would lose access at different income levels and explain how payment capacity identifies fraud. If additional oversight needs funding, DHS should evaluate proportionate alternatives supported by documented administrative costs. Legitimate students should not have to finance a prohibitive barrier in order to demonstrate that they deserve a lawful educational opportunity. Please withdraw the proposed fees.

Reference: Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566, sections IV.C and V.A (October 8, 2026).
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw them due to financial burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 2 of 10: Talent and scientific continuity.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose this proposal. Section V.A would impose an additional payment for subsequent OPT, including STEM extensions. Repeated financial hurdles can interrupt legitimate training after a graduate has already developed specialized knowledge and begun contributing to a team.

From a talent-development perspective, the relevant question is whether training is lawful, supervised, and educationally valuable. A large payment does not establish any of those facts. It may instead make continuation depend on the wealth of the sponsoring institution or access to a third-party payer.

I am concerned that the United States could train promising graduates and then make their lawful practical training financially inaccessible. The resulting loss could extend beyond an individual placement to unfinished experiments, interrupted collaboration, and recruitment decisions. These are risks to evaluate, not outcomes I claim to have personally observed.

DHS should analyze retention and project-continuity effects by field and institution and compare targeted compliance measures. The agency should also reject the alternative that would reimpose the initial fee at higher educational levels. Talent and integrity deserve substantive evaluation. Please withdraw this financial gatekeeping proposal.

Reference: NPRM, sections V.A and VII.A.5.b.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposal, arguing that financial hurdles on OPT extensions harm talent retention and continuity.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 3 of 10: Faculty mentorship and research.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fee structure because it risks replacing educational judgment with a funding test. Section III.D describes OPT as training related to the student's major. That relationship should be evaluated through the work, supervision, and learning objectives, rather than inferred from an institution's willingness to make a large payment.

Consider a hypothetical graduate whose technical knowledge is useful to a supervised research project. The project may be academically valuable without having unrestricted funds available for an OPT fee. Refusing the graduate a recommendation in that situation would establish a budget constraint, not a lack of educational value or evidence of misconduct.

The possibility that years of instruction and mentorship could end at such a financial barrier is deeply frustrating. DHS should examine research continuity, grant restrictions, and the ability of departments with different resources to support legitimate training. It should compare direct verification of supervision and educational relevance against the proposed payment mechanism.

Protect program integrity by examining the training itself. Please withdraw the prohibitive fees and preserve access to legitimate, supervised learning.

Reference: NPRM, sections III.D, IV.C, and V.A.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed fees, arguing they create financial barriers and do not reflect educational value.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 4 of 10: University budgets.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed institutional payment obligation. Calling a school the payer does not create new resources. Administrators would have to choose among absorbing the cost, finding outside funding, transferring it, or declining otherwise legitimate recommendations.

For illustration only, 100 initial recommendations at the proposed $70,000 rate would require $7 million before subsequent fees and administrative expenses. This is arithmetic, not a claim about any specific university. DHS should evaluate such budget scenarios against unrestricted resources and operating margins, rather than treating gross revenue as freely spendable cash.

Section IV.C expressly allows costs to be passed to all students. That possibility deserves particular scrutiny: domestic students could bear higher charges or reduced services without having participated in OPT at all. It is unacceptable to treat this shifting of burdens as though it solves the underlying economic harm.

Please assess effects on tuition, aid, student services, and institutions with limited reserves. A policy intended to improve oversight should not force universities to ration lawful educational opportunities according to their capacity to finance a new charge. Withdraw the proposed fees.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.C, V.A, and VII.B.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed institutional payment obligation and fees, arguing it causes economic harm.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 5 of 10: Employer planning.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose this proposal because it could disrupt legitimate recruitment without directly testing employer compliance. Section V.A makes payment depend on a school's OPT recommendation, rather than a particular employer. A careful, law-abiding employer could therefore lose access to a qualified candidate because of an independent institution's funding decision.

Section VII.A.5.b acknowledges possible productivity losses when employers cannot replace OPT participants with qualified workers. DHS should investigate that risk by occupation, location, recruitment lead time, and training needs. The existence of another lawful hiring category does not by itself establish that a suitable replacement is immediately available.

The practical cost of an interrupted placement may include delayed projects, repeated recruitment, and additional work for existing staff. These are potential mechanisms that require evidence, not personal experiences I am asserting.

I support meaningful verification of genuine jobs, supervision, and lawful working conditions. Those checks address conduct directly. A substantial payment imposed upstream does not demonstrate that a particular job is legitimate. DHS should withdraw the proposed fees and evaluate targeted oversight that preserves compliant employers' ability to plan and train responsibly.

Reference: NPRM, sections V.A, VI, and VII.A.5.b.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they strongly oppose the proposal and argues it disrupts recruitment and harms employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 6 of 10: Small-business access.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose a policy that could make lawful training opportunities depend on the financial strength of a school or potential employer. A small business can offer serious supervision and meaningful work while having far less cash available than a large corporation. Access to capital is not a reliable measure of compliance or training quality.

Although schools would formally owe the fees, section IV.C allows costs to be shifted to employers. If that occurs, smaller employers could face pressure to abandon a placement that a better-funded competitor could finance. Even without a direct charge, they could lose candidates when schools decline recommendations.

Section VII.B requests alternatives that minimize small-entity impacts. DHS should examine these financing constraints and downstream effects separately from its analysis of directly regulated schools. It should compare risk-based inspections, verification of genuine supervision, and enforcement against documented misconduct.

It is deeply concerning to create an entry barrier that may favor institutional wealth over a valuable learning opportunity. The agency should withdraw the proposed fee structure and develop an approach that tests integrity rather than purchasing power.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.C, V.A, and VII.B.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed fee structure because it harms small businesses and creates entry barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 7 of 10: Public-interest training.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees because an educational placement's public value cannot be judged by its capacity to finance a large upfront payment. Legitimate degree-related training in community research, environmental work, public policy, or nonprofit services may produce benefits that are not fully reflected in a starting salary or an organization's available cash.

Section VII.A.5.b suggests that parties could share costs when the benefits exceed the fees. That reasoning needs a much more careful examination. A project can benefit the public without giving the student, school, or host organization a way to capture those benefits as money available for payment. Benefits spread across a community do not automatically become a funding source.

I find it troubling that financially constrained public-interest placements could be excluded even when their educational merit and compliance are clear. DHS should analyze these settings separately, including restricted funding and benefits received by people outside the paying parties.

Please withdraw the proposed fees. Preserve meaningful oversight while evaluating training through its educational content, supervision, and actual compliance, rather than its ability to produce an immediate payment.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.C and VII.A.5.b.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly asks DHS to withdraw the proposed fees due to negative impacts on public-interest placements.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 8 of 10: U.S. workers and labor standards.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees and take the protection of U.S. workers seriously. Section IV.B should establish how this particular payment mechanism would improve wages and employment after accounting for different occupations, local conditions, and effects on employers' output.

A reduction in OPT participation does not, by itself, establish an equal increase in suitable jobs for U.S. workers. DHS should examine whether roles are filled, remain vacant, move elsewhere, or disappear when projects are reduced. It should also evaluate possible effects on U.S. colleagues whose work depends on a team's combined skills. I do not assume that every OPT placement is beneficial or that displacement never occurs; that is precisely why careful evidence is necessary.

Where exploitation, false employment, or unlawful working conditions are found, enforcement should address those practices directly. A large payment to the government does not by itself raise a worker's wage or improve supervision.

Workers deserve protections that can be shown to work. Please withdraw these fees and compare targeted labor-standard and anti-fraud measures using measurable outcomes and transparent assumptions.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.B, VII.A.5.b, and VII.A.6.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong opposition to the proposed fees and asks DHS to withdraw them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 9 of 10: Effective fraud prevention.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees while supporting serious enforcement against OPT fraud. Section IV.A identifies misconduct that deserves investigation. The critical question is whether a universal financial barrier detects or prevents it more effectively than direct, risk-based controls.

GAO-19-297 recommended improvements involving fraud-risk assessment, data analysis, school oversight, and DSO training. The report's online updates describe implementation of several recommendations and continuing work on training. These recommendations provide concrete oversight measures to evaluate; I am not claiming that every earlier deficiency remains unresolved.

Payment is not verification. A well-funded dishonest participant could still seek to evade requirements, while an honest participant with limited resources could lose access. DHS should show why the proposed amounts are necessary, compare less burdensome controls, and publish measurable criteria for success, such as confirmed violations detected and corrected.

It is profoundly frustrating to see legitimate educational access put at risk without a convincing demonstration that the chosen barrier addresses the actual misconduct. Withdraw the fee proposal and strengthen investigation, verification, and accountability directed at evidence of fraud.

References: NPRM, section IV.A; U.S. GAO, GAO-19-297, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-297.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they strongly oppose the proposed fees and asks DHS to withdraw the fee proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Samantha Green
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,By submitting this comment, I am expressing my opposition to this proposed rule. America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. I ask you to rescind this proposed rule. Laura De Santislauradesantis@umail.ucsb.eduSanta Barbara, California 93106
