comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT authorization.

Internships and other forms of experiential learning are a central part of modern higher education and early-career preparation. NACE reports that 67% of Class of 2024 bachelor’s graduates completed at least one internship and 86% participated in some form of experiential learning. Employers also use internship experience to distinguish otherwise similarly qualified candidates.

Internationally, access to work experience while studying is common. OECD research shows that international students in competing higher-education systems generally have access to part-time work, and study-related internships and work-based learning are often regulated separately from ordinary student employment.

The proposed OPT fee should also be considered together with the recent restrictions and uncertainty surrounding CPT. Under the government’s 2026 interpretation, many optional but academically relevant internships may no longer qualify for CPT if they are not required for all students in a curriculum. If students also become effectively priced out of pre-completion OPT, they may graduate from U.S. universities with substantially less practical experience than domestic classmates holding the same degree.

A U.S. degree alone does not necessarily make a graduate equally competitive. Domestic students may graduate with the same degree plus internships, industry experience, professional references, and employer networks. Restricting both major pathways to pre-graduation practical training could therefore disadvantage international graduates for reasons unrelated to academic ability or merit.

The fee itself is also extraordinary. DHS proposes $70,000 for the first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation. A student who uses pre-completion OPT and later post-completion OPT could therefore trigger $100,000 in fees even though standard pre- and post-completion OPT share the same 12-month aggregate limit. DHS itself anticipates that this structure will reduce participation in pre-completion OPT. This means the fee is not merely administrative; it is expected to change students’ educational and career decisions.

A financial deterrent also does not distinguish between fraud and lawful participation. A student with a legitimate degree, a genuine degree-related job, and a compliant employer faces the same $70,000 barrier as a higher-risk case. DHS should explain why these amounts are reasonably related to the actual administrative and enforcement costs attributable to an individual OPT participant.

The proposal may also create inequities among institutions and students. Two equally qualified students could receive different opportunities simply because one attends a university willing and able to absorb a $70,000 charge while the other does not. DHS estimates that the rule could generate approximately $12.4 billion annually under its primary scenario, demonstrating that the economic effects are substantial.

If DHS is concerned that F-1 employment could displace U.S. workers, less restrictive alternatives should be considered. At minimum, students should have a clear pathway to participate in academically relevant internships while physically outside the United States without jeopardizing F-1 status or future OPT eligibility. Overseas employment generally does not require U.S. CPT or OPT authorization, so this would allow students to gain professional experience without occupying U.S.-based internship positions.

DHS could also use more targeted anti-fraud measures, such as risk-based audits, stronger employer verification, enhanced reporting, and penalties for demonstrated violations. These approaches would address misconduct directly rather than imposing the same extraordinary financial barrier on every legitimate participant.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed fee structure and to evaluate its combined effects with recent CPT restrictions on practical training, graduate employability, university competitiveness, and the United States’ ability to attract and retain international talent.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they harm students' early-career preparation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule requiring schools to pay $70,000 for a student's initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

1. The fee exceeds DHS's fee-setting authority. Immigration fees are authorized to recover the cost of adjudication services. Reviewing a school's OPT recommendation and issuing an employment authorization document is a routine administrative act costing a fraction of the proposed amount. DHS's own estimate that the rule would collect $12.4 billion per year confirms the fee is not calibrated to cost recovery. A charge of this magnitude functions as a revenue measure, not a service fee, and therefore exceeds the authority Congress granted DHS to set fees.

2. The rule would effectively terminate OPT, contrary to its legislative purpose. OPT exists so F-1 students can obtain practical training related to their field of study. Schools that cannot absorb a $70,000 fee will either pass it on to students, most of whom cannot afford it, or stop recommending OPT altogether. Either way, OPT becomes unavailable to the overwhelming majority of students it was designed to serve. An agency may not use a fee schedule to accomplish indirectly what it has no authority to do directly. If OPT should be narrowed or eliminated, that is a decision for Congress, not for a fee rule.

3. The rule harms the American public interest. International students choose the United States in large part because OPT offers post-study work experience. If OPT becomes unaffordable, many will study in Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia instead. The United States would lose tuition revenue that sustains its universities, research contributions in university laboratories, and the companies and jobs these graduates would otherwise create here. American employers, especially startups and small businesses that cannot compete with large firms for experienced workers, would also lose a critical entry-level pipeline.

4. DHS has not provided evidence that a fee of this size is needed. The proposal does not demonstrate that fraud or abuse in OPT is of a scale that could justify $70,000, nor does it connect the size of the fee to any identified problem. Its figures describe the revenue the rule would generate, not the harm it would prevent. A fee imposed without an evidentiary basis linking its size to a documented problem is arbitrary: it burdens students, schools, and employers while the agency has not shown that those costs purchase any improvement in program integrity.

5. The burden will fall hardest on public universities and students of modest means. Well-resourced private institutions may absorb or subsidize the fee; public universities under tight budgets cannot, and will be forced to restrict OPT recommendations or shift the cost to students. OPT would thus become a privilege of wealthy institutions and wealthy families, while students at public universities and from modest backgrounds lose the practical training component of their education. This undermines the breadth of American higher education and one of its principal attractions to talented students worldwide.

For these reasons — unlawful fee-setting, inconsistency with OPT's purpose, lack of evidence, and damage to the American public interest — DHS should withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it due to excessive fees.

comments.commentText: I strongly disagree the proposed OPT fee increase. International students already pay high international tuition, living costs, visa fees, relocation expenses, and healthcare. Charging another substantial fee just to access practical training that is part of their educational pathway places an unreasonable burden on graduates who have already invested heavily in U.S. education. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international student in a STEM field and I don’t think this regulation benefits the United States, especially given how much the country says it wants legal pathways for immigration.
My own story is part of why. I chose to study here largely because of my brother, an engineer in the US who built his career in his field and encouraged me to follow the same path. Many students make this decision the same way: they see someone they trust succeed here and take the chance themselves. A $70,000 charge on OPT threatens that kind of pathway. OPT is when a student’s years of tuition and study start paying off, for the student and for the country that trained them.
The fee is technically charged to schools, but it will not stay there. DHS itself acknowledges that institutions could get the money from international students, and it concedes that some schools may stop funding OPT, which could sharply reduce participation. More than 56% of SEVP-certified institutions may qualify as small entities. For a small college, a bill like this could threaten its survival. I expect fewer schools to offer OPT and fewer international students to choose the US at all.
International students are not a burden on this country. They pay tuition, contribute to research, and after graduation fill roles that employers say they struggle to fill. Cutting that pipeline will not send those jobs to Americans. More likely the work moves to Toronto, London or Singapore and the future founders and engineers go with it. Those countries are already recruiting these students.
The fee also makes no distinction between employers. A fraudulent shell company and a hospital hiring a nurse researcher or a biotech lab hiring a bioinformatician pay the same price. If fraud is the concern, I would rather see enforcement aimed at the bad employers than a cost that shuts out honest students. The fee would rise roughly 13,900% from today’s $500 or so, which is hard to explain as covering administrative costs.
Students and families also read the headlines. A country that proposes this, while the H-1B fee fights are still going on, tells the world’s best students they are a revenue source and not a welcome investment. International enrollment was already projected to drop about 9.5 percent for fall 2026, before this proposal appeared. That kind of reputational damage builds slowly and takes far longer to repair.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the high OPT fee harms students, schools, and the U.S. economy, threatening legal immigration pathways.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee increase because it would weaken U.S. competitiveness. OPT helps American universities attract global talent, especially in STEM fields, and allows U.S. employers to recruit highly skilled graduates. Participants work, pay taxes, and contribute to research, innovation, and economic growth. Excessive fees would discourage talented students from choosing the United States over countries such as Canada or the United Kingdom, hurting universities, employers, and the broader economy. At a time when the United States seeks to lead in science and technology, creating unnecessary barriers for international graduates is counterproductive. I urge ICE to reconsider this proposal and preserve an accessible OPT program.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee hurts U.S. competitiveness, universities, and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As a professor teaching architecture to students, there are several reasons why this cost prohibitive proposal should not be implemented. Specifically:

1. Priced Out of Professional Practice: The $70,000 fee acts as a de facto ban on OPT for architecture schools, directly obstructing international graduates from completing required AXP hours and achieving professional licensure.

2. Unbearable Arbitrary Burden on Higher Ed: Shifting an administrative fee onto colleges and universities—amounting to tens of millions of dollars annually for modest-sized programs—violates administrative reasonableness and threatens program viability.

3. Devastating Impact on Design Innovation and STEM: Architecture programs (often STEM-designated) foster global perspectives essential for addressing the country’s policy priorities, including efficient design of cities and buildings, resilience against disasters, and robust infrastructure supporting American business interests. Cutting off international scholars harms national competitiveness in the architecture, engineering and construction industries.

4. Compounding Harm to Experiential Learning: Combined with recent regulatory rollbacks on CPT authorizations, this fee strips students of both in-school and post-graduation practical learning, undermining the ability of universities to thrive within their local communities across the nation.

This is an autocratic and destructive policy to limit international students in coming to the US. It is false that these valuable and beneficial programs—for students, employers, and US colleges and universities—create a "pipeline for cheap foreign labor." That is an absurd notion as is the idea that fraught with fraud and abuse. The fraud and abuse is within this administration.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee is cost-prohibitive, harms architecture students, and threatens higher education.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees. Charging $70,000 for initial OPT and another $30,000 for subsequent OPT is completely unreasonable. These amounts are so far beyond any reasonable administrative cost that it's hard to see them as anything other than an attempt to make OPT inaccessible.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. Schools would have to pay them before recommending a student for practical training. DHS has not shown that it has authority to charge them, or that payments this large would separate legitimate training from fraud.

DHS relies on INA § 214(a)(1), which lets it set the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission.[1] That provision says nothing about fees. DHS set the amounts to match the H-1B payment, not to recover a cost. The money would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, and ICE could neither keep nor use it.[2] Skinner requires Congress to speak clearly before an agency imposes financial burdens, "whether characterized as 'fees' or 'taxes,'" even to recover costs that do not benefit the payer.[3] A charge that recovers no cost at all needs at least as clear an authorization. When Congress authorizes immigration fees, it says so expressly and specifies how the money is collected and used. Examples include the H-1B/L fraud fee, adjudication fees, the SEVIS fee, and the 2025 visa integrity fee.[4] Section 214(a)(1) has nothing comparable. In July, the First Circuit relied on that pattern, on Skinner, and on Learning Resources. It held that the government had not made a strong showing of authority to require the $100,000 H-1B payment, which is the benchmark DHS used here.[5] Washington Alliance upheld DHS's authority over OPT; it did not consider any fee.[1]

The fraud DHS describes involves shell companies and fake worksites. Yet the school pays before recommending OPT, possibly before the student has a job offer, and the payment "would not be tied to a specific employer."[2] A school's willingness to pay says nothing about whether a future employer is legitimate. DHS rejected broader site visits, training plans, and reporting partly because enforcing them would take "substantial time and resources."[2] The fees would not fund that enforcement either. DHS's main evidence is also inconsistent. The text describes more than 10,000 students working for suspect employers, while footnote 56 describes 10,000 suspect employers. Both cite a video.[2] DHS should release the underlying data.

DHS's primary estimate after the transition year is $12.4 billion a year in fees from 2,478 schools, an average of about $5 million per school. Its low-participation scenario still assumes about 88,000 initial OPT participants a year, mostly STEM students, plus about 74,000 STEM extensions.[6] DHS does not explain why schools would keep paying at that scale. Using the unpaid fee as a proxy for lost opportunities does not capture enrollment lost over whole degree programs.[6] The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act discussion says in one paragraph that the rule would not reach the statutory threshold, and in the next that it would exceed it.[6]

DHS should also weigh this proposal together with its pending H-1B fee proposal. If both take effect, one graduate who uses OPT, receives a STEM extension, and is then sponsored for a cap-subject H-1B could trigger $203,265 in new payments by the school and the employer.[7]

Under the transition rule, if a student began OPT before the effective date, the school would owe $70,000 for a STEM extension recommended afterward, because no initial fee was ever paid.[8] DHS acknowledges that current students are differently situated from prospective ones,[2] but gives them no protection. Students enrolled before the final rule takes effect should be exempt for OPT and STEM extensions tied to their current degree.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposal. Any new proposal should cite specific statutory authority, disclose the fraud data, and support its participation and cost assumptions.

References:

[1] 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a)(1); Wash. All. of Tech. Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022).

[2] DHS, ICE, [Optional Practical Training Fees](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/08/2026-20660/optional-practical-training-fees), 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026), pp. 64570–71 & n.56, 64574–78 & n.124.

[3] Skinner v. Mid-America Pipeline Co., 490 U.S. 212, 224 (1989); see Nat'l Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336, 340–43 (1974).

[4] 8 U.S.C. §§ 1184(c)(12), 1356(m), (v), 1372(e); Pub. L. 119-21, § 100007, 139 Stat. 370 (2025).

[5] California v. Mullin, No. 26-1699, order at 4–6 (1st Cir. July 24, 2026) (denying stay pending appeal); Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229 (2026).

[6] 91 Fed. Reg. at 64582–83, 64587–89, 64597.

[7] $70,000 + $30,000 here, plus $103,265 under DHS, Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions, 91 Fed. Reg. 54817 (Aug. 25, 2026) (proposed).

[8] Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(3), 91 Fed. Reg. at 64599–600.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Acting Director Venturella:

I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an F-1 student’s initial OPT recommendation and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions. The proposal would impose a prohibitive barrier that effectively dismantles a longstanding program without clear congressional authorization. I urge DHS to withdraw it for the reasons below.

1. The fees exceed statutory authority and function as a general revenue tax.

Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act and established precedent, a user fee must reasonably relate to the cost of a specific service and the proceeds should support that program. The NPRM states that the projected $8.4 to $16.5 billion in annual collections would go to the general Treasury, not to SEVP compliance or anti-fraud work. The preamble also indicates the amounts were set as a deterrent, aligned with proposed H-1B fees, rather than calculated from the marginal cost of a DSO recommendation in SEVIS. Using a prohibitive price to reduce participation, and suggesting the program might otherwise be shut down, amounts to an attempt to curtail a regulatory program and raise general revenue without an Act of Congress.

2. The FICA tax rationale is mathematically implausible.

In the NPRM, DHS points to the FICA exemption (7.65% combined employee Social Security and Medicare) as creating an incentive for employers to prefer F-1 OPT students. For a 7.65% savings to equal the $70,000 initial fee over a 12-month OPT period, an entry-level graduate would need to earn more than $915,000. Typical OPT salaries are far lower. Treating a statutory payroll tax differential that Congress itself created as justification for a $70,000 to $100,000 per-student charge is arbitrary.

3. Requiring universities to pre-pay $70,000 before a DSO recommendation is unworkable.

The obligation falls on the school before any OPT recommendation is entered in SEVIS. At that stage, a student seeking initial post-completion OPT is not required to have an employer. Nonprofit universities are educational institutions, not staffing agencies. Forcing them to front $70,000 per graduate, or to build escrow and pass through arrangements with students or prospective employers before USCIS even adjudicates an EAD, creates an unnecessary administrative and financial burden. Grant-funded labs and early-stage employers often cannot absorb an additional $30,000 to $100,000 surcharge within existing budgets.

4. The rule harms U.S. STEM capacity while failing to target actual fraud.

International graduate students contribute substantially to research and innovation in fields such as artificial intelligence, biomedical engineering, and other critical STEM areas. OPT and STEM OPT provide a bridge from graduate training to practical work. DHS has identified concerns about shell companies and other abuse, but ICE and USCIS already have targeted tools such as SEVIS reporting, Form I-983 reviews, and site visits to address bad actors. Applying a six figure charge across all certified institutions and compliant students, rather than focusing enforcement on fraudulent employers, is not a reasoned response.

5. Reliance interests and less burdensome alternatives were not adequately considered.

Hundreds of thousands of current F-1 students entered multi-year programs in reliance on the existing OPT framework. Even with grandfathering of prior recommendations, students who have not yet graduated, and those on initial OPT who will need a subsequent recommendation for a STEM extension after the effective date, face sudden disruption. DHS has not meaningfully evaluated more targeted measures, such as cost based compliance fees or strengthened employer verification, that could address integrity concerns without broadly reducing access to practical training.

For these reasons, the proposed rule is arbitrary, capricious, and in excess of statutory authority. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

Respectfully submitted.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed exorbitant OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations. Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate goals, but the proposed approach imposes broad costs without adequately establishing that these particular fees are necessary or effective. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal and evaluate more targeted alternatives.

1. A high fee is not a reliable fraud screen.

DHS expects these fees to deter bad actors and encourage schools to scrutinize OPT requests. Yet ability to pay is not the same as compliance. A legitimate school could be priced out while a well-funded fraudulent operator could pay. DHS should provide evidence linking the proposed dollar amounts to reductions in fraudulent authorizations and distinguish that outcome from a reduction in legitimate participation. What proportion of discouraged applicants is expected to be fraudulent, and on what evidence is that estimate based?

2. The projected costs require a stronger accounting of benefits.

DHS's regulatory impact analysis estimates annualized economic costs of about $4.1 billion in its primary scenario, with substantial uncertainty [1]. The agency should compare these modeled costs with quantified estimates of avoided fraud, enforcement savings, and measurable gains for U.S. workers. Lower OPT participation alone is not proof of better wages or employment outcomes. Without such a comparison, the public cannot assess whether the fees are proportionate to the stated objectives.

3. The fees do not directly finance stronger oversight.

DHS states that fee receipts would go to the U.S. Treasury rather than be earmarked for SEVP enforcement [1]. The agency proposes deterrence and stronger school incentives, but it should demonstrate why those indirect mechanisms would outperform risk-based school audits, employer verification, data-driven fraud detection, and mandatory DSO training. GAO identified specific SEVP oversight vulnerabilities and recommended stronger fraud-risk controls [3]. DHS should compare these alternatives using estimated effectiveness and cost rather than assume a uniform fee is preferable.

4. The effects on U.S. education and research deserve fuller analysis.

OPT can influence where students pursue degrees and where graduates develop their skills. Research on earlier STEM OPT expansions found increases of approximately 14–15% in STEM degree completions, including gains among domestic students [2]. That finding does not directly predict the effect of this proposal, but it cautions against assuming that opportunities for international graduates necessarily disadvantage U.S. students. DHS should evaluate impacts on university enrollment, research capacity, domestic STEM training, and innovation.

5. A uniform charge creates uneven burdens and reliance concerns.

A $70,000 obligation may have vastly different effects on large universities, smaller colleges, and the students they recommend, irrespective of compliance history. Students and institutions also make multi-year educational commitments under existing OPT expectations. DHS should examine these distributional and reliance effects and explain why its proposed 60-day transition is adequate.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees and instead evaluate evidence-based, risk-targeted oversight measures, including their expected fraud-reduction benefits, costs, and effects on U.S. workers and universities. An effective rule should target misconduct rather than treat financial capacity as a proxy for program integrity.

Thank you for considering this comment.

References

[1] DHS (2026), “Optional Practical Training Fees,” 91 FR 64566–64600, Docket ICEB-2026-0100. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm

[2] Amuedo-Dorantes & Shih (2026), “OPT Reforms and the Relative Supply of STEM Skills,” AEA Papers and Proceedings 116:351–355. https://doi.org/10.1257/pandp.20261100

[3] U.S. GAO (2019), “Student and Exchange Visitor Program: DHS Can Take Additional Steps to Manage Fraud Risks,” GAO-19-297. https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-297

comments.submitterName: the Associated Students of the University of California (ASUC)
comments.commentText:
Submitted electronically via Regulations.gov
Docket No.: ICEB-2026-0100
RIN: 1653-AB01

October 21, 2026

To:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Department of Homeland Security

Re: Public Comment in Strong Opposition to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566)

This comment is submitted on behalf of the Associated Students of the University of California. As the student government representing all students at the University of California, Berkeley, we strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training Fee, as we are deeply concerned about its potential consequences for the international student community. We respectfully urge DHS to consider and provide further explanations regarding the following concerns:
We are concerned about the rationale behind this proposed rule. In the Summary, DHS’s main justifications are to combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers. However, in Section VI, DHS’s own evidence suggests that most students do not come to the United States with employment as the ultimate goal of their education. Therefore, we question whether this proposed rule would effectively address the aforementioned goals, as it may not only undermine the attractiveness of U.S. higher education, to which international students contribute billions of revenue, with approximately $43 billion during the last academic year, but also fail to achieve its primary purpose. This directly raises questions about DHS’s justification mentioned in footnote 124. We therefore urge DHS to provide a detailed accounting of the proposed rule’s potential economic losses in other sectors of the U.S. economy.
We question whether the proposed rule provides a reasonable amount of time for transition. In Section V.C, DHS provides DSOs and international students with only 60 days after the final rule is published. However, particularly at a time when most of the U.S. universities and colleges have already begun their semesters or quarters, some students may have decided to pursue higher education in the United States specifically because of the practical training opportunities offered by specific businesses they are interested in that are primarily operating in the United States. Therefore, we urge DHS to explain what measures it would take to accommodate these students and how it intends to address the harm to their reasonable expectations.
We demand calculations and accounting of how DHS determined the $70,000 initial OPT authorization fee and another $30,000 for each subsequent or STEM authorization. What mathematical reasoning supports such a substantial fee, and how would it effectively achieve the objectives stated in the proposal? We noticed in section V.A compares the proposed fee amounts with the tuition costs that international students pay for one or two years of education in the United States. However, the fact that international students already pay substantial tuition fees does not necessarily make the proposed fees economically reasonable or effective, and we would like to kindly remind DHS of its own stated objectives to “combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers.” We do not see how the proposed fee would effectively address these objectives, instead, such high costs could potentially favor wealthier institutions and students with greater financial resources while disadvantaged students who lack financial support, especially for public universities such as UC Berkeley.
With these in mind, ASUC respectfully urges DHS to respond to the concerns raised above and reconsider the proposed rule.
Sincerely,
Associated Students of the University of California

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, published on October 8, 2026 (91 FR 64566). The proposal would impose a fee of $70,000 for an initial period of Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT period. I respectfully urge the Department to withdraw this proposal.

1. Disproportionate financial burdens on international students and universities

OPT is an important component of the F-1 student program, allowing international graduates to apply their academic knowledge and skills in professional settings. The proposed fees are so substantial that they risk making OPT practically inaccessible. Although educational institutions would formally bear the payment obligation, these costs could ultimately be passed on to students, employers, or other members of university communities. This would create significant financial barriers for international students, many of whom have already made substantial investments in their education in the United States.

2. Insufficient justification and lack of proportionality

The Department identifies fraud prevention, immigration system integrity, and the protection of U.S. workers as justifications for the proposed fees. While these are legitimate governmental objectives, the Department should demonstrate how fees of this extraordinary magnitude are reasonably related to the actual administrative and enforcement costs of the OPT program. The proposal raises serious questions about the methodology used to calculate these amounts and whether they are necessary to achieve the stated objectives. The Department should provide a transparent, evidence-based justification before imposing such substantial financial obligations.

3. Negative consequences for U.S. higher education and research

International students contribute significantly to American universities, research institutions, and the broader economy. They participate in academic research, support innovation, contribute specialized expertise, and enrich the intellectual life of university communities. OPT provides an important pathway through which these contributions extend beyond the classroom. By imposing prohibitive fees, the proposed rule could discourage universities from facilitating OPT and employers from recruiting international graduates. In the long term, this could weaken the competitiveness of U.S. higher education and undermine the country's ability to attract and retain international talent.

4. Unequal access to professional opportunities

The proposed fees would disproportionately disadvantage international students with limited financial resources and institutions unable to absorb additional costs. For many graduates, OPT provides an essential opportunity to gain professional experience and establish careers after completing their degrees. Making access to this opportunity dependent on an institution's or employer's capacity to absorb extraordinarily high fees risks creating unequal access to professional development and employment opportunities.

5. Less restrictive alternatives are available

The Department's objectives of preventing fraud and ensuring program integrity do not necessarily require prohibitive fees. More targeted measures, including strengthened institutional oversight, improved verification procedures, risk-based compliance reviews, and enhanced reporting requirements, could address documented abuses without undermining access for otherwise eligible students. The Department should meaningfully consider these less burdensome alternatives.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge the Department to withdraw the proposed rule. Its extraordinarily high fees are insufficiently justified and risk imposing disproportionate burdens on international students, universities, and employers. The objectives of protecting U.S. workers and maintaining immigration system integrity are important, but they should be pursued through proportionate, evidence-based, and carefully tailored regulatory measures.

OPT should remain an accessible pathway for international graduates to contribute their knowledge, skills, and professional expertise to American society. A regulatory framework that effectively restricts access on the basis of institutional or financial resources would undermine the educational, economic, and research interests that OPT helps advance.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges the Department to withdraw the proposal.

If the objective is to strengthen the American economy, encourage innovation and maintain global competitiveness, the country should be making it easier for talented graduates to contribute, not introducing substantial financial barriers to their employment.

If schools must pay $70,000 per student, they will restrict recommendations, raise costs, or lose applicants to Canada, Britain, and Australia. Withdraw this rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security:

I am a doctoral student in biostatistics, and I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training recommendation and $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations. Protecting U.S. workers and preventing fraud are important objectives. However, the proposed fees could undermine American research, weaken employers’ access to qualified graduates, and restrict legitimate training opportunities without adequately distinguishing them from fraudulent activity. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

My training focuses on statistical methods used to evaluate health interventions and improve the reliability of medical evidence. In biostatistics, the value of a researcher’s work extends beyond an individual position: rigorous study design and analysis help researchers determine whether treatments are effective, identify safety concerns, and draw reliable conclusions from clinical data. These contributions benefit American patients, clinicians, and research teams. A substantial financial barrier to retaining U.S.-trained graduates could interrupt this work and reduce the future domestic benefits of investments in their education and training.

I am particularly concerned about the economic reasoning in Section VII.A.5.b of the proposal. DHS assumes that, when the benefits of OPT exceed the proposed fees, affected parties could collectively share the costs to preserve participation.[1] This assumption overlooks the distinction between social value, private financial returns, and the availability of funds. Patients who may benefit from better medical evidence cannot readily finance a researcher’s employment authorization. A university or nonprofit may recognize the value of a graduate’s contributions while lacking unrestricted funds to cover the fee. An inability to pay therefore does not demonstrate that an opportunity offers insufficient value to the United States. DHS should explicitly evaluate these financing constraints and the benefits of research that extend beyond the student, institution, and employer.

The proposed fee would also make financial resources a major determinant of access to practical training. Two equally qualified graduates pursuing equally legitimate opportunities could face different outcomes because one has access to a wealthy employer or personal resources and the other does not. A flat fee does not directly measure competence, compliance, or educational value. It could disadvantage smaller employers and nonprofit research organizations even when they offer appropriate supervision and competitive compensation.

Protecting American employment also requires examining whether international graduates complement U.S. workers, rather than assuming that excluding one graduate creates one job for an American. A 2024 study by Guo, Gong, and Pang found that an expansion of STEM OPT increased domestic employment in STEM occupations, with stronger effects in information technology.[2] This finding does not establish that every worker benefits or predict the effects of the proposed fee. It does, however, demonstrate why DHS should assess potential effects on team productivity, business expansion, and demand for American workers before imposing a substantial barrier to participation.

Fraud should be addressed through measures that identify and penalize misconduct. Payment of a large fee does not establish that an employer exists, that appropriate training occurs, or that wages and working conditions comply with applicable requirements. DHS should compare the proposal with targeted employer verification, risk-based inspections, and enforcement against documented violations. Reducing legitimate participation alongside fraudulent participation is not sufficient evidence that a policy improves program integrity or benefits the country overall.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees and evaluate proportionate alternatives supported by evidence. Any future proposal should account for effects on American research, smaller employers, domestic workers, and students already investing years in U.S. education. Preserving legitimate practical training while enforcing meaningful safeguards would better serve the interests of the United States.

Thank you for considering my comment.

References:

[1] Department of Homeland Security. “Optional Practical Training Fees.” Proposed rule, October 8, 2026, particularly Section VII.A.5.b.
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm

[2] Guo, X., Gong, J., and Pang, M.-S. (2024). “Creation or Destruction? STEM OPT Extension and Employment of Information Technology Professionals.” MIS Quarterly, 48(2), 715–730.
https://aisel.aisnet.org/misq/vol48/iss2/15/
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees harm research, employers, and students, and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Public Comment Opposing Proposed OPT Fees
Docket No.: ICEB-2026-0100

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent or STEM OPT fee. Although preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives, these extraordinary fees threaten America's ability to attract and retain international talent.

IV.A - Combating Fraud and Abuse

Fraud prevention is important, but imposing excessive fees on legitimate students is not an effective substitute for targeted enforcement. DHS should prioritize employer verification, compliance audits, and penalties for fraudulent entities. Financially excluding legitimate graduates wastes talent and research investments that strengthen America's innovation economy.

IV.B - Protecting American Workers

OPT participants are highly educated graduates who contribute specialized knowledge to research, technology, and other industries. Protecting domestic workers should involve enforcing wage protections and labor standards rather than imposing blanket financial barriers. Preventing qualified graduates from contributing could reduce U.S. productivity, innovation, and advanced technology development.

V.A - Establishing OPT Fees

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent or STEM OPT fee are excessive and disproportionate to reasonable administrative costs. International students already pay substantial tuition and living expenses. These fees would make practical training accessible primarily to those with exceptional financial resources. Such barriers could drive talented graduates toward competing countries, weakening America's scientific leadership and skilled workforce.

Additional fees associated with higher educational levels would discourage advanced education and professional development. This risks losing future researchers, scientists, and innovators whose contributions could benefit the United States for decades.

Educational Cost Comparisons

Tuition and educational expenses cannot justify extraordinary immigration-related fees. Students pay universities for instruction and educational services, not for the ability to afford an additional $70,000 employment authorization charge. Such policies could undermine America's attractiveness as a global destination for higher education and intellectual talent.

Institutional and Employer Costs

If universities or employers must pay these fees, they may reduce recruitment, employment opportunities, compensation, or research funding. Small businesses and research institutions may be particularly unable to absorb these costs. Reduced access to international researchers could slow American scientific discoveries, technological advancement, and economic growth.

V.C - Transition Period

A 60-day transition period is inadequate for universities, employers, and students to adjust budgets and existing employment commitments. Students have made substantial educational and financial decisions based on the existing OPT framework. Abrupt implementation could disrupt research projects and jeopardize investments in American education and innovation.

VII - Economic and Regulatory Impact

The proposed rule risks discouraging international students from attending U.S. universities and encouraging qualified graduates to pursue opportunities abroad. This could reduce research productivity, STEM workforce retention, institutional revenue, and U.S. competitiveness. Losing these graduates means losing future entrepreneurs, researchers, inventors, and contributors to America's economic and intellectual leadership.

DHS should thoroughly evaluate impacts on universities, small employers, research organizations, and students and provide transparent evidence supporting the proposed fee calculations.

Alternatives and Recommendation

Fraud prevention and program integrity can be achieved through targeted enforcement, reasonable administrative fees, employer accountability, and improved compliance mechanisms. These alternatives are less burdensome and preserve access to qualified international talent.

I respectfully urge DHS and ICE to withdraw the proposed rule. The fees would disproportionately burden legitimate international graduates, undermine research and workforce development, and weaken America's global competitiveness.

OPT should remain accessible through a reasonable, transparent, and proportionate regulatory framework that protects program integrity without creating prohibitive financial barriers.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule and recommend its withdrawal. Preserving access to qualified international graduates is an investment in America's economic prosperity, scientific leadership, and intellectual future.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they are excessive and harm talent retention.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Leo Irakliotis
comments.commentText:
I write in opposition to this proposed rule. I support genuine reform of Optional Practical Training where fraud is demonstrated — fictitious worksites, "visa mill" schools, and employers using OPT to undercut wages are legitimate targets for enforcement. This rule, however, is not that reform. Rather than directing resources at the specific institutions and employers implicated in the fraud cases cited in the preamble, the rule imposes a blanket $70,000/$30,000 fee on every SEVP-certified institution, for every student, regardless of merit or risk. That is not a fraud-deterrence mechanism; it is a tax on universities large enough to end OPT participation outright for all but a handful of wealthy institutions.

As a university professor, I have seen the caliber of international students OPT allows to apply an American education in the American economy. A rule that prices out that pathway does not improve immigration policy — it abandons the distinction between fraudulent actors and legitimate ones, punishing both equally. DHS should withdraw this rule and pursue targeted enforcement against documented bad actors rather than a blunt fee that falls indiscriminately on universities.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
ICEB-2026-0100 is harmful to students, schools, and the U.S. as a whole. OPT fees currently don't get higher than $520. $70,000 is an astronomical leap. DHS calls this a "fee," but a fee is meant to recoup the cost of providing a service; this is a tax.

International students contributed $42.9 billion and 355,736 jobs in the 2024-2025 academic year (1). NAFSA estimated a loss of 111,000 international students at U.S. colleges, $3.4 billion in revenue, and up to 39,000 jobs in the 2026-2027 academic year given recent changes, and that's not counting OPT students (2). Those numbers will get even higher with that added variable.

Over 400,000 students worked on OPT in 2024 (3). If taken today, we'd be depleting schools of over $28 billion. But, DHS has stated schools could pass the cost off to students. The average American doesn't have $70,000 on hand, let alone someone who's spent tens of thousands of dollars on flight tickets, visas, tuition, etc. Most would be paying more than they even earn from OPT.

The tax will also affect U.S. students. High international student enrollment leads to more U.S. student enrollment and lower fees and tuition for them (4). For grad programs, Kevin Shih estimates an increase of 8 domestic students per 10 international students (5).

The Institute for Progress surveyed 734 current and former F-1 students (6). 87% of current students said they'd pursue OPT. 80% fewer said they'd stay under the new rule (82% fewer STEM students). 69% said they wouldn't have even enrolled in a U.S. program under the new rule. Michael Clemens estimates a 79% decline in OPT starts under an imposed tax of $100,000 on schools (7). When schools and employers inevitably refuse to pay, this number will sink even lower.

The tax would have a huge impact on STEM programs and graduate programs. A large percentage of students in STEM programs across the U.S. in the 2021-2022 academic year were international, and most worked in OPT (8). They would be even more affected due to the added $30,000 tax for STEM OPT extension. Looking at international student program completions in the top public university STEM master's programs in the U.S. from 2022-2025, nearly all percentages fell in the 80's and 90's, with the University of Central Missouri's Computer Science program being just under 100% (9). It's also worth noting 70& of full‑time graduate students in AI‑related fields are international (10).

These programs will dwindle or discontinue altogether if this rule comes to pass. Most OPT students will study and work elsewhere, namely countries with strong STEM presences like China (some already have, with significant impact (10)). Lower international enrollment means lower U.S. enrollment and, thus, a decreased workforce.

OPT leads to increased innovation, opportunities, and wages for U.S. workers (11). With the STEM OPT Extension in 2016, areas with more OPT workers led to expansion of operations among employers and an increase in the hiring of U.S. workers, about 450 for every 10,000 residents (12).

DHS makes claims of OPT fraud, but they’ve been known to give biased and propagandized data with little to no credible sources (13, 14, 15). This was further compounded by the administration downsizing DHS’s oversight offices such as CRCL and OIDO while DHS forced institutions to terminate any attempts to hold them accountable (16).

Regardless, it makes no sense to punish schools or students seeking to hone their skills and contribute to our society based on the actions of a few. If anything, this will increase fraud. If your response to grocery store theft is raising the price of a carton of eggs to $1000, you're giving people more of a reason to steal. That's just common sense.

This rule is meant to "combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers." It will do none of those. DHS themselves admits they "cannot precisely quantify opportunity costs" and "cannot accurately predict how many schools or OPT participants would be affected due to lack of funding." So, their plan is to increase costs (which would go to the Treasury instead of towards addressing their "concerns") by over 13,000% and just hope for the best, not knowing or caring what the consequences will be. It offers no compensation for schools who will face opportunity costs and doesn't account for students working in OPT for under a year or over two years. DHS's true goal here is to end OPT.

Alternatives:
1. Reallocating some of ICE's increasingly large funds towards fraud detection.
2. Revising SEVP fees to cover fraud detection and prevention.
3. Keeping the fee as is until accurate data is provided that proves a change is necessary. If so, consider one that's more prudent.

I also request an extended commenting period, as 30 days is not enough time to properly evaluate everything the rule entails or for institutions affected to gather necessary data.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is an astronomical tax that harms students, schools, and the U.S. economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write to strongly oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety. A $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee would effectively end Optional Practical Training for most international students. That would harm American science, the American economy, and the United States’ standing in the world, without meaningfully serving the rule’s stated goals.

First, the fee does not fit its stated purpose. DHS justifies the rule as a way to strengthen program integrity, but a flat fee of this size applies equally to every student, and the overwhelming majority of OPT participants are doing exactly what the program intends: gaining practical experience in their field at universities, hospitals, laboratories, and companies. DHS already has oversight tools, such as training plans, employer reporting, and site visits, and the rule itself discusses extending these measures more broadly. That approach would strengthen oversight without making OPT unaffordable for the students it exists to serve.

Second, in practice the cost will fall on students. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the fee on to students or employers. $70,000 exceeds the annual stipend of most PhD students in the United States and the first-year salary of many new graduates. Few students could pay it, and few employers will pay it to hire an entry-level graduate. Universities will face the same pressure, so whether a student is recommended for OPT would depend on the institution’s budget rather than the student’s merit. Students at less wealthy institutions would be hurt most.

Third, the rule would undermine practical training as part of education. DHS expects schools to steer students away from pre-completion OPT, because splitting OPT would cost $100,000. Pre-completion OPT is how many students gain internship and research experience while they study. Discouraging it makes American degrees less valuable and less competitive with programs abroad.

Fourth, comparing OPT to H-1B misunderstands the program. OPT is time-limited practical training directly related to a student’s field of study. It is an extension of education, not a substitute for a work visa. Setting fees to “align” with H-1B treats training as a labor loophole and ignores the long-standing recognition that practical experience is part of an education.

Fifth, the rule wastes public investment. Many international graduate students are trained with support from federal research grants, which U.S. taxpayers fund. OPT is often the main way the country gets a return on that investment: graduates apply what they learned in American labs and companies, pay taxes, start businesses, and often stay to fill critical roles. This rule would ensure that federally funded training mostly benefits other countries’ economies.

Sixth, the rule would weaken American leadership in science and technology. The best students choose where to study based partly on post-study work opportunities, and competitor countries such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia offer post-graduation work pathways without anything like this fee. If OPT becomes unaffordable, top talent will go elsewhere, and so will the research, patents, and companies they produce. The United States has also gained enormous soft power from generations of international students who trained and worked here and went on to become leaders in science, business, and government around the world. Closing that pathway gives up an advantage that cannot easily be regained.

Finally, the rule is unfair to students already enrolled. Current international students made multi-year commitments to American institutions based on a program that has existed for decades. Changing its terms this drastically, mid-degree, breaks faith with them.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it due to high fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations. I support efforts to prevent fraud, but these fees are so high that they would effectively shut many qualified students out of a lawful program.

OPT is not a loophole. It is an established part of the F-1 system, with eligibility rules, school oversight, and government authorization. Students come to the United States legally, pay tuition, complete their degrees, and follow the rules with the understanding that they may apply for practical training in their field. OPT is not guaranteed, but people who meet the requirements should have a fair chance to apply. Making that chance depend on whether a school, student, or employer can come up with $70,000 is not reasonable enforcement.

It also makes little sense from the standpoint of American competitiveness. The U.S. spends years educating talented people from around the world. American employers and research teams then have a chance to benefit from the skills those graduates developed here. Why would we want to train these people and then put up a financial wall just as they are ready to contribute? Other countries are competing for the same talent, and they will be happy to welcome graduates who find the U.S. route too expensive.

Universities would pay a price as well. The chance to gain relevant work experience after graduation is one reason students choose to study in America. If OPT becomes financially unrealistic, some students will choose another country before they ever enroll. That means fewer tuition dollars for U.S. schools and less spending at local businesses. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs in the 2024–25 academic year. This proposal puts part of that value at risk.

What concerns me most is the weak connection between the size of these fees and the stated goal of fighting fraud. The proposed rule says the money would go into the U.S. Treasury and would not be specifically set aside for OPT investigations or enforcement. If the goal is to stop fraudulent employment, why not direct resources toward checking employers, verifying job arrangements, and investigating violations? A $70,000 charge does not tell us whether a job is legitimate. It mainly tells us who can afford to pay.

The burden on smaller institutions is especially troubling. DHS’s own analysis estimates that 98 small institutions could face annual fee costs exceeding 20% of their estimated revenue after the transition period. For some schools, that is money that could otherwise support teaching, student services, and research.

Fraud should be taken seriously. But legitimate students and the schools that educate them should not be priced out of OPT because of wrongdoing by others. I urge DHS to withdraw this fee proposal and pursue targeted, evidence-based enforcement instead.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they harm students and U.S. competitiveness.

However, from a perspective of an international student, I think that OPT is an great opportunity for us to evaluate and apply our study in real situations. It helps us not only gain new experiences but also see the grap between books and reality. You give us a chance to study here. I'm appreciate it. But, it is difficult to us to see how it works in reality if the fee is too high as you plan on the new rule. I hope you please consider it again. Thank you.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is too high and asks DHS to reconsider.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: A fee set high enough to price graduates out of participating is not meaningfully different from ending the program outright. If the practical effect of this charge is that large numbers of eligible graduates cannot use OPT, then the agency will have cancelled OPT in substance while claiming only to have priced it. I oppose the rule for that reason. OPT should remain valid and accessible, not be charged out of existence.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the high fees will effectively price graduates out of OPT and opposes the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I am a US citizen and I fully support this rule. By adding the fee for initial approval and extensions, the fees will help DHS/USCIS to combat fraud and also de-incentivize employers and SEVIS schools to give preference for students on OPT since they do not have to pay FICA taxes. But the best result from this rule is that it would eliminate students who are part of pay for play schemes thereby giving more opportunities for US citizen/national graduates.
comments.reason: The commenter supports the rule to combat fraud, reduce hiring preference for OPT students, and help US graduates.
